meta.label: Digital services
meta.attribution: Curated from public privacy policies, security docs, open-source/self-hosting docs, export docs and pricing pages - not measured data. Every criterion has a cited basis; reviewed 2026-06. Suggest changes via Contribute.

reads.text: Compare digital services by privacy, cost, openness, and data portability.

axes.label: Cost or overall fit
axes.question: Lower cost or a stronger overall fit?

consumer.axes: Round 8 practical decision dials, with the S4 cost-or-values default where evidence permits.
consumer.budget: Round 8 honest budget eligibility, with S4 refusing to guess missing cost data.
consumer.archetypes: Round 8 computed answer slots matched to available category evidence.
consumer.page: Round 7 personal precedence extended in Round 9 to the shared decision page for every live category.

products.name: Signal

privacy.note: Signal says messages and calls are end-to-end encrypted and it is designed not to collect sensitive information.

openness.note: Signal publishes client and server source repositories publicly.

portability.note: Accounts remain tied to Signal identity/phone-number workflows, so switching protocols is not as portable as federated messaging.

respect.note: Signal is nonprofit, donation-supported and has no advertising business.

accessibility.note: Free apps cover iOS, Android, desktop and basic calling/messaging flows.

economical.note: Signal is free to download and use.

products.description: A nonprofit, end-to-end encrypted messenger that minimizes stored data and keeps clients/source code public.

products.name: Element (Matrix)

privacy.note: Element markets Matrix-based end-to-end encrypted messaging and calls for privacy-sensitive communication.

openness.note: Matrix is an open network/protocol, and Element publishes open-source projects publicly.

portability.note: Matrix federation and self-hosting support make identity and hosting more portable than closed messengers.

respect.note: The model centers encrypted, interoperable communication rather than ads or behavioral profiling.

accessibility.note: Usable apps exist, but server/federation concepts add friction for casual users.

economical.note: Core Matrix/Element client use can be free; hosted enterprise deployments are paid.

products.description: A Matrix-based messenger for encrypted, federated communication, strong on sovereignty but less effortless than mainstream chat.

products.name: Threema

privacy.note: Threema Private says chats, calls and files are end-to-end encrypted and a phone number/email is optional.

openness.note: Threema lists open-source apps as part of its private product claims.

portability.note: Threema IDs avoid phone-number dependence, but the network itself remains a separate proprietary service.

respect.note: Threema identifies app users as its funding source rather than an ad model.

accessibility.note: Polished mobile/desktop options, but paid adoption can limit network effects.

economical.note: One-time paid app model is inexpensive but not free.

products.description: A Swiss paid messenger with end-to-end encryption, no phone-number requirement, and a user-funded business model.

products.name: iMessage

privacy.note: Apple documents end-to-end encryption for iMessage between Apple devices.

openness.note: iMessage is a closed Apple service and protocol, despite some underlying open web standards elsewhere.

portability.note: The service is tied to Apple devices and Apple IDs, so cross-platform portability is limited.

respect.note: No ad-supported messaging feed, but ecosystem lock-in is central to the product.

accessibility.note: Highly polished and integrated on Apple devices, with poor accessibility for non-Apple contacts.

economical.note: Free with Apple devices, but unavailable without buying into the Apple ecosystem.

products.description: Apple's polished encrypted messaging for Apple users, strong inside the ecosystem and weak for cross-platform freedom.

products.name: Telegram

privacy.note: Telegram's FAQ distinguishes cloud chats from optional Secret Chats, so ordinary chats are not end-to-end encrypted by default.

openness.note: Telegram clients are open source, but server software and the full cloud service are not open in the same way.

portability.note: Telegram provides an export tool for chats/media, improving data exit compared with many messengers.

respect.note: A freemium platform with premium subscriptions and public channels; less surveillance-heavy than Meta but not as aligned as nonprofit tools.

accessibility.note: Fast cross-platform apps and cloud sync make it very easy to adopt.

economical.note: Free core service with optional Telegram Premium.

products.description: A fast, highly usable messenger with cloud sync and exports, but ordinary chats are not end-to-end encrypted by default.

products.name: WhatsApp

privacy.note: WhatsApp says personal messages, calls, photos and videos are end-to-end encrypted so not even WhatsApp can see them.

openness.note: WhatsApp is a closed-source Meta service rather than an open protocol or open client stack.

portability.note: Chat export and backups exist, but moving conversations/networks to another protocol is limited.

respect.note: Meta-company information sharing and business integrations remain trade-offs for people trying to exit surveillance platforms.

accessibility.note: Huge global adoption and simple mobile UX make it one of the easiest messengers to use with existing contacts.

economical.note: WhatsApp is free for personal users.

products.description: A ubiquitous Meta messenger with default end-to-end encryption for personal chats, but metadata, business surfaces, and Meta ecosystem sharing remain trade-offs.

products.name: Proton Mail

privacy.note: Proton Mail says end-to-end and zero-access encryption mean Proton cannot view email contents and attachments.

openness.note: Proton publishes open-source client code and security/audit materials for its apps.

portability.note: Proton provides import/export tools, but encrypted-mail ecosystems still have migration friction.

respect.note: Proton says it does not sell ads and funds through paid privacy services.

accessibility.note: Web/mobile apps and a free tier help adoption, but encrypted-email behaviors can be less familiar than Gmail.

economical.note: Free tier exists, with paid plans for more storage and features.

products.description: An encrypted email service with zero-access storage, open-source clients, and a freemium privacy-suite model.

products.name: Tuta (Tutanota)

privacy.note: Tuta says it encrypts email, calendars, contacts, attachments and even subject lines end-to-end where possible.

openness.note: Tuta publishes its app source code publicly.

portability.note: Strong encryption and lack of standard IMAP/POP workflows improve security but reduce ordinary email-client portability.

respect.note: Tuta presents itself as ad-free privacy software funded by users.

accessibility.note: Free and paid apps are available, but encryption-specific workflows add some friction.

economical.note: Free private email exists, with paid plans for more features/storage.

products.description: A German encrypted email and calendar service with open-source clients, strong encryption claims, and some interoperability tradeoffs.

products.name: Fastmail

privacy.note: Fastmail is privacy-respecting and paid, but its normal hosted email model is not end-to-end encrypted from the provider.

openness.note: Fastmail supports open mail standards such as IMAP/SMTP/CardDAV/CalDAV, though the service itself is proprietary.

portability.note: Standards support and export/import tooling make it comparatively easy to leave or use external clients.

respect.note: Paid email model avoids ads and advertising-profile incentives.

accessibility.note: Polished web/mobile apps plus standard-client compatibility make it easy for ordinary email users.

economical.note: Low-cost paid plans, with no long-term free consumer tier.

products.description: A paid standards-friendly email provider that is respectful and portable, but not an end-to-end encrypted mailbox.

products.name: Gmail

privacy.note: Google's privacy policy covers broad collection/use across services, including data controls and personalization.

openness.note: Gmail is a closed Google service despite supporting standard mail protocols in many clients.

portability.note: Google Takeout lets users export Google account data, including Gmail data where selected.

respect.note: Gmail sits inside Google's advertising and account ecosystem, even though Google says users can control ad personalization.

accessibility.note: Highly polished web/mobile UX, search, spam filtering and broad integrations make it very accessible.

economical.note: Consumer Gmail is free with paid storage/Workspace upgrades.

products.description: The dominant free email service: excellent UX and portability tools, but deeply integrated into Google's data ecosystem.

products.name: Outlook.com Mail

privacy.note: Outlook.com sits inside Microsoft's broad account, advertising and cloud ecosystem and is governed by the Microsoft Privacy Statement.

openness.note: Outlook.com is a proprietary Microsoft service, even though Outlook can connect to standard mail accounts.

portability.note: Microsoft documents Outlook.com mailbox export, but it requires desktop Outlook rather than a simple web self-export.

respect.note: Free Outlook.com shows inbox ads unless users pay for Microsoft 365, keeping it tied to Microsoft's account and subscription funnel.

accessibility.note: A mature web/mobile app, familiar Microsoft account model and Office integration make it easy for many users to adopt.

economical.note: The basic consumer mailbox is free, with paid Microsoft 365 plans for ad-free use, more storage and advanced security.

products.description: A highly accessible mainstream email floor with strong Microsoft integration, but closed, ad-supported on free accounts, and awkward to export cleanly.

products.name: Yahoo Mail

privacy.note: Yahoo's 2026 privacy policy says it analyzes and stores communications content, including email content, to deliver and personalize features, ads and services.

openness.note: Yahoo Mail is a proprietary hosted email service.

portability.note: Yahoo documents downloading mailbox content through IMAP into third-party email apps.

respect.note: Yahoo's privacy policy describes targeted advertising, cross-device association and email-content analysis, so it is a clear advertising-supported floor.

accessibility.note: Yahoo Mail is familiar, free, web-based and broadly available, though less central to modern workflows than Gmail or Outlook.

economical.note: Yahoo Mail is available as a free consumer mailbox, with paid upgrades for more features and fewer ads.

products.description: A free, familiar email floor that is useful to compare against privacy-respecting mail because its own policy plainly supports email-content analysis and targeted advertising.

products.name: iCloud Mail

privacy.note: Apple's iCloud security overview says iCloud Mail is encrypted in transit and on server, but Apple holds the keys and Mail is not end-to-end encrypted.

openness.note: iCloud Mail is a proprietary Apple service built around Apple ID and iCloud.

portability.note: Apple Mail can export mailboxes as .mbox packages, and iCloud Mail can also be used through standard mail clients.

respect.note: It is ad-free and bundled, but strongly tied to Apple devices, Apple ID and iCloud storage.

accessibility.note: For Apple users it is built in across devices and available on iCloud.com, but less attractive outside the Apple ecosystem.

economical.note: The mailbox is included with Apple ID/iCloud, though heavy use may require paid iCloud storage.

products.description: A bundled, ad-free Apple mailbox with decent standards support, but not end-to-end encrypted and still very ecosystem-bound.

products.name: Zoho Mail

privacy.note: Zoho Mail says it does not sell data, does not data-mine mail for targeted ads, and restricts employee access to customer data.

openness.note: Zoho Mail is a proprietary hosted service, though it supports conventional mail administration and client workflows.

portability.note: Zoho documents account and folder-specific export/backup options, including ZIP/PST exports for administrators and user folder export.

respect.note: The service is ad-free and paid-business oriented rather than advertising-funded.

accessibility.note: Zoho is strong for custom-domain and organization email, but less frictionless for ordinary personal email than Gmail or Outlook.

economical.note: Zoho lists a limited free plan and low-cost paid Mail Lite/Premium business plans.

products.description: A business-friendly ad-free email option with stronger privacy posture than big ad ecosystems, but proprietary and less simple for a casual personal mailbox.

products.name: Mailbox.org

privacy.note: Mailbox.org advertises ad-free, tracking-free German email with TLS plus optional PGP/S/MIME end-to-end encryption.

openness.note: The hosted service is proprietary, but supports open mail protocols such as IMAP, POP3 and SMTP.

portability.note: Mailbox.org added a user data export feature covering email, calendars, contacts, files and tasks in open data formats.

respect.note: The service is paid, ad-free, tracking-free and hosted under German data-protection claims rather than an advertising model.

accessibility.note: It offers webmail and standards support, but it is less mainstream and polished for casual users than the big free providers.

economical.note: Private plans start at EUR 1/month, with higher tiers for more storage, aliases, office and support.

products.description: A strong paid privacy-mail option: ad-free, standards-friendly and export-conscious, but not as open-source or beginner-simple as the best privacy-first apps.

products.name: Posteo

privacy.note: Posteo emphasizes anonymous signup/payment separation, no tracking, optional crypto mail storage, TLS and optional PGP/S/MIME workflows.

openness.note: Posteo is not a fully open-source hosted service, but it supports open standards such as IMAP, POP3, CalDAV/CardDAV and PGP/S/MIME.

portability.note: Standards support and external-client access make mailbox migration possible, though it is not a one-click export-first product.

respect.note: Posteo is paid, ad-free, privacy-focused, sustainability-oriented and says it does not connect payment data with email accounts.

accessibility.note: It provides webmail, client support and multilingual help, but privacy-mail workflows remain less mainstream than Gmail or Outlook.

economical.note: A Posteo account costs EUR 1/month, with low-cost add-ons for storage, aliases, calendars and S/MIME certificates.

products.description: A lean paid privacy mailbox with excellent ethics signals, strong standards support and low cost, but less hand-holding than big free webmail.

products.name: StartMail

privacy.note: StartMail says its core values include privacy by design, encryption made easy and minimal data retention.

openness.note: StartMail is a proprietary hosted email service rather than an open-source mailbox platform.

portability.note: StartMail supports IMAP access through trusted-device passwords, making standard-client export and migration practical.

respect.note: The product is paid privacy email with aliases and encryption rather than an advertising-funded free mailbox.

accessibility.note: It is available through webmail and standard clients, but has no permanent free tier and a smaller ecosystem than mainstream mail.

economical.note: StartMail offers a short free trial, but ongoing personal use is paid annually or monthly.

products.description: A paid privacy-mail service with aliases and IMAP support, useful for escaping ad mail but less open and less cheap than some European alternatives.

products.name: Mailfence

privacy.note: Mailfence says it offers ad-free private email with no tracking and browser-based end-to-end encrypted email.

openness.note: Mailfence uses interoperable email standards but is not presented as an open-source hosted mail platform.

portability.note: Mailfence supports backups/exports for account data and recommends IMAP clients for large email backups, though email backup is not available on the free tier.

respect.note: Mailfence says it has no ads, trackers, solicitations, backdoors or targeted-ad data commercialization.

accessibility.note: It offers a full email suite and free entry point, but encrypted/PGP workflows can be less familiar than mainstream email.

economical.note: A free tier exists, with paid tiers needed for fuller storage, aliases and export/backup capability.

products.description: A Belgian privacy-mail suite with a free entry point, no-ad stance and PGP-style encryption, balanced by proprietary hosting and some export limits on free accounts.

products.name: SimpleLogin

privacy.note: SimpleLogin creates email aliases so users can hide their real address and protect against spam and phishing.

openness.note: SimpleLogin publishes its backend, web app and clients as public source code and documents self-hosting.

portability.note: Self-hosting and custom-domain aliasing make SimpleLogin more portable than closed relay services.

respect.note: SimpleLogin is an open-source email-alias service owned by Switzerland-based Proton AG.

accessibility.note: Web, browser-extension and mobile apps make alias creation practical, though the full workflow is more advanced than ordinary email.

economical.note: SimpleLogin offers free aliases with paid premium upgrades for heavier use.

products.description: A strong open-source email-alias service for using a different address on every site without exposing your real inbox.

products.name: addy.io

privacy.note: addy.io creates forwarding aliases so users can share an alias instead of their main email and disable it if it leaks.

openness.note: addy.io publishes its service, browser extension, mobile apps and Docker image as public source repositories.

portability.note: The open-source service can be self-hosted and supports alias workflows across web, browser and mobile clients.

respect.note: The service is built around user-controlled aliases rather than advertising or attention capture.

accessibility.note: addy.io is powerful and flexible, though usernames, custom domains and self-hosting options add some learning curve.

economical.note: addy.io has a free plan plus paid plans for higher limits and advanced alias features.

products.description: A highly portable open-source email-alias service with self-hosting options and strong control for privacy-minded users.

products.name: Firefox Relay

privacy.note: Firefox Relay provides email and phone masks so users can sign up without exposing their primary identity.

openness.note: Mozilla publishes the Firefox Relay service source code publicly under the fx-private-relay repository.

portability.note: Relay works as a web service and browser add-on, but it remains tied to Mozilla's hosted account flow for ordinary users.

respect.note: Mozilla positions Relay as identity protection rather than an ad-surveillance product.

accessibility.note: Firefox Relay is easy to use through Firefox and its dashboard, with free masks and paid upgrades.

economical.note: Relay offers a free tier with paid premium options for more masking features.

products.description: Mozilla's masking service is an easy on-ramp to email privacy, especially for Firefox users who want less setup.

products.name: DuckDuckGo Email Protection

privacy.note: DuckDuckGo Email Protection conceals a user's address with personal and private Duck Addresses.

openness.note: DuckDuckGo publishes some privacy extension code, but the hosted Email Protection service is not a fully open, self-hostable stack.

portability.note: The service forwards to an existing inbox and works across DuckDuckGo apps/extensions, but aliases stay inside DuckDuckGo.

respect.note: DuckDuckGo says Email Protection removes email trackers it can find while protecting a user's real address.

accessibility.note: Free Duck Addresses and browser/app integration make the service very easy to adopt.

economical.note: DuckDuckGo describes Email Protection as a free forwarding service.

products.description: A very simple free email-protection layer that hides your real address and strips some trackers, but keeps aliases in DuckDuckGo's hosted service.

products.name: Apple Hide My Email

privacy.note: Apple says Hide My Email generates unique random addresses that forward to a personal inbox while keeping the real address private.

openness.note: Hide My Email is a proprietary Apple/iCloud feature rather than an open-source alias service.

portability.note: Aliases are useful but tied to iCloud+ and Apple account management.

respect.note: The feature reduces email exposure, but it deepens reliance on Apple's closed ecosystem.

accessibility.note: Hide My Email is easy for Apple users through Safari, iCloud settings and Sign in with Apple.

economical.note: Standalone Hide My Email creation requires an iCloud+ subscription, though Sign in with Apple can generate relay addresses in supported flows.

products.description: A polished email-masking feature for Apple users, valuable but closed and hard to take with you outside iCloud.

products.name: Fastmail Masked Email

privacy.note: Fastmail Masked Email creates unique addresses for each login so a real address stays private and leaks can be isolated.

openness.note: Fastmail is a proprietary hosted email service, not an open-source alias stack.

portability.note: Fastmail supports aliases and standard mail workflows, but Masked Email is strongest when paired with Fastmail and 1Password.

respect.note: Fastmail says it provides private email with no ads and no data mining.

accessibility.note: The 1Password integration makes masked addresses easy at signup, but requires paid services for the smoothest flow.

economical.note: Fastmail is a paid email service, and the best masked-email workflow often assumes 1Password as well.

products.description: A paid masked-email workflow that pairs especially well with 1Password and Fastmail's non-ad email model.

products.name: Cloaked

privacy.note: Cloaked offers masked email addresses and phone numbers with dedicated inboxes to reduce exposure of real contact details.

openness.note: Cloaked is a proprietary commercial privacy suite rather than an open-source alias service.

portability.note: Cloaked identities work inside Cloaked's hosted app, browser extension and paid suite rather than a self-hostable standard.

respect.note: The product is privacy-oriented, but its privacy policy still describes commercial data handling and third-party controls.

accessibility.note: Cloaked bundles aliases, phone numbers, passwords and data removal in a polished app/extension workflow.

economical.note: Cloaked plans start at a paid monthly price and bundle aliases with data removal and identity-protection features.

products.description: A polished commercial identity-masking suite with email and phone aliases, useful but closed and relatively expensive.

products.name: IronVest

privacy.note: IronVest consumer apps include masked email addresses, masked mobile numbers and other privacy-wallet features.

openness.note: IronVest is a proprietary commercial privacy and fraud-prevention product, not an open-source alias service.

portability.note: Masked identity features live inside IronVest apps and extensions rather than a self-hostable or open service model.

respect.note: IronVest is useful for masking, but its privacy policy and terms describe significant personal-data and payment-service processing.

accessibility.note: Apps and browser extensions make masked email, phone and card workflows accessible for people who prefer an all-in-one product.

economical.note: IronVest has consumer app access with free and paid feature tiers, but advanced masking and payment tools can add cost and complexity.

products.description: An all-in-one commercial masking and security wallet; convenient, but closed and heavier than simple email-alias tools.

products.name: Permission Slip by Consumer Reports

privacy.note: Consumer Reports says Permission Slip helps users send delete and stop-sale requests to companies, with Plus adding data-broker automation.

openness.note: The app is run by a nonprofit consumer organization, but the mobile app and automation workflow are not presented as open source.

portability.note: The value is in delegated rights requests rather than account migration or self-hostable infrastructure.

respect.note: Consumer Reports frames the project around consumer privacy rights, transparency and fairness rather than advertising or resale.

accessibility.note: The app is designed to make privacy-rights requests simpler, including one-tap deletion and stop-sale actions.

economical.note: Permission Slip has a free app path, while Plus adds paid automation and human help.

products.description: A nonprofit data-rights app for sending deletion and stop-sale requests; useful for learning privacy rights, but not a full substitute for every broker opt-out.

products.name: EasyOptOuts

privacy.note: EasyOptOuts says it removes personal information from Google results and 200+ data brokers and people-search sites.

openness.note: EasyOptOuts is a proprietary paid service, not open-source removal tooling.

portability.note: The service submits removals for users, but the process is service-bound rather than self-hostable or easily portable.

respect.note: EasyOptOuts says it collects minimal data and never shares it with third parties; the model still requires trusting a remover with sensitive identifiers.

accessibility.note: The product emphasizes automated opt-outs and a five-minute signup flow for people-search/data-broker removals.

economical.note: EasyOptOuts advertises a $19.99/year price, making it one of the lower-cost managed removal services.

products.description: A low-cost automated people-search and data-broker opt-out service; strong value, with the normal caveat that no removal service can erase everything.

products.name: Optery

privacy.note: Optery offers a free exposure report and paid removals, with its Ultimate plan claiming automated removals from 630+ sites and custom requests across 945+ sites.

openness.note: Optery describes patented proprietary opt-out technology rather than open-source removal tooling.

portability.note: The screenshots and reports improve transparency, but removal work remains tied to Optery's hosted service.

respect.note: Optery states it has no affiliation with data brokers and provides screenshot-backed reports, but the service still handles sensitive personal data.

accessibility.note: Free exposure reports make discovery accessible, while managed removals require paid tiers.

economical.note: The free tier is useful for exposure discovery, but the broadest automated removal coverage is reserved for higher paid plans.

products.description: A high-coverage exposure-report and removal service with useful proof reports; strong for visibility, but meaningful coverage costs more.

products.name: Incogni

privacy.note: Incogni says it covers 420+ data brokers with automated removals and identifies private brokers by region before sending periodic opt-out requests.

openness.note: Incogni is a proprietary subscription service, not open-source data-removal software.

portability.note: Removal requests are handled inside Incogni's managed workflow rather than a portable, self-run opt-out system.

respect.note: Incogni automates opt-out requests across brokers, but users must share identifying data with a commercial remover to run the process.

accessibility.note: The service is designed as a hands-off removal workflow with automated requests and progress tracking.

economical.note: Incogni is paid subscription software; pricing is more accessible than concierge removers but not free.

products.description: A subscription data-broker remover with broad automated coverage; convenient and international-facing, but closed and still trust-based.

products.name: DeleteMe

privacy.note: DeleteMe plans remove people from major data-broker websites for a year and include custom removal requests plus reports.

openness.note: DeleteMe is a proprietary commercial removal service run by Abine, not open-source removal software.

portability.note: DeleteMe manages removals and reports for subscribers, so continuity depends on the hosted service and renewal.

respect.note: DeleteMe has long-running data-broker removal expertise, but plans require sharing sensitive identifiers with a commercial provider.

accessibility.note: Plans include automated services, custom removals, privacy reports and email/chat/phone support.

economical.note: DeleteMe is a paid annual or biennial service, with lower affordability than budget opt-out tools.

products.description: A long-running paid data-broker removal service with reports and support; accessible for US residents, but more expensive than lightweight opt-out tools.

products.name: Kanary

privacy.note: Kanary describes a platform that identifies exposed personal information, removes it and helps prevent future leaks.

openness.note: Kanary combines proprietary technology with a US-based privacy team rather than open-source removal tooling.

portability.note: Removal and monitoring are handled through Kanary's account workflow, not through a portable or self-hostable system.

respect.note: Kanary positions itself around stalking, harassment, doxxing and deepfake risk reduction, a higher-safety use case than generic reputation cleanup.

accessibility.note: Kanary offers self-guided and managed options, with family-account support for people protecting more than one person.

economical.note: Kanary offers a free-start/self-guided path and paid managed plans, so cost depends on how much help is needed.

products.description: A personal safety-oriented exposure removal service for doxxing and harassment risk; more protective than DIY opt-outs, but still closed and service-bound.

products.name: Privacy Bee

privacy.note: Privacy Bee's paid plans cover data brokers, custom sites, search-result monitoring and additional exposure-remediation features.

openness.note: Privacy Bee is proprietary commercial privacy-remediation software, not open-source removal tooling.

portability.note: The service centers on Privacy Bee's takedown workflow and analysts rather than portable user-controlled removal tooling.

respect.note: Privacy Bee includes extensive exposure-reduction features, though the higher-touch model requires sharing sensitive information with a commercial service.

accessibility.note: Plans range from mostly automated takedowns to analyst-supported options, reducing the amount of user labor.

economical.note: Annual prices start around $8/month for Essentials and rise materially for Pro or high-risk Signature support.

products.description: A broad exposure-remediation service with broker removals, monitoring and analyst-backed tiers; powerful for high-risk users, but relatively expensive.

products.name: Have I Been Pwned

privacy.note: HIBP lets users check whether an email address appears in known data breaches and sign up for breach notifications.

openness.note: The service has public web checks, domain search and an API, though the breach corpus and service are not a self-hostable open-source stack.

portability.note: HIBP does not lock users into an account to understand exposure; email checks and notifications are separate from broader identity services.

respect.note: The notification page states HIBP will never share the submitted email address with anyone else.

accessibility.note: The basic workflow is simple: enter an email, check breach history and opt into free future notifications.

economical.note: Breach search and email notifications are free for individual users.

products.description: A free breach-exposure check and notification service; not a removal tool, but essential literacy for knowing when credentials or emails are exposed.

products.name: Mozilla Monitor

privacy.note: Mozilla Monitor checks known breaches for exposed data and provides steps to fix affected accounts.

openness.note: Mozilla explains the breach-alert service and its HIBP basis publicly, but Monitor itself is a hosted Mozilla service rather than a self-hostable open tool.

portability.note: Free breach monitoring can cover multiple email addresses without locking users into a broader identity-protection bundle.

respect.note: Mozilla shut down Monitor Plus data-broker removals while keeping core breach alerts, making the current service narrower but clearer.

accessibility.note: The main workflow is a simple email check and free scan for breach exposure.

economical.note: Core breach alerts remain available for free after the paid Monitor Plus removal service shut down.

products.description: A Mozilla breach-alert service that helps users find exposed accounts and act, now best understood as monitoring rather than broker removal.

products.name: VirusTotal

privacy.note: VirusTotal is useful for suspicious files, URLs and domains, but public submissions are shared with the security community, so private files should not be uploaded.

openness.note: VirusTotal publishes API documentation, but the service and scanning corpus are Google-operated rather than open-source or self-hostable.

portability.note: The public web tool and API can analyze files, URLs, domains and IP addresses across platforms without installing a local app.

respect.note: VirusTotal offers private scanning for organizations, but the ordinary public workflow is built around community sharing of submitted samples.

accessibility.note: The basic workflow is simple: paste a URL or upload a suspicious file and read multi-engine security results.

economical.note: VirusTotal provides public scanning on the web, with paid/private and API capacity tiers for heavier use.

products.description: A mainstream suspicious-file, URL, domain and IP scanner; powerful for literacy, but public submissions can expose private material.

products.name: Jotti's malware scan

privacy.note: Jotti warns that submitted files are shared with antivirus companies to improve detection, so users should not upload sensitive documents.

openness.note: Jotti is a hosted multi-engine scanner; the site does not present itself as open-source or self-hostable.

portability.note: The scanner runs in a browser and accepts multiple files, with a 250 MB per-file limit.

respect.note: The service is clear about file sharing with antivirus vendors, but that sharing model is a major privacy tradeoff.

accessibility.note: Jotti offers a straightforward file-upload workflow for people who want a second opinion on suspicious files.

economical.note: Jotti describes the malware scan as a free service.

products.description: A simple multi-antivirus file scanner that is useful for second opinions, with the important caveat that uploaded files are shared with antivirus companies.

products.name: urlscan.io

privacy.note: urlscan.io distinguishes Public, Unlisted and Private scans; public scans are visible to other users, so private links need private visibility.

openness.note: urlscan.io provides public docs and an API, but it is an operated hosted scanner rather than a reusable open-source service.

portability.note: The web scanner can load a URL from different country contexts and returns a reusable report with screenshots, requests and indicators.

respect.note: The service publishes scan-visibility guidance warning users not to make sensitive or proprietary URLs public.

accessibility.note: The interface is powerful but more analyst-oriented than one-click consumer phishing checks.

economical.note: urlscan.io offers free public use and free private-scan quotas, with paid tiers for heavier usage.

products.description: A web-page scanner for suspicious URLs, phishing pages and redirect chains; excellent for learning, but scan visibility must be chosen carefully.

products.name: PhishTank

privacy.note: PhishTank's privacy policy says submitted suspected phishing emails may include personal information, so submissions require care.

openness.note: PhishTank provides phishing data through open API/download formats for developers and researchers.

portability.note: The phishing feed is available in XML, CSV, JSON and other formats for reuse in other tools.

respect.note: The project is a collaborative clearinghouse for phishing data rather than an ad-funded consumer profiling service.

accessibility.note: Anyone can submit, verify, track and share phishing data, though the interface is more community/security-oriented than polished consumer software.

economical.note: PhishTank says the website and data API are free for everyone.

products.description: A community phishing-clearinghouse and free API that helps people and tools check whether a URL has been reported as phishing.

products.name: AbuseIPDB

privacy.note: AbuseIPDB lets users report and check suspicious IPs, but its API docs warn reporters to remove personally identifiable information from comments.

openness.note: The service provides public lookups and a documented API for checking and reporting abusive IP addresses, though the service itself is operated by AbuseIPDB.

portability.note: AbuseIPDB supports web checks, API checks, reports, bulk checking and integrations for security tools.

respect.note: The project is centered on community IP abuse reports for administrators and interested parties rather than consumer advertising.

accessibility.note: The home page exposes a direct IP, domain, subnet and ASN lookup box, while deeper reporting workflows are more administrator-oriented.

economical.note: AbuseIPDB lists an individual plan as free forever with 1,000 checks and reports per day.

products.description: A community IP reputation database for checking whether an address has been reported for abuse; useful for suspicious logins and admin triage, but report comments need privacy care.

products.name: Cisco Talos Intelligence Center

privacy.note: Talos lookups focus on IP, domain, URL and file-hash reputation rather than uploading private documents.

openness.note: Talos publishes reputation-center guidance, but the underlying threat intelligence and classification systems are Cisco-operated and proprietary.

portability.note: Cisco documents Talos URL and IP lookup as an online tool for understanding FQDN, URL, category and web-reputation classifications.

respect.note: Talos exposes reputation signals for defensive checking, though users still rely on a large vendor's classification system.

accessibility.note: The reputation center is public but more technical than a one-button consumer safety checker.

economical.note: Cisco's public reputation center is available on the web without a listed consumer fee.

products.description: A Cisco reputation lookup for domains, IPs, URLs and file hashes; useful for technical cross-checking, but not open infrastructure.

products.name: Norton Safe Web

privacy.note: Norton Safe Web checks web safety inside Norton's ecosystem, so privacy depends on Norton's product and service practices.

openness.note: Safe Web is a proprietary Norton/Gen Digital safety product rather than an open blocklist or self-hostable tool.

portability.note: Norton offers site safety ratings through Safe Web and related Safe Search/browser-safety surfaces.

respect.note: Safe Web is meant to warn users about scams and dangerous websites, but the protection is vendor-mediated.

accessibility.note: The public Safe Web page and search-oriented safety rating flow make it approachable for ordinary users.

economical.note: The public lookup and safe-search surfaces are accessible without buying a full suite, while broader protection is tied to Norton products.

products.description: A mainstream site-safety checker and browser-safety surface from Norton; easy for suspicious links, but proprietary and vendor-bound.

products.name: Trend Micro Site Safety Center

privacy.note: The Site Safety Center checks a submitted URL and does not require uploading files, but the query still goes to Trend Micro.

openness.note: Trend Micro ratings are based on Trend Micro research and sources, but the classification system is proprietary.

portability.note: The public web checker returns website safety rating and category without installing a client.

respect.note: Trend Micro provides a reclassification request path for sites that appear misrated.

accessibility.note: The workflow is simple: paste a website link, click Check Now and read the current rating and category.

economical.note: Trend Micro describes Site Safety Center as a free service for checking suspicious URLs.

products.description: A straightforward free URL safety checker from Trend Micro, useful for quick second opinions on suspicious sites.

products.name: ScamAdviser

privacy.note: ScamAdviser checks websites and shops, but queries and trust-score generation are handled by a commercial service.

openness.note: ScamAdviser describes an algorithm and many data points, but the trust-score model is not an independently reproducible open method.

portability.note: ScamAdviser offers a web checker and a business API for domain trust scoring.

respect.note: The tool can help consumers pause before trusting a shop or link, but a trust score should not be treated as a final verdict.

accessibility.note: The homepage is built around checking whether a site or online store looks safe or scammy.

economical.note: The public website checker is free to use, while API and business services are separate.

products.description: A consumer-friendly trust-score checker for suspicious shops and websites; useful as a pause button, not proof that a site is safe.

products.name: URLVoid

privacy.note: URLVoid says data submitted to the checker is shared with security companies, so users should not submit private or sensitive URLs casually.

openness.note: URLVoid aggregates many blocklists and reputation engines, but it is a NoVirusThanks/APIVoid-operated service rather than an open tool.

portability.note: The safety report includes multiple engines, IP address details, domain creation date, server location and related report links.

respect.note: URLVoid explicitly warns that a clean result cannot guarantee a website is harmless.

accessibility.note: The web form is a simple website reputation checker with no local setup.

economical.note: URLVoid describes itself as a free service for scanning websites with multiple reputation engines.

products.description: A multi-engine website reputation checker that helps compare suspicious domains across blocklists, with an important submission-sharing caveat.

products.name: Hybrid Analysis

privacy.note: Hybrid Analysis says uploaded file collections are made available to the community YARA/String search, so sensitive files should not be submitted.

openness.note: The public service exposes reports, search and API documentation, but the sandbox is powered by CrowdStrike Falcon Sandbox rather than open-source infrastructure.

portability.note: The service supports file and URL analysis, report search, YARA search, string search and IOC search through a browser.

respect.note: The public sharing model is useful for community defense but makes this unsuitable for private documents or confidential incident data.

accessibility.note: Drag-and-drop upload is simple, but interpreting sandbox output is more analyst-oriented than beginner-friendly.

economical.note: Hybrid Analysis describes itself as a free malware analysis service for the community.

products.description: A free malware sandbox and report search service for suspicious files and URLs; powerful, but public/community sharing makes privacy caution essential.

products.name: ANY.RUN

privacy.note: ANY.RUN's pricing page says private analyses are available only on paid Hunter and Enterprise plans, while the free plan is public-analysis oriented.

openness.note: ANY.RUN is a proprietary hosted sandbox and threat-intelligence platform rather than open-source malware-analysis infrastructure.

portability.note: The platform supports interactive browser-based sandboxing and threat-intelligence lookup for malicious files, URLs and behaviors.

respect.note: Interactive analysis can teach real behavior, but free public tasks can expose artifacts and should not be used for confidential samples.

accessibility.note: ANY.RUN offers a free sign-up path and visual sandbox sessions, though the concepts remain security-analyst oriented.

economical.note: ANY.RUN lists a free Community plan with unlimited public analyses, while private analysis requires paid tiers.

products.description: An interactive malware sandbox for watching suspicious files and URLs behave in a virtual environment; useful for learning, but free analyses are public.

products.name: Joe Sandbox Cloud Basic

privacy.note: Joe Sandbox Cloud Basic is a community cloud sandbox, so users should avoid submitting private files or live credentials.

openness.note: Joe Sandbox is a proprietary Joe Security service rather than an open sandbox engine.

portability.note: Joe Sandbox analyzes files and URLs across Windows, macOS and Linux environments and generates detailed behavior reports.

respect.note: The community tier helps researchers inspect malicious behavior, but limited output and cloud sharing make it a triage tool rather than private incident handling.

accessibility.note: Cloud Basic provides browser access, but sandbox terminology and reports are oriented toward malware analysts.

economical.note: Joe Sandbox Cloud Basic allows 15 analyses per month and 5 per day with limited analysis output.

products.description: A limited free cloud sandbox for malware and phishing analysis, with strong technical reports but a narrow, analyst-style workflow.

products.name: EmailRep

privacy.note: EmailRep evaluates email addresses using many public and security signals, so checking a personal email address is itself a sensitive query.

openness.note: Sublime Security publishes the EmailRep public API repository and response details on GitHub.

portability.note: The API returns JSON reputation and detail fields for email addresses, making it easy to integrate into defensive workflows.

respect.note: The tool can support anti-phishing and fraud checks, but its own documentation also acknowledges offensive reconnaissance uses.

accessibility.note: The service is simple for API users, but less approachable for nontechnical people than a web-only checker.

economical.note: EmailRep lists a free community API key with 250 queries per month and up to 10 queries per day.

products.description: An email reputation API for phishing, fraud and throwaway-account checks; helpful for defenders, but personal email lookups deserve care.

products.name: MxToolbox Blacklist Check

privacy.note: MxToolbox blacklist checks use a domain or server IP rather than file upload, but queries still go through a commercial diagnostic service.

openness.note: The tool checks more than 100 DNS-based email blacklists, but MxToolbox is a proprietary diagnostic platform.

portability.note: The web checker works with a server IP or domain and links into related MX and DNS diagnostics.

respect.note: The knowledge base explains what blacklists are and how monitoring works, though results can be alarming without mail-delivery context.

accessibility.note: The Blacklist Check form is simple for a domain or IP, especially for people troubleshooting email delivery.

economical.note: MxToolbox provides a free online blacklist check and free monitoring options, with paid support and deeper monitoring tiers.

products.description: A practical blacklist checker for mail-server IPs and domains, strongest for email administrators and small sites troubleshooting deliverability.

products.name: URLhaus

privacy.note: URLhaus submissions are shared with security solution providers, antivirus vendors and blocklist providers, so private URLs should not be submitted.

openness.note: URLhaus provides public browsing, APIs, feeds and bulk data for malicious URLs used in malware distribution.

portability.note: The platform supports database browsing, malware URL reporting, APIs and feeds for integration into defensive tools.

respect.note: The platform has a narrow malware-URL mission and explains that it collects, tracks and shares malware URLs to help defenders protect networks and users.

accessibility.note: The database is public, but APIs, feeds and malware URL handling are more technical than consumer scam-checking tools.

economical.note: URLhaus exposes public browse and API paths without listing a consumer subscription requirement.

products.description: A public malware-URL exchange from abuse.ch and Spamhaus, strong for threat-intelligence and blocklist workflows but too technical for casual link checking.

products.name: Wayback Machine

privacy.note: Wayback captures and serves public web pages; it is essential for public evidence, but not a private note or sensitive-page archive.

openness.note: The Wayback Machine is an Internet Archive initiative, part of a nonprofit digital library of internet sites and cultural artifacts.

portability.note: Save Page Now can capture a page as it appears now for trusted citation in the future.

respect.note: The service is public-interest web preservation rather than an ad or engagement platform.

accessibility.note: Users can paste a URL into Save Page Now or browse historic captures in a public web interface.

economical.note: The Wayback Machine is free to use, with the Internet Archive supported by donations and institutional services.

products.description: The public web-archive default for checking deleted pages, changed claims and source history; very useful, but public archiving is not private storage.

products.name: TinEye

privacy.note: TinEye says reverse-image searching is private and that it does not save or index uploaded search images.

openness.note: TinEye is a proprietary reverse-image search service rather than open-source image-search infrastructure.

portability.note: TinEye supports image upload, image URL, drag-and-drop, copy/paste and browser extensions for reverse-image searching.

respect.note: The product emphasizes private search and does not position uploaded images as training/indexing material.

accessibility.note: TinEye offers a simple web search box and extensions, but the index is narrower than major image-search platforms.

economical.note: The public TinEye reverse-image search is free for ordinary manual searching, with paid commercial/API products separately.

products.description: A privacy-friendlier reverse-image search option for checking where an image appeared before, whether it is stock, or whether it has been reused out of context.

products.name: Google Lens

privacy.note: Google says Visual Search History can save images used with Google Lens to Web & App Activity when the setting is on.

openness.note: Google Lens is a proprietary Google visual-search service, not an open-source or self-hostable verification tool.

portability.note: Lens is widely available across Google apps and Chrome, but results/history live inside Google's account and search ecosystem.

respect.note: Lens is powerful for visual search, but Google's support page says saved visual-search images may be used to improve recognition technologies.

accessibility.note: Google Lens lets users search with a photo, camera or almost any image across common Google surfaces.

economical.note: Google Lens is free to use in the Google app, Chrome and related Google surfaces.

products.description: The easiest visual-search default for finding similar images and context, with the usual Google tradeoff: excellent access, weaker privacy and openness.

products.name: InVID-WeVerify Plugin

privacy.note: The plugin is a browser verification toolkit; privacy depends on which external checks/tools a user invokes during an investigation.

openness.note: The InVID Verification Plugin is provided as open source on GitHub under an MIT license.

portability.note: The plugin bundles multiple verification workflows for images and videos, including keyframes and reverse-search assists.

respect.note: The tool is explicitly designed for journalists, fact-checkers, human rights defenders, academics and OSINT researchers.

accessibility.note: It is powerful for verification work but expects a user who understands source-checking and investigation context.

economical.note: The plugin is free to install and use.

products.description: A serious browser toolkit for verifying images and videos in journalism/OSINT workflows, best for users ready to learn investigative habits.

products.name: FotoForensics

privacy.note: FotoForensics is an online service, so users upload or submit images for analysis and should avoid sensitive/private material.

openness.note: FotoForensics provides public tools and training, but it is not presented as an open-source image-forensics app.

portability.note: The service offers tools and tutorials for digital picture analysis, including error level analysis and metadata.

respect.note: The FAQ frames ELA as one limited technique rather than proof of manipulation, which is useful for careful media literacy.

accessibility.note: FotoForensics is web-based and educational, but interpretation of image-forensics output requires caution and practice.

economical.note: FotoForensics makes public image-analysis tools available on the web, with separate training and expert services.

products.description: An educational image-forensics service for ELA/metadata-style checks; useful for learning, risky for private images, and never proof on its own.

products.name: Forensically

privacy.note: Forensically is described by its creator as a set of tools for performing photo forensic analysis in the browser.

openness.note: Forensically is publicly available and free, but the creator's post does not present it as released open-source software.

portability.note: Forensically includes clone detection, error level analysis, metadata extraction and other web-based photo-forensics tools.

respect.note: It is a focused toolset for examining images rather than a platform feed or ad product.

accessibility.note: The browser workflow is approachable, but photo-forensics outputs require interpretation and should not be treated as automated truth.

economical.note: Forensically is provided as a free online photo-forensics toolset.

products.description: A free browser-based photo-forensics workbench for clone detection, ELA and metadata checks, useful as a learning tool when used cautiously.

products.name: SunCalc

privacy.note: SunCalc-style verification can be done with location/time inputs rather than uploading private media.

openness.note: The SunCalc JavaScript library is public on GitHub and calculates sun/moon positions, phases and times.

portability.note: The underlying library can calculate sun position, sunlight phases, moon position and lunar phase for any location and time.

respect.note: SunCalc is a focused calculation/visualization tool, useful for geolocation checks without an account or feed.

accessibility.note: The public map interface is easy for basic sun-position checks, though geolocation verification still takes practice.

economical.note: The public SunCalc tool and library are free to use.

products.description: A simple sun-position checker for geolocation and chronology work: not a verdict machine, but a useful sanity check for shadows and timestamps.

products.name: SecurityHeaders.com

privacy.note: SecurityHeaders scans a submitted public URL and returns HTTP-response header findings, so private or unpublished URLs should not be pasted casually.

openness.note: SecurityHeaders.com is a hosted scanner rather than an open-source self-hosted tool.

portability.note: The FAQ explains the grades and checked HTTP response headers, making findings understandable and repeatable.

respect.note: The tool is a focused website-hardening checker rather than an advertising or profiling product.

accessibility.note: The basic workflow is simple: enter a website URL and get a grade with missing/present header guidance.

economical.note: SecurityHeaders.com provides free public checks.

products.description: A quick HTTP-security-header checker that helps users learn why sites need CSP, HSTS and related protections.

products.name: MDN HTTP Observatory

privacy.note: HTTP Observatory scans public websites and security headers, so users should avoid submitting private/internal URLs.

openness.note: Mozilla's HTTP Observatory scanner, CLI and website projects are published as open-source tools.

portability.note: The project includes a web scanner, command-line interface and API for testing website security configuration.

respect.note: MDN describes the Observatory as an educational security assessment tool for website administrators and developers.

accessibility.note: The MDN web interface provides detailed, actionable feedback on HTTP headers and security configuration.

economical.note: MDN HTTP Observatory is free to use.

products.description: A stronger open-source website-security checker for learning how headers and key web-security settings protect visitors.

products.name: ICANN Lookup

privacy.note: ICANN Lookup exposes current public registration data; useful for source-checking, but domain registrants must understand privacy/proxy options.

openness.note: ICANN provides a public registration-data lookup for domain names and internet number resources.

portability.note: The lookup tool returns current public registration data such as registrar, dates and resource records where available.

respect.note: The service is internet-governance infrastructure rather than a commercial attention platform.

accessibility.note: The public web form is easy to use, though modern redaction means many registrant contact details may not be visible.

economical.note: ICANN Lookup is free to use on the web.

products.description: A practical first stop for checking domain age, registrar and registration context, with the caveat that modern privacy redaction limits what it can show.

products.name: crt.sh

privacy.note: crt.sh searches public Certificate Transparency records; CT improves accountability but can reveal certificate/subdomain information by design.

openness.note: crt.sh is a public certificate search operated by Sectigo for Certificate Transparency data.

portability.note: The tool can search by domain name, organization name, certificate fingerprint or crt.sh ID.

respect.note: Certificate Transparency is public-accountability infrastructure for the WebPKI, not an ad or engagement product.

accessibility.note: crt.sh is powerful for security/OSINT users, but the interface is technical for everyday source checking.

economical.note: crt.sh is freely available on the web.

products.description: A certificate-transparency lookup for checking what certificates and subdomains appear for an identity, useful but more technical than ordinary domain lookup.

products.name: Google Fact Check Explorer

privacy.note: Fact Check Explorer is a Google service, so searching is governed by Google's privacy and account ecosystem.

openness.note: Google exposes Fact Check Tools APIs, but the explorer itself is a proprietary Google-hosted service.

portability.note: The API lets users query the same set of Fact Check results available through Fact Check Explorer.

respect.note: The tool points users toward published ClaimReview fact checks, but coverage depends on participating publishers and Google's indexing.

accessibility.note: Fact Check Explorer provides a searchable web interface for recent and topic-based fact checks.

economical.note: Google Fact Check Explorer is free to use on the web.

products.description: A useful searchable layer over published fact checks, strongest as a starting point and weakest if treated as complete coverage of every claim.

products.name: Content Credentials Verify

privacy.note: The public Verify tool inspects Content Credentials metadata supplied by the user, but users should still treat uploaded or selected media as sensitive.

openness.note: Content Credentials are based on the open C2PA standard for media provenance and authenticity signals.

portability.note: C2PA provenance data is designed to travel with digital media across compatible tools and platforms.

respect.note: The standard helps creators and viewers see origin and edit-history signals, while C2PA cautions that missing credentials do not prove media is fake.

accessibility.note: Content Credentials offers a public web verification path for checking whether an asset carries provenance metadata.

economical.note: The public Content Credentials Verify site is free to access.

products.description: A public C2PA and Content Credentials inspection path for checking whether media carries provenance metadata; useful, but absence of credentials is not proof of fakery.

products.name: Adobe Content Authenticity

privacy.note: Adobe Content Authenticity is tied to Adobe's app and account ecosystem, so privacy depends on Adobe's service practices.

openness.note: The app works with Content Credentials, but the creator-facing service is an Adobe product rather than an independent open tool.

portability.note: Adobe describes the tool as attaching Content Credentials that can show attribution and preference information across supported services.

respect.note: Adobe frames the tool around creator attribution and a signal for generative-AI training and use preferences.

accessibility.note: Adobe launched a public beta for creators, with a web app path for applying and managing Content Credentials.

economical.note: Adobe describes the public beta as available to creators without a paid Creative Cloud plan.

products.description: A creator-facing Content Credentials tool for attaching attribution and AI-training preference signals; useful for provenance, but still sits in Adobe's account and tool ecosystem.

products.name: c2patool

privacy.note: c2patool can inspect and work with C2PA manifests locally, reducing the need to upload sensitive media to a third-party verifier.

openness.note: The Content Authenticity Initiative publishes c2patool documentation and open-source C2PA tooling on GitHub.

portability.note: The tool reads and creates C2PA manifests for media files, aligning with portable Content Credentials workflows.

respect.note: Local inspection supports careful verification without treating provenance as a centralized platform verdict.

accessibility.note: c2patool is a command-line tool, powerful for technical users but less approachable for casual media verification.

economical.note: The open-source c2patool project is available freely through the Content Authenticity Initiative tooling.

products.description: A local command-line C2PA tool for reading, adding and inspecting manifests; excellent for technical users, too technical for casual verification.

products.name: C2PA Viewer

privacy.note: C2PA Viewer says files are verified in the browser and are not uploaded to a server.

openness.note: The viewer uses the C2PA standard, but the page itself is a third-party viewer rather than the standards body's canonical verifier.

portability.note: The viewer checks C2PA metadata carried in selected media files through a browser interface.

respect.note: A client-side viewer helps people inspect provenance without assuming a platform account or a single gatekeeper.

accessibility.note: The web interface is simpler than command-line C2PA tooling, though it is still oriented around people who understand provenance metadata.

economical.note: C2PA Viewer is presented as a free browser-based inspection tool.

products.description: A free browser-based C2PA inspector that says verification happens client-side; useful for quick checks, but it is a third-party viewer rather than the standards body.

products.name: Proofmode

privacy.note: Proofmode is built for privacy-aware evidence capture and lets users control whether sensitive metadata is collected and shared.

openness.note: Proofmode is published as free and open-source software by Guardian Project and WITNESS.

portability.note: Proofmode creates signed proof bundles that can accompany photos and videos outside the app.

respect.note: The project is designed for journalists, activists and human-rights defenders who need evidence integrity without surrendering control.

accessibility.note: Proofmode is available through Android app distribution, though its evidence-capture concepts require user understanding.

economical.note: Proofmode is free software with public source code.

products.description: A free open-source camera and provenance tool that signs captures and lets users control metadata; strong for chain-of-custody when privacy settings are understood.

products.name: Tella

privacy.note: Tella emphasizes encrypted, hidden and protected documentation workflows for people working in high-risk environments.

openness.note: Tella is published as open-source software by Horizontal.

portability.note: Tella supports documentation collection and submission workflows rather than locking evidence only into one consumer account.

respect.note: The app is designed for human-rights defenders, journalists and civil-society groups documenting sensitive events.

accessibility.note: Tella is distributed through mobile app stores, though its security features require careful setup and context.

economical.note: Tella is available as a free app and open-source project.

products.description: A free open-source documentation app for human-rights work, with encryption, hiding and evidence collection for challenging environments.

products.name: eyeWitness to Atrocities

privacy.note: eyeWitness collects verification metadata and sends footage to secure storage for legal use, which is valuable but sensitive.

openness.note: The app and legal-evidence pipeline are specialized and not presented as open-source software.

portability.note: The workflow is built around preserving evidence and chain of custody for legal accountability rather than general consumer export.

respect.note: The project exists to help authenticate potential evidence of atrocity crimes and support accountability processes.

accessibility.note: eyeWitness is available on Android, while the project states that the iOS app is not currently available.

economical.note: The Android app listing presents eyeWitness to Atrocities as a free app.

products.description: A specialized Android tool for documenting atrocities with metadata and secure chain-of-custody for legal evidence; powerful, but not a casual everyday verifier.

products.name: OpenTimestamps

privacy.note: OpenTimestamps can timestamp hashes, allowing proof that data existed before a time without publishing the full underlying file.

openness.note: The OpenTimestamps client and protocol tooling are published openly on GitHub.

portability.note: The project is designed around portable timestamp proofs that can be verified later.

respect.note: Timestamping proves existence-before-time without asking a central content platform to judge the content itself.

accessibility.note: OpenTimestamps is powerful but technical, with command-line client workflows for many users.

economical.note: The OpenTimestamps client is an open-source project that users can run without a commercial subscription.

products.description: An open timestamping protocol and tool for proving data existed before a point in time; privacy-friendly because hashes can be timestamped without uploading full files, but technical.

products.name: GPTZero

privacy.note: GPTZero publishes privacy and security materials, but users still submit text to a commercial detection service.

openness.note: GPTZero is a proprietary AI-detection product rather than an open model or open benchmark users can independently inspect.

portability.note: The product supports web and workflow use, but results remain tied to GPTZero's service and detector design.

respect.note: AI-text detection should be treated as one review signal with human context, not a final verdict on authorship.

accessibility.note: GPTZero offers public-facing web access and plans aimed at education and professional users.

economical.note: GPTZero offers a free tier alongside paid plans.

products.description: A widely recognized AI-text detector for education and workplace workflows; useful as one signal with human review, not a verdict on authorship.

products.name: Originality.ai

privacy.note: Originality.ai is a commercial service where users submit text and content into a proprietary detection workflow.

openness.note: Originality.ai is a proprietary paid product rather than an open-source detector or independently reproducible model.

portability.note: The service is built for publisher and team workflows, but its scoring is bound to the Originality.ai platform.

respect.note: The suite can support review workflows, but AI-detection results should be interpreted cautiously and not as a stand-alone accusation.

accessibility.note: Originality.ai is web-based and aimed at professional teams, with less fit for casual free public checking.

economical.note: Originality.ai presents paid plans rather than a durable broad free consumer tier.

products.description: A paid AI, plagiarism and fact-checking suite for publishers and teams; stronger for professional workflow than open or privacy-minimal values.

products.name: Copyleaks

privacy.note: Copyleaks publishes data-protection materials, but users are still submitting content into a commercial scanning service.

openness.note: Copyleaks is a proprietary AI and plagiarism detection platform, not an open-source detector.

portability.note: The platform supports multiple education and business workflows, while scores and integrations remain platform-specific.

respect.note: Detection can help triage review, but authorship and academic-integrity decisions require careful human process.

accessibility.note: Copyleaks offers a web platform and integrations for organizations, schools and businesses.

economical.note: Copyleaks publishes paid pricing, making it less economical for casual users than free verification tools.

products.description: A commercial AI and plagiarism detection suite with compliance claims and education/business workflows; useful for triage, but not an open or low-risk verdict engine.

products.name: Reality Defender

privacy.note: Reality Defender is an enterprise detection platform, so privacy depends on organizational deployment and vendor handling of submitted media.

openness.note: Reality Defender is a proprietary platform rather than an open-source deepfake detector.

portability.note: The product is positioned for enterprise and government detection workflows rather than portable public self-verification.

respect.note: Deepfake detection can reduce impersonation and fraud harms, but enterprise detection should still be paired with due process.

accessibility.note: Reality Defender is aimed at organizations rather than everyday public use, which lowers accessibility for ordinary consumers.

economical.note: The product is sold as an enterprise platform rather than a free public verification tool.

products.description: An enterprise deepfake-detection platform for organizations and governments; relevant to media authenticity, but not a public/open everyday consumer tool.

products.name: Google Safe Browsing Site Status

privacy.note: The Site Status tool lets users check a URL against Google's unsafe-site detection without uploading a private file.

openness.note: Google publishes a Safe Browsing Transparency Report and FAQs, but the detection service itself is proprietary.

portability.note: The lookup is web-based and Safe Browsing protections are used across browsers, Search and web security integrations.

respect.note: Safe Browsing is a harm-prevention service, though it remains part of Google's broader web-security ecosystem.

accessibility.note: Users can paste a site into the Transparency Report Site Status diagnostic tool and get a plain safety result.

economical.note: The public Safe Browsing Site Status lookup is free to use.

products.description: A simple Google lookup for whether a site is currently flagged as unsafe, useful as a low-friction first check for suspicious links.

products.name: Malwarebytes Browser Guard

privacy.note: Browser Guard blocks trackers, ads, phishing and malicious content, but it is still a proprietary browser extension operating in browsing context.

openness.note: Malwarebytes Browser Guard is distributed as a vendor-managed extension rather than a public-source tool.

portability.note: Malwarebytes offers Browser Guard for Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari.

respect.note: The extension is aimed at blocking scam, malware, phishing, ad and tracker abuse rather than adding a social or advertising layer.

accessibility.note: Installation is a normal browser-extension flow and the product is designed for everyday users rather than analysts.

economical.note: Malwarebytes describes Browser Guard as a free extension.

products.description: A free mainstream browser extension for scam, phishing, malware, ad and tracker blocking, with the tradeoff of trusting a proprietary browser-security vendor.

products.name: Bitdefender TrafficLight

privacy.note: TrafficLight scans pages users visit for malware and phishing attempts, which helps safety but requires trusting Bitdefender's extension layer.

openness.note: TrafficLight is a proprietary Bitdefender extension rather than an open-source browser-defense tool.

portability.note: Bitdefender documents TrafficLight support for Safari, Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox.

respect.note: TrafficLight focuses on phishing, malware, malvertising and unsafe-page blocking, but the model is vendor trust rather than user-controlled rules.

accessibility.note: The extension offers visible browser warnings and search-result safety cues that non-experts can understand.

economical.note: Bitdefender describes TrafficLight as a free browser protection add-on.

products.description: A free proprietary browser add-on for malware and phishing protection, helpful for mainstream users who want warnings without learning analyst tools.

products.name: Netcraft Extension

privacy.note: Netcraft's privacy policy says blocked-site analytics can include the blocked URL, reason, extension version and country.

openness.note: The extension is a free Netcraft product, but not presented as open-source or self-hostable.

portability.note: Netcraft says the browser extension works with major browsers including Chrome, Firefox and Edge.

respect.note: The extension is built for phishing, fake-shop and malicious-script protection and allows users to report malicious URLs to Netcraft.

accessibility.note: Netcraft packages site information and cybercrime protection into a browser extension rather than requiring a separate analyst workflow.

economical.note: Netcraft describes its browser extension as free.

products.description: A free anti-phishing browser extension with strong cybercrime focus, balanced by proprietary implementation and some blocked-URL analytics.

products.name: CyberChef

privacy.note: CyberChef runs entirely in the browser with no server-side component, so inputs and recipes are not sent anywhere in the official app.

openness.note: GCHQ publishes CyberChef as open-source software on GitHub.

portability.note: CyberChef can run in a browser or as a downloaded standalone copy, making it practical across operating systems.

respect.note: The local-processing design lets users decode, hash, inspect and transform data without sending inputs to a remote analysis service.

accessibility.note: CyberChef is visual and powerful, but its many operations can still be intimidating for non-technical users.

economical.note: CyberChef is free to use and download.

products.description: A local-in-browser cyber literacy tool for decoding, hashing, inspecting and transforming data without sending inputs to a server.

products.name: ExifCleaner

privacy.note: ExifCleaner strips EXIF data from photos, videos and PDFs locally, helping remove hidden location, device and timestamp metadata before sharing.

openness.note: ExifCleaner publishes its source code publicly.

portability.note: ExifCleaner is a cross-platform desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux.

respect.note: The tool is focused on local metadata removal rather than uploading files to an online cleaner.

accessibility.note: ExifCleaner's drag-drop-clean workflow is easier for ordinary users than command-line metadata tools.

economical.note: ExifCleaner is free to download and use.

products.description: A free open-source desktop app for stripping hidden metadata from photos, videos and PDFs before sharing.

products.name: MAT2

privacy.note: MAT2 removes metadata from a wide range of common file formats, but users must remember it does not anonymize file contents themselves.

openness.note: MAT2 is published as free software under the LGPL-3.0 license.

portability.note: MAT2 is mainly a Python command-line/library and Linux file-manager workflow, so it is portable for technical users but not as consumer-polished.

respect.note: The local command-line design avoids uploading documents to a third-party metadata-cleaning website.

accessibility.note: MAT2 is powerful but command-line oriented, making it less approachable than drag-and-drop metadata cleaners.

economical.note: MAT2 is free and open-source software.

products.description: A serious open-source metadata-removal toolkit for people who need local, scriptable file cleaning and understand the limits.

products.name: ExifTool

privacy.note: ExifTool can read, write and edit metadata locally across many file formats, helping users inspect or remove sensitive embedded information.

openness.note: ExifTool publishes source code and is released as a Perl library plus command-line application.

portability.note: ExifTool is platform-independent and supports a wide range of image, video and document metadata formats.

respect.note: Because ExifTool runs locally, users can inspect and edit metadata without uploading files to a web service.

accessibility.note: ExifTool is extremely capable but command-line heavy, so it is less friendly for non-technical users than GUI metadata cleaners.

economical.note: ExifTool is free to download and use.

products.description: The classic local metadata inspection and editing tool: very powerful and portable, but best suited to users comfortable with command-line workflows.

products.name: Aegis Authenticator

privacy.note: Aegis emphasizes encrypted vault storage and backups for TOTP/HOTP tokens on Android.

openness.note: Aegis describes itself as free and open source and publishes its Android app code publicly.

portability.note: Aegis supports encrypted backups and imports from other authenticator apps, making migration practical for Android users.
