respect.note: The app is free, open source and local-first rather than tied to an advertising or account-sync business model.

accessibility.note: Aegis is strong for Android users but does not cover iOS or desktop as a first-party app.

economical.note: Aegis is offered as a free authenticator app through Google Play and F-Droid.

products.description: A local-first, open-source Android authenticator with encrypted backups; excellent for Android users who want control without a cloud account.

products.name: 2FAS

privacy.note: 2FAS says it uses local, on-device encryption and is free from invasive data gathering and profiling.

openness.note: 2FAS publishes official open-source app repositories, including its iOS code.

portability.note: 2FAS emphasizes migration from existing authenticators and backup/restore options, though sync still depends on mobile platform choices.

respect.note: The project positions itself around privacy, open code and no profiling rather than surveillance or account lock-in.

accessibility.note: 2FAS is available on major mobile platforms and includes browser-extension workflows for easier code entry.

economical.note: 2FAS advertises the authenticator as 100% free.

products.description: A free, open-source authenticator with a friendlier mainstream feel than many privacy tools, especially for mobile users.

products.name: Ente Auth

privacy.note: Ente Auth offers end-to-end encrypted cloud backups and sync for authenticator codes.

openness.note: Ente publishes its end-to-end encrypted platform and Auth app code publicly.

portability.note: Ente Auth works across mobile, desktop and web, with codes syncing across devices under end-to-end encryption.

respect.note: The service is built around encrypted backup and open-source transparency rather than ad tracking.

accessibility.note: Cross-platform apps and web access make Ente easier for people who do not want a phone-only authenticator.

economical.note: Ente Auth is described as a free authenticator app.

products.description: A free, open-source authenticator with end-to-end encrypted sync across phones, desktop and web.

products.name: Proton Authenticator

privacy.note: Proton describes its authenticator as open source, end-to-end encrypted and private.

openness.note: Proton Authenticator is presented as open source, with code available for public inspection through Proton's repositories.

portability.note: Proton says the app supports sync or backup of 2FA codes and works without requiring a Proton Account.

respect.note: The download page explicitly says Proton Authenticator has no ads and no tracking.

accessibility.note: Proton lists Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS downloads for the authenticator.

economical.note: Proton describes the authenticator as simple and free to use.

products.description: A free cross-platform authenticator from Proton, aiming to combine encrypted sync, open-source transparency and mainstream ease.

products.name: Google Authenticator

privacy.note: Google Authenticator can now sync one-time codes to a Google Account, improving recovery while adding account-level cloud dependence.

openness.note: Google Authenticator is a proprietary Google app rather than an open-source authenticator project.

portability.note: Google documents setup and transfer workflows for Authenticator, but the cloud-sync path is tied to a Google Account.

respect.note: The app is simple and free, but its most convenient recovery path now sits inside Google's account ecosystem.

accessibility.note: Google Authenticator is widely recognized and available on Android and iOS with a simple offline code workflow.

economical.note: The app is free to install and use.

products.description: The familiar mainstream authenticator: easy and free, but proprietary and increasingly tied to Google Account sync for recovery.

products.name: Microsoft Authenticator

privacy.note: Microsoft Authenticator backs up account credentials through platform cloud backup, but restore is limited to the same device type.

openness.note: Microsoft Authenticator is a proprietary Microsoft app and service component.

portability.note: Microsoft says backed-up accounts can be restored only on the same device type, reducing cross-platform portability.

respect.note: Authenticator still supports MFA and passkeys, but Microsoft has moved password autofill out of the app and toward Edge.

accessibility.note: The app is a very accessible default for Microsoft accounts, work accounts, push approvals and passkeys.

economical.note: Microsoft Authenticator is free to install and use for MFA workflows.

products.description: A convenient Microsoft-account authenticator and passkey app, strongest for Microsoft ecosystems but weaker on openness and cross-platform backup portability.

products.name: Authy

privacy.note: Authy offers encrypted cloud backups, but account recovery and setup are tied to phone-number identity and Twilio's hosted service.

openness.note: Authy is a proprietary Twilio authenticator app rather than open-source software.

portability.note: Authy's multi-device and backup model is convenient but keeps tokens inside Authy's hosted sync and recovery system.

respect.note: The app is useful for avoiding lockout, but the phone-number identity and Twilio account-recovery flow create more service dependence than local-first authenticators.

accessibility.note: Authy is easy to set up and supports encrypted backups and multiple mobile/tablet devices, but its desktop app reached end of life in 2024.

economical.note: Authy is free for end users.

products.description: A still-recognizable authenticator with convenient encrypted backups, but closed, phone-number-bound and less appealing after desktop support ended.

products.name: Yubico Authenticator

privacy.note: Yubico says OATH/TOTP secrets are stored and processed on the YubiKey secure element rather than on the phone or computer.

openness.note: Yubico publishes the current Authenticator code for desktop and Android under an Apache-2.0 license.

portability.note: The same YubiKey credentials can be used across desktop and mobile authenticator apps, but losing the key without backups can be disruptive.

respect.note: Hardware-backed TOTP avoids cloud-sync dependence and keeps secrets under user possession, at the cost of key management.

accessibility.note: Yubico Authenticator works across major desktop and mobile platforms, but requires a compatible YubiKey and more setup comfort.

economical.note: The app is free, but practical use requires buying and managing one or more compatible hardware security keys.

products.description: A hardware-backed authenticator for people willing to manage YubiKeys so TOTP secrets live on a physical key rather than in a phone cloud.

products.name: Cover Your Tracks

privacy.note: Cover Your Tracks tests how visible a browser is to trackers, including tracking protection and fingerprint uniqueness.

openness.note: EFF publishes the Cover Your Tracks code under the AGPL-3.0 license.

portability.note: The browser test runs from the web and can compare different browsers, devices and add-on setups without installing an app.

respect.note: EFF frames the tool as user education and research into tracker behavior rather than as a commercial profiling service.

accessibility.note: Users can run a browser test and read plain-language suggestions about tracker blocking and fingerprinting.

economical.note: Cover Your Tracks is free to use on the public web.

products.description: A free EFF browser-privacy test that teaches users what trackers can see and why fingerprinting is different from ordinary cookies.

products.name: Exodus Privacy

privacy.note: Exodus analyzes Android apps to list embedded trackers and risky permissions so users can see what is inside an app.

openness.note: Exodus publishes its privacy-auditing platform source code publicly.

portability.note: Reports are available on the web, and the Android app downloads reports from the Exodus platform for installed apps.

respect.note: Exodus is run by a French nonprofit and focuses on making app trackers visible rather than monetizing user behavior.

accessibility.note: The reports are useful but require users to search apps and interpret tracker and permission findings.

economical.note: The public report database and Android app are available without a subscription.

products.description: An open Android app-tracker report database that helps people learn which trackers and permissions are embedded in mobile apps.

products.name: Apple App Store

privacy.note: Apple requires App Store privacy details so users can see some data collection and tracking practices before downloading.

openness.note: The App Store is Apple's curated proprietary distribution channel, governed by Apple's review rules and platform policies.

portability.note: Purchases, subscriptions, reviews and update history are tied to Apple ID and Apple platforms, so moving outside the ecosystem is limited.

respect.note: Privacy labels and review rules are useful user protections, but distribution remains tightly gatekept by Apple.

accessibility.note: The App Store is the default app discovery, purchase and update path across iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch and Apple TV.

economical.note: The store is free to browse and includes many free apps, but paid apps, subscriptions and in-app purchases are central to the model.

products.description: The default Apple app marketplace: highly convenient and privacy-labeled, but closed, curated and strongly tied to Apple ID and Apple platforms.

products.name: Google Play Store

privacy.note: Google Play requires Data safety disclosures and Play Protect scans apps, but Play Protect and Play services collect device, app and security signals.

openness.note: Google Play is a proprietary Google marketplace even though Android can install apps from some other sources.

portability.note: Android permits apps from sources beyond Google Play, but Play purchases, reviews, licensing and updates stay within Google's marketplace.

respect.note: Play Protect improves safety and permission hygiene, but it can also send app details and device/app signals to Google for scanning.

accessibility.note: Google Play is the mainstream Android app store with broad device support, search, updates, payments and account recovery.

economical.note: The store is free to use and includes many free apps, alongside paid apps, subscriptions and in-app purchases.

products.description: The default Android marketplace: huge, convenient and protected by Play Protect, but deeply tied to Google accounts, telemetry and platform rules.

products.name: F-Droid

privacy.note: F-Droid foregrounds user freedom and labels anti-features such as tracking so users can avoid apps with unwanted behavior.

openness.note: F-Droid describes itself as the Android app distribution ecosystem for free and open-source mobile apps.

portability.note: Apps are distributed as Android packages outside a Google account model, though F-Droid is Android-specific.

respect.note: F-Droid's acceptance criteria and anti-feature labels are explicitly framed from the user's point of view.

accessibility.note: F-Droid is easy for privacy-curious Android users, but catalog coverage and sideloading setup are less familiar than Google Play.

economical.note: F-Droid apps and the store client are free to use, with the project supported by donations.

products.description: A values-first Android app store for free/open-source apps, with anti-feature warnings that make tracking and proprietary dependencies visible.

products.name: Aurora Store

privacy.note: Aurora Store reduces direct dependence on the Play Store app, but it still fetches apps from Google Play infrastructure.

openness.note: The Aurora Store project describes itself as an unofficial FOSS client to Google Play and publishes GPL-licensed source code.

portability.note: Aurora can help install Play-hosted apps without the official Play Store client, but the app catalog remains Google's catalog.

respect.note: As a community FOSS client, Aurora is more user-controlled than Google Play, with the caveat that it depends on an unofficial access path.

accessibility.note: It is powerful for Android users comfortable with sideloading, but less stable and official than using Google Play directly.

economical.note: Aurora Store is free/open-source software.

products.description: An unofficial open-source Google Play client for Android users who want Play catalog access with less direct Google-app dependence.

products.name: Obtainium

privacy.note: Obtainium gets Android app updates directly from release pages instead of using a centralized app-store account.

openness.note: Obtainium is GPL-licensed open-source software with public source code.

portability.note: It supports many app sources such as GitHub, GitLab, F-Droid, APKPure and direct APK links, but users must manage source choices carefully.

respect.note: The model favors direct upstream releases and user choice over a central app-store recommendation or advertising system.

accessibility.note: Obtainium is powerful, but it requires users to understand APK sources, release pages and update configuration.

economical.note: Obtainium is free open-source software.

products.description: A source-first Android updater for people who want apps from upstream releases rather than a single marketplace catalog.

products.name: APKMirror

privacy.note: APKMirror is a web APK repository rather than an account-based app store, but it remains a proprietary hosted download site.

openness.note: APKMirror publishes APK files and FAQs but is not an open-source distribution project.

portability.note: APK files can be installed outside Google Play, but users must handle compatibility, signatures and update tracking themselves.

respect.note: APKMirror says hosted APKs are signed with official release keys, which supports authenticity checks compared with random APK downloads.

accessibility.note: The site is easy for downloading known APKs, but sideloading and signature mismatch errors create friction for less technical users.

economical.note: APKMirror provides free APK downloads.

products.description: A popular Android APK download site, useful for version access and sideloading but not as open or governance-transparent as F-Droid.

products.name: Uptodown

privacy.note: Uptodown is a commercial app-download platform, so users trade easier open access for a proprietary hosted intermediary.

openness.note: Uptodown is not an open-source app-store project, though it promotes free access to a broad app catalog.

portability.note: Direct APK downloads and previous-version access make it more portable than locked platform stores.

respect.note: Uptodown says files undergo security checks using VirusTotal, but users still rely on its curation and hosting model.

accessibility.note: Uptodown is easy to use across platforms and does not require the official Google Play Store for Android app downloads.

economical.note: Uptodown provides free access to app downloads.

products.description: A broad third-party app download store with security scanning and easier APK access, but proprietary governance and a commercial web model.

products.name: Flathub

privacy.note: Flathub requires limited permissions and encourages portals and XDG standards, though individual app permissions still vary.

openness.note: Flathub is a community Linux app store with public source links and documentation.

portability.note: Flathub advertises apps for any Linux distribution through Flatpak, making Linux app distribution more portable.

respect.note: Its app-author requirements emphasize safe integration, stable releases, redistributable content and limited permissions.

accessibility.note: Flathub is easy for Linux users once Flatpak is set up, but it is still less familiar than phone app stores.

economical.note: Flathub is free to browse and install apps from, with optional developer support and donation pathways depending on the app.

products.description: The main Flatpak app store for Linux, making desktop apps easier to install across distributions while preserving more openness than proprietary stores.

products.name: Microsoft Store

privacy.note: Windows lets users manage many Microsoft Store app permissions, but desktop apps and broader Windows account data remain outside that narrow store model.

openness.note: The Microsoft Store is a proprietary Windows marketplace governed by Microsoft Store policies.

portability.note: Windows can install apps from outside the Store, but Store purchases, app identity and update flows stay tied to Microsoft's marketplace.

respect.note: Microsoft Store policies require privacy-policy access for apps that collect or transmit personal information, but the store remains a centralized commercial gatekeeper.

accessibility.note: The Store is integrated into Windows and offers an easy path for apps, games and updates.

economical.note: The Store includes free apps and paid products, with many installs available without an upfront store fee.

products.description: The Windows app marketplace: convenient and integrated, but proprietary and less central to Windows than app stores are on phones.

products.name: GitHub

privacy.note: GitHub's privacy statement covers account, content, usage, device, cookie, marketing, affiliate and AI-related processing.

openness.note: GitHub hosts open-source projects at massive scale, but the GitHub service itself is a proprietary Microsoft-owned platform.

portability.note: GitHub supports repository migration exports, while issues, pull requests, discussions, stars and network effects remain partly platform-bound.

respect.note: The privacy statement describes personalization, product improvement, AI and affiliate sharing, making GitHub less quiet than user-funded or self-hosted forges.

accessibility.note: GitHub is the most recognizable code forge for many developers, with broad collaboration, CI, package, issue and documentation workflows.

economical.note: GitHub pricing lists a free tier with unlimited public and private repositories, with paid Pro, Team and Enterprise tiers.

products.description: The default global software forge: extremely useful and affordable, but proprietary, Microsoft-owned, and hard to leave socially once a project's community lives there.

products.name: GitLab

privacy.note: GitLab can be used as hosted SaaS or self-managed, giving privacy-conscious teams a stronger control path than SaaS-only forges.

openness.note: GitLab describes the GitLab project as an open-source DevSecOps platform, while some product features sit in paid commercial tiers.

portability.note: GitLab file exports provide a portable package for project data, including repositories, issues, merge requests and comments.

respect.note: Self-managed GitLab offers infrastructure and data control, but GitLab.com remains a commercial SaaS with paid tiers and AI-era platform incentives.

accessibility.note: GitLab offers hosted, self-managed and dedicated deployment paths with integrated source control, CI/CD, security and planning tools.

economical.note: GitLab pricing includes a free tier and paid Premium and Ultimate tiers for broader team and enterprise features.

products.description: A broad code hosting and DevSecOps platform with a meaningful self-managed route, stronger portability than many SaaS defaults, and commercial tier complexity.

products.name: Codeberg

privacy.note: Codeberg describes itself as a privacy-friendly, non-commercial alternative to commercial software forges.

openness.note: Codeberg is operated by Codeberg e.V. around a Forgejo-based software forge for Free Software projects.

portability.note: Codeberg documents repository migration and is based on Forgejo, so projects keep the underlying Git repository portable.

respect.note: The service is run by a democratic non-profit association whose mission is to avoid dependence on commercial external or proprietary services.

accessibility.note: Codeberg is free to use, but it is focused on Free Software and has a smaller ecosystem than GitHub or GitLab.

economical.note: Codeberg's FAQ says a user account is free-as-in-beer and free-as-in-freedom under its terms of use.

products.description: A community-run, nonprofit Forgejo instance for Free Software projects, strong on openness and independence but smaller and more mission-bounded than the mainstream forges.

products.name: SourceHut

privacy.note: SourceHut states that it uses absolutely no tracking or advertising and that all features work without JavaScript.

openness.note: SourceHut describes the platform as 100% free and open-source software.

portability.note: SourceHut advertises the hut CLI for backing up all user data and moving to or from a self-hosted SourceHut instance.

respect.note: SourceHut explicitly rejects tracking, ads and AI features, and frames itself as user-funded free-software infrastructure.

accessibility.note: SourceHut supports Git, Mercurial, mailing lists, CI and ticketing, but its email-centered workflow is less familiar to many mainstream developers.

economical.note: SourceHut expects users who host projects to pay according to their means through equal-feature subscription tiers.

products.description: A deliberately minimal, user-funded software forge for people who prefer standards, email workflows, no tracking, and free-software infrastructure over mainstream polish.

products.name: Bitbucket

privacy.note: Atlassian's privacy policy governs Bitbucket Cloud and describes account, usage, device, cookie, analytics and marketing data processing.

openness.note: Bitbucket Cloud is a proprietary Atlassian product rather than an open-source or federated software forge.

portability.note: Bitbucket Cloud documents issue export/import and Git repositories remain clonable, but Jira integration, pipelines and team context are platform-bound.

respect.note: The product is tightly connected to Atlassian's AI, Jira and Teamwork Graph ecosystem, which is useful but commercially sticky.

accessibility.note: Bitbucket is strong for teams already using Jira, with built-in CI/CD, code review, governance and Atlassian integrations.

economical.note: Bitbucket pricing includes a free cloud plan for small teams and paid Standard and Premium plans.

products.description: A proprietary Atlassian forge that makes sense for Jira-centered teams, but is less open, less portable socially, and more commercially embedded than independent alternatives.

products.name: Gitea

privacy.note: Gitea is primarily self-hosted, so privacy depends on the operator's deployment, logs, backups and account policies.

openness.note: Gitea describes itself as a free self-hosted Git service under the MIT license.

portability.note: Gitea is Git-based and self-hostable, with repositories, issues and project features under the operator's own infrastructure.

respect.note: Self-hosted Gitea gives teams direct control over their forge rather than depending on an advertising or commercial SaaS platform.

accessibility.note: Gitea is lighter and familiar for GitHub-style workflows, but still requires hosting and administration for the self-managed route.

economical.note: The self-managed Gitea software is free, while managed cloud and enterprise options are paid.

products.description: A lightweight self-hosted Git forge for teams that want GitHub-like basics under their own control, with the usual responsibility of running the server well.

products.name: Forgejo

privacy.note: Forgejo focuses on security, scaling, federation and privacy, with self-hosting as the central model.

openness.note: Forgejo says it will always be Free and Open Source Software and is developed under the Codeberg e.V. umbrella.

portability.note: Forgejo is self-hosted Git forge software, allowing projects to run on their own instance or on public Forgejo instances.

respect.note: The project is backed by an inclusive community under a democratic non-profit organization rather than a commercial SaaS owner.

accessibility.note: Forgejo offers a familiar GitHub-like environment and aims for low maintenance, but users still need an instance or a public host such as Codeberg.

economical.note: Forgejo itself is free software; costs come from hosting, support, maintenance or donations rather than a required software license.

products.description: A community-governed free-software forge for self-hosting or public instances, especially strong for people who want Codeberg-like values on infrastructure they control.

products.name: Radicle

privacy.note: Radicle uses peer-to-peer replication, cryptographic identities and user-run nodes rather than a single controlling code-hosting provider.

openness.note: Radicle describes itself as an open-source, peer-to-peer code collaboration stack built on Git.

portability.note: Radicle stores social artifacts in Git, is local-first, and says users own their data for easier migration, backup and offline access.

respect.note: Radicle is designed to avoid reliance on third parties and central platform control over code collaboration.

accessibility.note: Radicle provides CLI, desktop and web interfaces, but its peer-to-peer workflow is still less familiar than mainstream hosted forges.

economical.note: Radicle can be installed and run directly by users, with costs mainly in hosting seed nodes or maintaining the workflow.

products.description: A peer-to-peer, local-first software forge for people who want code collaboration without a central host, trading mainstream convenience for sovereignty.

products.name: WordPress.org

privacy.note: Self-hosted WordPress can keep site data under the owner's chosen host, and core includes personal-data export tools, but privacy depends on the operator and plugins.

openness.note: WordPress.org describes WordPress as open-source software licensed under GPLv2 or later.

portability.note: WordPress documents a built-in export tool for posts, pages, comments, custom fields, terms, navigation menus and custom post types.

respect.note: The project frames itself around democratizing publishing and user freedoms rather than a proprietary hosted platform.

accessibility.note: WordPress says the basic software is designed to work with minimum setup, while deeper customization still takes hosting and maintenance skill.

economical.note: The WordPress software is free under the GPL, though users still pay for hosting, domains, themes, plugins or support as needed.

products.description: The open-source CMS route: excellent for ownership, portability and customization, but it asks the user to choose hosting and manage privacy, security and plugins responsibly.

products.name: WordPress.com

privacy.note: Automattic's privacy policy covers account, usage, transaction, device, cookie and hosted-content data across its services.

openness.note: WordPress.com is built around WordPress, but the hosted service, plans and managed platform features are Automattic-run.

portability.note: WordPress.com documents export tools for moving site content to another WordPress site or other platform.

respect.note: The hosted service preserves a real export path, but the privacy policy and plan structure reflect a broad commercial platform relationship.

accessibility.note: WordPress.com bundles hosting, editing, domains and support into hosted plans, making WordPress easier for non-technical users.

economical.note: WordPress.com pricing includes a free starting point and paid Personal, Premium, Business, Commerce and Enterprise-style paths.

products.description: A hosted, easier WordPress path with real export options and less server work, trading some sovereignty for managed convenience and plan complexity.

products.name: Ghost

privacy.note: Ghost Foundation's privacy policy says it does not sell personal data, while Ghost(Pro) still processes account, billing and hosted-site information.

openness.note: Ghost publishes its source code on GitHub under the MIT license and describes itself as independent technology for modern publishing.

portability.note: Ghost documents JSON and CSV exports for content, members, theme files and post analytics.

respect.note: Ghost(Pro) revenue funds the Ghost Foundation and the open-source project, aligning the hosted service with project maintenance.

accessibility.note: Ghost offers a polished managed service plus self-hosting, but it is still more publishing-focused and less all-purpose than broad website builders.

economical.note: Ghost(Pro) pricing starts with paid hosted plans, while the codebase can be self-hosted for users able to manage their own server.

products.description: A publishing-first platform for blogs, newsletters and memberships: strong ownership and export signals, especially for people comfortable with self-hosting or paying for Ghost(Pro).

products.name: Squarespace

privacy.note: Squarespace's privacy policy describes personal information collection, processing, sharing and user rights for its hosted platform.

openness.note: Squarespace is a proprietary hosted website builder rather than open-source or self-hostable software.

portability.note: Squarespace documents import and export for content, products and contacts, but this is not the same as exporting the full hosted builder experience.

respect.note: The service offers a clean hosted experience and some export paths, but site design, commerce tools and account workflows stay inside Squarespace.

accessibility.note: Squarespace bundles templates, hosting, commerce and site management for non-technical users who want a polished site quickly.

economical.note: Squarespace pricing is subscription-based after trial, with higher tiers needed for more business and commerce features.

products.description: A polished mainstream website builder for portfolios and small businesses, strong on convenience and design, weaker on openness and full-platform portability.

products.name: Wix

privacy.note: Wix's privacy policy describes personal information collection, use, sharing and rights for users of its services.

openness.note: Wix is a proprietary hosted website builder, not open-source or self-hostable software.

portability.note: Wix documents domain transfer and embedding options, but its official help does not present full static-code export as a normal portability path.

respect.note: Wix is very convenient, but its builder, apps and paid-site features keep finished sites closely tied to Wix hosting and account systems.

accessibility.note: Wix offers a broad visual builder, templates, AI and business features aimed at non-technical site creators.

economical.note: Wix offers a free starting path and multiple paid website and business plans, with custom domains tied to upgrades.

products.description: A highly accessible mainstream builder with a free entry point and many business tools, but one of the weaker choices for openness and leaving with your finished site intact.

products.name: Webflow

privacy.note: Webflow's privacy policy describes account, billing, platform-use, website-content, log, cookie and end-user technical data processing.

openness.note: Webflow is proprietary SaaS for visual website design, hosting, CMS and optimization rather than open-source builder software.

portability.note: Webflow documents code export to a ZIP file, while also noting exported code cannot be reimported into Webflow.

respect.note: Code export is a useful ownership signal, but CMS, hosting, collaboration, forms and optimization remain tied to Webflow plans.

accessibility.note: Webflow gives designers a powerful visual interface, but its professional design model has a steeper learning curve than simpler builders.

economical.note: Webflow offers a free starting point and paid site and workspace plans, with meaningful publishing features depending on paid tiers.

products.description: A professional no-code design platform with better static-code export than many builders, but still a proprietary SaaS workflow with plan and CMS lock-in.

products.name: Carrd

privacy.note: Carrd's privacy policy explains what personal information it collects, uses and shares for visitors, accounts and sites operated through the platform.

openness.note: Carrd is a proprietary hosted builder, with use governed by a service license rather than open-source software freedoms.

portability.note: Carrd supports publishing simple hosted sites and custom domains on paid plans, but its public docs emphasize hosted site operation rather than full code export.

respect.note: Carrd keeps the product narrow and inexpensive, but users still rely on a closed hosted builder for edits and publishing.

accessibility.note: Carrd is explicitly designed for simple, free, fully responsive one-page sites and is easy for non-technical pages.

economical.note: Carrd advertises a free basic path and low-cost Pro plans starting annually for custom domains and additional features.

products.description: A low-cost, very approachable builder for simple one-page sites, best when speed and price matter more than full ownership or complex migration.

products.name: Neocities

privacy.note: Neocities publishes a privacy policy for its service, while static sites expose only what creators intentionally publish.

openness.note: Neocities' backend source is published on GitHub, though the hosted community service itself is still a managed platform.

portability.note: Neocities hosts static HTML, CSS and JavaScript sites and supports tools such as a site editor, CLI, WebDAV and one-click backups.

respect.note: Neocities advertises free static web hosting with zero ads and frames the service around individual creativity on the web.

accessibility.note: The service makes static hosting approachable, but users still need more direct HTML/CSS comfort than drag-and-drop builders require.

economical.note: Neocities lists a free plan and a paid Supporter tier with more storage, bandwidth and features.

products.description: A zero-ad static-hosting community for the indie web: wonderfully portable and low-cost if you are comfortable making pages closer to the metal.

products.name: Plausible Analytics

privacy.note: Plausible says it uses no cookies, no persistent identifiers and no cross-site or cross-device tracking.

openness.note: Plausible publishes an open-source analytics repository and offers managed cloud or self-hosted community edition paths.

portability.note: Plausible documents dashboard CSV exports, stats API access and import paths for historical analytics data.

respect.note: The company says it is independent, bootstrapped and subscription-funded rather than surveillance-ad funded.

accessibility.note: Plausible emphasizes a simple one-page dashboard and lightweight script for site owners who do not want complex GA-style reporting.

economical.note: Hosted Plausible is paid after a trial, while self-hosting gives technically capable users a lower-cost route.

products.description: A simple, privacy-first Google Analytics alternative with an open-source/self-host route and paid hosted plans; strong when site owners need enough insight without tracking visitors across the web.

products.name: Matomo

privacy.note: Matomo says both cloud and on-premise hosting give website owners full data ownership and privacy compliance controls.

openness.note: Matomo On-Premise is described as free to download and open-source analytics that can be hosted on the user's own servers.

portability.note: Matomo On-Premise supports raw data access and can connect analytics data to warehouses or BI workflows.

respect.note: The platform frames the relationship as remaining between the website owner and visitor rather than outside analytics intermediaries looking in.

accessibility.note: Matomo offers cloud hosting for ease and on-premise hosting for control, but the deeper self-host route requires technical administration.

economical.note: The on-premise software is free to download, while Matomo Cloud and enterprise support are paid.

products.description: A mature analytics platform for people who want stronger ownership and self-hosting than mainstream analytics, with more complexity than the smallest privacy-first dashboards.

products.name: Simple Analytics

privacy.note: Simple Analytics says it works without cookies or personal data and is EU-hosted and compliant by design.

openness.note: Simple Analytics is a hosted analytics product with APIs and docs, not a self-hosted open-source analytics stack.

portability.note: The docs describe dashboard CSV export, a raw data Export API and APIs for aggregated stats and administration.

respect.note: The service is built around collecting analytics without cookies or personal data rather than increasing visitor profiling.

accessibility.note: The product emphasizes a one-page dashboard with no configuration and no consent banner for ordinary website traffic understanding.

economical.note: Simple Analytics is a paid hosted service starting at a monthly plan, so it is calmer than free ad-tech but not the cheapest option.

products.description: A polished hosted analytics product for people who want a no-cookie, no-personal-data dashboard and usable exports, trading openness and price for simplicity.

products.name: Fathom Analytics

privacy.note: Fathom says it anonymizes IP addresses and other visitor data without using cookies.

openness.note: Fathom is a proprietary hosted analytics service rather than an open-source or self-hostable analytics stack.

portability.note: Fathom documents custom CSV exports and API access for generating reports and controlling account entities.

respect.note: The product centers on cookie-free analytics and a paid subscription model rather than ad-tech profiling.

accessibility.note: Fathom focuses on simple site analytics with a lightweight script and dashboard that avoids GA-style complexity.

economical.note: Fathom is a paid hosted service, with pricing positioned for sites willing to pay for simpler privacy-first analytics.

products.description: A very approachable cookie-free analytics service with solid export/API support, best for people who want to pay for a calm hosted alternative instead of running analytics themselves.

products.name: Umami

privacy.note: Umami describes itself as a privacy-focused Google Analytics alternative that is cookie-free and can be self-hosted.

openness.note: The Umami repository describes the project as open source and lists the code under the MIT license.

portability.note: Umami Cloud documents CSV exports of collected analytics data, and the API returns data in JSON for self-hosted instances.

respect.note: Self-hosting and cookie-free measurement make Umami a strong fit for sites avoiding visitor profiling and ad-tech analytics.

accessibility.note: Umami is simple and fast, but self-hosting or choosing a smaller hosted analytics provider is less turnkey than using a default big-tech dashboard.

economical.note: The open-source self-host route is free software, while Umami Cloud uses hosted plans for users who want less administration.

products.description: A lean open-source analytics option for people who want self-hosting or a smaller hosted cloud, with more setup tradeoff than polished paid alternatives.

products.name: PostHog

privacy.note: PostHog's privacy policy covers hosted services and self-managed installations and says the company aims to minimize collected and shared personal information.

openness.note: PostHog's repository describes an all-in-one open-source product platform with web analytics, session replay, feature flags and more.

portability.note: PostHog documents real-time destinations, batch exports and migration guides for moving analytics data.

respect.note: The product can be self-hosted and open, but richer product analytics, replays and activation tooling can collect more behavioral data than simple web counters.

accessibility.note: PostHog Cloud is the recommended start path and bundles many tools for product teams, but it is more complex than single-purpose web analytics.

economical.note: PostHog pricing starts at zero with a generous monthly free tier and usage-based billing after free limits.

products.description: A powerful open-source product analytics stack for teams that need funnels, events and experiments; far more controllable than many SaaS suites, but heavier and more behavior-data-oriented than simple web analytics.

products.name: Cloudflare Web Analytics

privacy.note: Cloudflare says Web Analytics uses no cookies or localStorage and does not fingerprint individuals via IP, user agent or other data.

openness.note: Cloudflare Web Analytics is a hosted Cloudflare product rather than open-source or self-hostable analytics software.

portability.note: The product is centered on Cloudflare's dashboard and lightweight beacon, so analytics context remains more service-bound than file/API-first tools.

respect.note: Cloudflare frames the product as non-invasive essential analytics that respects visitor privacy.

accessibility.note: Cloudflare says users can add a lightweight JavaScript beacon and view essential stats from a dashboard quickly.

economical.note: Cloudflare advertises Web Analytics as free, making it one of the lowest-cost privacy-friendlier analytics options.

products.description: A free, easy Cloudflare-hosted analytics layer that avoids cookies and fingerprinting, but keeps the analytics workflow tied to a large infrastructure provider.

products.name: Google Analytics

privacy.note: Google Analytics offers privacy controls, but it still collects event-based website/app analytics inside Google's broader measurement and advertising ecosystem.

openness.note: Google Analytics is a proprietary Google Marketing Platform service rather than open-source or self-hostable analytics software.

portability.note: GA4 can export raw event data to BigQuery, which improves data access for teams able to use Google's cloud data tooling.

respect.note: Google documents controls to limit analytics data use for advertising personalization, but those controls exist because analytics can connect to ad use cases.

accessibility.note: Google Analytics is free of charge and deeply integrated into common marketing workflows, making it the easiest default for many site owners.

economical.note: Google says Analytics tools are available free of charge for understanding customer journeys and marketing return.

products.description: The mainstream analytics floor: free, powerful and familiar, with real BigQuery export for teams, but weaker for people trying to minimize Google dependence and advertising-adjacent measurement.

products.name: Substack

privacy.note: Substack's privacy policy describes collection, use and sharing of personal information across its site and services.

openness.note: Substack is a proprietary hosted publishing network governed by its service terms rather than open-source software freedoms.

portability.note: Substack documents exports for posts, subscriber lists and related statistics from publication settings.

respect.note: The creator business model is transparent, but paid publications still give Substack a 10% platform fee on transactions.

accessibility.note: Publishing is free on Substack regardless of subscriber count, making it easy for non-technical writers to start.

economical.note: Free publications cost nothing to run, while paid publications pay Substack plus payment-processing fees.

products.description: A very accessible newsletter and publishing default with real export paths, but also a closed network and a platform fee on paid-reader relationships.

products.name: Medium

privacy.note: Medium's privacy policy describes collection, sharing, third-party embeds and vendor processing, including content and account data.

openness.note: Medium is proprietary SaaS; its terms give users content ownership but not software or platform portability rights.

portability.note: Medium lets users export personal data and stories as HTML files in a ZIP archive.

respect.note: Medium's model supports writers through membership, but the platform still controls distribution, paywalling and platform surfaces.

accessibility.note: Medium makes writing and reading widely accessible through a mainstream hosted editor and free sign-up path.

economical.note: Readers can start free and pay for unlimited member access; writers do not need to run their own website to publish.

products.description: A polished, mainstream place to publish and read essays, with easy authoring and account export but limited control over distribution, data use and the platform layer.

products.name: beehiiv

privacy.note: beehiiv's privacy policy details broad categories of personal information collected for accounts, purchases, support and service use.

openness.note: beehiiv is a proprietary hosted newsletter, website, analytics and monetization platform rather than open-source publishing software.

portability.note: beehiiv has import tools for Substack, WordPress, Ghost and Mailchimp, while direct outbound portability is less prominent in public docs.

respect.note: The product emphasizes growth, analytics, ad network and AI features, which is useful for publishers but less calm than simpler newsletter tools.

accessibility.note: beehiiv's free Launch plan includes newsletters, website, podcast, analytics, custom domains and a recommendation network up to 2,500 subscribers.

economical.note: beehiiv advertises a free Launch plan and 0% take rate on paid subscriptions on paid tiers, with Stripe fees still applying.

products.description: A powerful newsletter-growth suite with a generous free tier and strong monetization terms, but it is built around proprietary analytics, growth and ad-network tooling.

products.name: Buttondown

privacy.note: Buttondown describes itself as privacy-first and says it avoids using customer or subscriber data as a revenue stream.

openness.note: Buttondown is a proprietary hosted product, though it publishes detailed docs, API references and migration guidance.

portability.note: Buttondown documents CSV exports for subscriber data and separate exports for emails, events, surveys and API-request data.

respect.note: Buttondown states that paid newsletter creators keep revenue without extra platform fees from Buttondown.

accessibility.note: Buttondown offers a focused newsletter workflow with hosted archives, markdown/rich text editing and migration docs.

economical.note: Buttondown's pricing page lists a free path for the first 100 subscribers and paid add-ons for advanced features.

products.description: A smaller, calmer newsletter tool that is not open source, but scores well for privacy posture, data export and avoiding a take from paid subscriptions.

products.name: Write.as

privacy.note: Write.as states that privacy is central to the service and says it minimizes and does not share user data.

openness.note: Write.as is the flagship hosted instance of WriteFreely, which is free AGPL open-source publishing software.

portability.note: Write.as support discussions document export options for posts as TXT, CSV or JSON, including Markdown-formatted text files.

respect.note: WriteFreely frames the platform around distraction-free publishing without feeds, alerts or social-media engagement loops.

accessibility.note: Write.as emphasizes simple writing and publishing, including Markdown and a clean hosted editor.

economical.note: Write.as pricing lists simple paid publishing starting at a monthly plan rather than a broad free hosted tier.

products.description: A minimal, privacy-forward writing host backed by open-source WriteFreely, best for people who want a quiet blog more than a growth machine.

products.name: Micro.blog

privacy.note: Micro.blog says it has no ads, does not sell data and collects only enough information to run the service.

openness.note: Micro.blog supports open-web flows such as personal domains, RSS/JSON feeds and ActivityPub interoperability with Mastodon.

portability.note: Micro.blog documents export options including Markdown, WordPress format, Blog Archive Format and Internet Archive backup support.

respect.note: Micro.blog explicitly avoids ads, user tracking and algorithmic main timelines in favor of personal-domain publishing.

accessibility.note: Micro.blog is approachable for hosted blogging but assumes some comfort with feeds, domains and indie-web concepts.

economical.note: Micro.blog pricing lists paid annual plans for hosted microblogs, premium features and family use.

products.description: A paid indie-web service for owning a blog and social presence, strong on export, no ads and open protocols, with a higher learning curve than mainstream publishers.

products.name: Tumblr

privacy.note: Tumblr's privacy policy describes personal-data processing and says blog export and privacy-data download options exist.

openness.note: Tumblr is a proprietary hosted social-blogging platform, not open-source publishing software.

portability.note: Tumblr documents full blog export as a ZIP backup, with primary and secondary blogs exported separately.

respect.note: Tumblr offers real blog export, but its privacy policy also describes platform data processing and social-product personalization.

accessibility.note: Tumblr remains a low-friction hosted social blog for text, images, reblogs and community publishing.

economical.note: Tumblr is broadly usable as a free hosted publishing platform, with account and blog controls handled through the web product.

products.description: A familiar social-blogging floor: easy, cheap and exportable, but proprietary and more platform-shaped than calm ownership-first publishing.

products.name: Blogger

privacy.note: Blogger is covered by Google's privacy policy, which describes broad Google data collection, controls, export and deletion.

openness.note: Blogger is a proprietary Google-hosted blogging service, though it exposes feeds, templates and an API.

portability.note: Google documents Blogger backup through Google Takeout, theme backup and import of feed.atom or XML files.

respect.note: Blogger's official page highlights AdSense monetization, built-in analytics and optional Google Analytics integration.

accessibility.note: Blogger offers a simple hosted blog builder with templates, blogspot.com domains and custom-domain support.

economical.note: Blogger provides hosted blogspot.com publishing without requiring users to run their own hosting stack.

products.description: A still-useful free Google blogging floor with real backup/import paths, but weaker fit for people trying to minimize Google dependence, analytics and ad infrastructure.

products.name: Feedly

privacy.note: Feedly says users should own and control their personal information, but its privacy policy still describes account/contact data, visitor data, service analytics and marketing communications.

openness.note: Feedly is a proprietary hosted news reader, even though it is built around open RSS feeds.

portability.note: Feedly documents OPML feed export, but notes that OPML export does not include Boards, Read Later articles, AI Feeds or Reddit feeds.

respect.note: Feedly helps people follow chosen sources outside social feeds, but the product is increasingly tied to AI and business-intelligence features.

accessibility.note: Feedly provides a mainstream web and mobile reading experience for RSS, newsletters and saved articles.

economical.note: Feedly offers Free, Pro, Pro+, and Enterprise plans, with the free tier intended for basic reading needs.

products.description: Mainstream RSS and news-reading floor: easy to use and widely recognized, but proprietary and only partly portable beyond feed subscriptions.

products.name: Inoreader

privacy.note: Inoreader's privacy policy says it does not transfer personal data outside the EEA and uses access controls for staff and partners with a business need.

openness.note: Inoreader is a proprietary hosted reader and monitoring service, though it supports open feed standards such as RSS and OPML.

portability.note: Inoreader describes OPML import and export as integral to reader portability and switching without lock-in.

respect.note: Inoreader supports user-chosen feeds, newsletters, filters and monitoring rather than a single algorithmic social feed.

accessibility.note: The hosted product covers RSS feeds, saved web pages, newsletters, filters, rules and social/web feeds for nontechnical users.

economical.note: Inoreader's pricing page lists a Pro plan at $7.50/month when billed annually, with higher custom plans for heavier use.

products.description: Power-user hosted RSS reader with strong filtering and monitoring features, good feed portability, and the usual proprietary-hosted-service tradeoffs.

products.name: NewsBlur

privacy.note: NewsBlur's privacy policy says email addresses are not sold, read-state is stored for syncing, aggregate stats are collected, and personal information is not sold or given to outside parties except as needed for functionality.

openness.note: NewsBlur is open source and can be self-hosted from the public repository.

portability.note: NewsBlur supports OPML import, and its public repo supports running a self-hosted instance for fuller data control.

respect.note: NewsBlur is built around chosen feeds, training, saved stories and optional self-hosting rather than advertising-driven social feed capture.

accessibility.note: NewsBlur offers web, iOS and Android apps, but the open-source and training model is more complex than simple mainstream readers.

economical.note: NewsBlur lists a free tier, a 30-day premium trial, and paid plans starting at $36/year.

products.description: Open-source RSS reader with hosted and self-hosted paths, good data-control upside, and more complexity than the easiest mainstream readers.

products.name: Feedbin

privacy.note: Feedbin's privacy policy says it is private by design, has no ads or tracking scripts, and uses feed/read/starred data to provide the service.

openness.note: Feedbin's source is public under the MIT license, though the project says it does not recommend running the full production stack casually.

portability.note: Feedbin supports OPML import/export for moving subscriptions between RSS readers.

respect.note: Feedbin is a paid reader for RSS, newsletters, podcasts and YouTube, with no advertising-tracking business model.

accessibility.note: Feedbin provides a polished hosted web reader and APIs for client apps, but it is paid after the trial.

economical.note: Feedbin lists a 30-day free trial followed by $7/month or $70/year.

products.description: Independent paid RSS reader with no-ad privacy posture and public source code, best for people who will pay for a quiet hosted reading service.

products.name: FreshRSS

privacy.note: FreshRSS can be self-hosted, so feed subscriptions and reading state can live on infrastructure the user controls.

openness.note: FreshRSS is free software under AGPL-3.0 with public source code.

portability.note: FreshRSS supports APIs for clients and can reshare selected articles by HTML, RSS and OPML.

respect.note: FreshRSS is community-friendly free software for chosen feeds rather than a hosted advertising or algorithmic feed product.

accessibility.note: FreshRSS offers demos and existing servers, but the strongest privacy/control path requires hosting and maintenance.

economical.note: FreshRSS is free and self-hostable, though users still need their own hosting, updates and backup discipline.

products.description: Self-hosted RSS aggregator for people who want feed independence and control, with the usual maintenance cost of running a small service.

products.name: Miniflux

privacy.note: Miniflux says it removes pixel trackers and tracking parameters, uses a media proxy, does not forward referrers, and has no telemetry or advertising.

openness.note: Miniflux is a free and open-source project distributed under the Apache 2.0 License.

portability.note: Miniflux is self-hosted and standards-based, with a simple feed-reader role rather than a proprietary discovery platform.

respect.note: The project is deliberately minimal, self-hosted and free from telemetry and advertising.

accessibility.note: Miniflux is lightweight and simple for technical users, but setup still expects server or package/Docker comfort.

economical.note: Miniflux is free open-source software; the main cost is whatever infrastructure the user runs it on.

products.description: Minimal, privacy-conscious self-hosted RSS reader for technically comfortable users who want quiet feeds without telemetry or ads.

products.name: NetNewsWire

privacy.note: NetNewsWire can download feeds directly and avoids routing all reading through a hosted proprietary reader account by default.

openness.note: NetNewsWire is a free and open-source feed reader for macOS and iOS, with public source code under the MIT license.

portability.note: NetNewsWire supports RSS, Atom, JSON Feed and RSS-in-JSON, and imports/exports OPML feed lists.

respect.note: NetNewsWire explicitly positions RSS as a way to read chosen sources instead of relying on big-tech social algorithms.

accessibility.note: The app is fast and polished on Mac, iPhone and iPad, but it is limited to Apple's platforms.

economical.note: NetNewsWire is free software and the repository explicitly says users should not send money to support it.

products.description: Free open-source RSS reader for Apple devices, strong for algorithm escape and local control but not useful outside the Apple ecosystem.

products.name: Apple Podcasts

privacy.note: Apple says podcast listening and interaction data is collected for improvement and personalization, but is not associated with the Apple Account.

openness.note: Apple Podcasts participates in the public podcast directory/RSS ecosystem, but the client and account sync are proprietary Apple services.

portability.note: Apple highlights syncing shows across Apple devices, but this is ecosystem sync rather than a broad export-first workflow.

respect.note: Apple's privacy notice says the service is designed to let users choose what they share, while still using recommendations and personalization.

accessibility.note: Apple Podcasts is bundled into Apple's device ecosystem and supports offline playback, charts, categories, subscriptions, and video/audio playback.

economical.note: The Apple Podcasts app is free to use, though individual shows and subscriptions may charge separately.

products.description: The default podcast app for Apple users: very accessible and relatively restrained for a platform service, but closed and most convenient inside Apple's ecosystem.

products.name: Spotify Podcasts

privacy.note: Spotify's privacy policy covers extensive account, usage, and personalization data processing across the Spotify service.

openness.note: Spotify supports many podcasts, but listening happens inside a closed platform with proprietary recommendation, ad, and account systems.

portability.note: Spotify provides personal-data downloads, but subscriptions and listening habits are not an open OPML-first podcast library workflow.

respect.note: Spotify's podcast experience is embedded in a personalized, ad-supported media platform rather than a neutral RSS client.

accessibility.note: Spotify offers free podcast listening across mobile, tablet, and desktop apps with search, browse, and playback features.

economical.note: Spotify's app offers podcast listening on the free tier, with Premium mainly changing music and offline/listening controls.

products.description: Huge and easy podcast discovery inside Spotify's media platform, useful for convenience but weak for privacy, openness, and escaping recommendation-driven listening.

products.name: YouTube Music Podcasts

privacy.note: YouTube Music podcast listening is governed by Google's privacy policy and Google account data practices.

openness.note: YouTube Music supports podcasts and RSS delivery for creators, but the listener experience remains inside Google's closed YouTube platform.

portability.note: Google Takeout supports exports of Google data, but YouTube Music podcast libraries are not a simple OPML-first podcast-client workflow.

respect.note: The Explore and Library podcast features sit inside YouTube Music's recommendation and Google-account media environment.

accessibility.note: YouTube Music exposes podcasts through Explore and Library tabs across Google-supported platforms.

economical.note: Podcast listening is available through YouTube Music without requiring a paid podcast-client subscription.

products.description: Google's replacement path for mainstream podcast listening, strongest on reach and weak when the priority is a quiet, portable, open podcast library.

products.name: Pocket Casts

privacy.note: Pocket Casts publishes a detailed privacy policy for app and site data, including account and listening-related service data.

openness.note: Pocket Casts publishes open-source Android and iOS mobile app repositories under the Automattic organization.

portability.note: Pocket Casts supports OPML export so followed podcasts can be moved between podcast applications.

respect.note: Pocket Casts remains a podcast-first client with RSS/OPML portability, though sync and discovery still run through a hosted account service.

accessibility.note: Pocket Casts is available across mobile, web, desktop, wearables, speakers, and car integrations.

economical.note: Pocket Casts is available free, with optional Plus and Patron plans for extra features.

products.description: A polished podcast client with strong cross-platform convenience and OPML portability; more open than most mainstream clients, but still partly account/cloud based.

products.name: AntennaPod

privacy.note: AntennaPod says it is built by volunteers without commercial interest and designed to respect privacy while giving users control.

openness.note: AntennaPod is an open-source podcast manager for Android, with public code on GitHub.

portability.note: AntennaPod supports RSS/Atom feeds and OPML import/export for moving subscriptions between podcast apps.

respect.note: AntennaPod says the app itself contains no ads and that publisher ads in media files remain with publishers.

accessibility.note: AntennaPod is a strong Android client, but official publishing and support are limited compared with big cross-platform services.

economical.note: AntennaPod is completely free and volunteer-built.

products.description: The privacy/open-source benchmark for Android podcast listening: local, ad-free, RSS-native and portable, with the tradeoff that it is not a full Apple/web ecosystem.

products.name: Overcast

privacy.note: Overcast's privacy policy says it stores podcast, episode, and listening activity for sync, and collects aggregate popularity/activity stats.

openness.note: Overcast is proprietary, but it works with the open standard world of public podcast RSS feeds rather than requiring separate distribution terms.

portability.note: Overcast's podcaster information emphasizes standard RSS feed handling and direct downloads from publishers' servers.

respect.note: The App Store listing says Overcast has no third-party analytics, ad services, or tracking code, though it is funded by podcast-promo ads.

accessibility.note: Overcast supports iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, CarPlay, offline playback, smart playlists, and enhanced playback features.

economical.note: Most Overcast features are free, with an optional Premium subscription for hiding ads and supporting the app.

products.description: A strong independent Apple podcast client: less extractive than platform feeds and RSS-friendly, but closed-source and Apple-ecosystem focused.

products.name: Podcast Addict

privacy.note: Podcast Addict says it does not collect personal information, while feed URLs and listening data can be collected anonymously unless private-feed settings are used.

openness.note: Podcast Addict is a proprietary Android app, but it supports open podcast feeds and OPML migration.

portability.note: Podcast Addict documents OPML import for moving subscriptions from another podcast app.

respect.note: The app is ad-supported, and Podcast Addict says personalized-ad consents are disabled by default in its GDPR consent flow.

accessibility.note: Podcast Addict is a powerful Android-focused podcast player with broad subscription and playback features.

economical.note: Podcast Addict says the full-featured app has long been free and ad-supported, with Premium available for support/ad removal.

products.description: Feature-heavy Android podcast client with good RSS/OPML flexibility; better than platform defaults for portability, but still proprietary and ad-supported unless paid.

products.name: Castbox

privacy.note: Castbox's privacy policy describes account/data deletion rights and data processing for its podcast services.

openness.note: Castbox is a proprietary podcast app and directory rather than an open-source podcast client.

portability.note: Castbox documents OPML import for bringing subscriptions from other podcast apps.

respect.note: Castbox is free and broad, but the service uses personalized recommendations and app-level data practices.

accessibility.note: Castbox advertises broad availability across Android, iPhone, Alexa, Google Home, CarPlay, and Android Auto.

economical.note: Castbox positions itself as a free podcast app for streaming and downloading podcasts.

products.description: A very accessible free podcast app with broad device reach; useful as a mainstream option but weaker for privacy and open-source values.

products.name: Podbean

privacy.note: Podbean's privacy policy says it collects podcast-consumption data for analytics, advertising measurement, and service improvement.

openness.note: Podbean is a proprietary podcast app and hosting platform, not an open-source client.

portability.note: Podbean's hosting pricing pages emphasize RSS migration/import for podcasters, while listener-app portability is less central than in OPML-first clients.

respect.note: Podbean's app promotes personalized recommendations and operates inside an analytics/advertising-supported podcast platform.

accessibility.note: Podbean markets its app as a cross-device podcast player with search, downloads, speed controls, volume boost, and playlists.

economical.note: The listener app is positioned as free to download and use for podcast listening.

products.description: Convenient podcast listening tied to a broader podcast hosting and analytics platform, with good reach but lower privacy and openness than RSS-first clients.

products.name: Podverse

privacy.note: Podverse says it will never sell or share private user data and will not insert ads next to podcast content without podcaster permission.

openness.note: Podverse describes itself as a FOSS podcast manager for iOS, Android, F-Droid, and web.

portability.note: Podverse supports custom RSS feeds, Podcasting 2.0 features, and cross-platform sync for premium accounts.

respect.note: Podverse is built around open podcast files hosted by publishers rather than rehosting podcast audio/video itself.

accessibility.note: Podverse is available for Android, F-Droid, iOS, and the web, with Podcasting 2.0 features such as chapters, transcripts, and comments.

economical.note: Podverse has a free tier and a paid Premium membership for server-backed sync and creation features.

products.description: A FOSS podcast app for people who care about open podcasting, RSS, and Podcasting 2.0 features, with some sync and social features behind Premium.

products.name: gPodder

privacy.note: gPodder is a local desktop podcast client, with optional gpodder.net sync rather than a mandatory centralized listening account.

openness.note: gPodder describes itself as a simple open-source podcast client with a mature codebase.

portability.note: gPodder supports podcast subscriptions and optional gpodder.net synchronization across devices.

respect.note: The project is a focused media aggregator/podcast client rather than an ad-driven discovery platform.

accessibility.note: gPodder is mature and desktop-oriented, but less polished for mainstream phone-first podcast listening.

economical.note: The gPodder repository is GPL-licensed free software.

products.description: A mature open-source desktop podcast client: excellent for local control and low-surveillance listening, less convenient for phone-first mainstream use.

products.name: Kasts

privacy.note: Kasts is a KDE podcast client with local app use and optional sync paths rather than a mandatory commercial listening account.

openness.note: Kasts is developed in the open under KDE, with a public GitHub mirror for the source code.

portability.note: Kasts supports playback-position sync through gpodder.net or gpodder-nextcloud.

respect.note: Kasts is a focused podcast application in KDE's free-software ecosystem rather than an ad or recommendation platform.

accessibility.note: Kasts is convergent across desktop and mobile and has Android/Windows availability, but remains more niche than mainstream podcast apps.

economical.note: Kasts is distributed as a KDE free-software application.

products.description: A KDE/free-software podcast client for people who want open local listening and optional open sync, with a more technical/niche audience than the big apps.

products.name: wallabag

privacy.note: Self-hosting wallabag gives users control over saved links, tags and reading archives on an instance they manage.

openness.note: wallabag is free and open-source read-it-later software that can be installed on a user's own server.

portability.note: wallabag.it highlights export-anytime portability, and self-hosted wallabag supports imports, apps, browser extensions, RSS-reader and e-reader workflows.

respect.note: wallabag is designed around saving articles without giving up control of the reading archive, with both self-hosted and hosted paths.

accessibility.note: People can self-host wallabag or use the hosted wallabag.it service if they do not want to maintain a server.

economical.note: Self-hosting is free software, while wallabag.it lists hosted plans from EUR 11/year after a 14-day trial.

products.description: Open-source read-it-later app for people who want a controlled article archive, with either self-hosted ownership or low-cost hosted convenience.

products.name: Instapaper

privacy.note: Instapaper is a proprietary hosted reading account; its privacy policy covers collection, use and disclosure of user information.

openness.note: Instapaper is a proprietary hosted service, though it provides developer APIs.

portability.note: Instapaper documents account export as CSV and article download as PDF, ePub or RSS.

respect.note: Instapaper is focused on saving and reading articles without a social timeline, but permanent archive and advanced reading tools are paid features.

accessibility.note: Instapaper syncs saved articles and videos across web, iOS, Android and e-readers, including offline reading.

economical.note: Instapaper offers a free tier, with Premium listed at $5.99/month or $59.99/year.

products.description: Long-running mainstream read-it-later app: very accessible and calmer than social feeds, but closed and less values-aligned than open or self-hosted readers.

products.name: Raindrop.io

privacy.note: Raindrop.io says bookmarks, files and personal data are private by default, with no ads, no tracking and no selling of user data.

openness.note: Raindrop.io says every app is open source on GitHub, while the hosted cloud service itself remains a proprietary account service.

portability.note: Raindrop.io documents full-account, collection and selected-item export in HTML, CSV and TXT formats.

respect.note: Raindrop.io says it is independent and subscription-funded, with no advertising, data mining or selling user data.

accessibility.note: Raindrop.io offers browser extensions plus Windows, Mac, iPad, iPhone and Android apps.

economical.note: Raindrop.io's limits page says the free plan has unlimited bookmarks, collections and sync devices, with Pro unlocking extras.

products.description: Cross-platform bookmark and web-archive manager with strong export and no-ad posture, but still centered on a hosted cloud account.

products.name: Readwise Reader

privacy.note: Readwise's privacy policy says it uses personal information to provide the service and may share data with service providers for hosting, analytics, email, payments and related operations.

openness.note: Readwise Reader is a proprietary hosted reading and highlighting service.

portability.note: Readwise highlights automatic export of enriched highlights to tools such as Notion, Obsidian and Evernote.

respect.note: Reader is built around intentional reading, highlighting and review rather than social-feed engagement, but it remains a paid proprietary workflow hub.

accessibility.note: Reader is powerful for heavy readers, researchers and note-takers, but its workflow and subscription make it less casual than simple save-for-later apps.

economical.note: Readwise offers a 30-day free trial, with the Full plan listed at $9.99/month when billed annually.

products.description: Premium reading and highlighting hub for serious readers, strong on workflow/export integrations but expensive and closed compared with simpler reader tools.

products.name: Apple Screen Time

privacy.note: Apple's platform security guide says Screen Time protects the privacy and security of usage data gathered and shared between Apple devices.

openness.note: Screen Time is a proprietary Apple operating-system feature rather than open-source or cross-platform software.

portability.note: Screen Time works across Apple devices, but its controls and usage history are tied to Apple's platform rather than portable to other ecosystems.

respect.note: Screen Time provides built-in usage summaries, app limits, downtime and content controls without requiring a separate attention-economy app.

accessibility.note: Screen Time is integrated into iPhone, iPad and Mac settings, so many users can try app limits and downtime without installing anything.

economical.note: Screen Time is included with supported Apple devices and does not require a separate subscription.

products.description: The sensible Apple-device first step for app limits and downtime: private enough, free and accessible, but locked to Apple's ecosystem.

products.name: Android Digital Wellbeing

privacy.note: Digital Wellbeing shows app, website, unlock and notification usage inside Android, while Google services are still governed by Google's broader privacy policy.

openness.note: Digital Wellbeing is a Google Android app/feature rather than an independent open-source blocker.

portability.note: Digital Wellbeing is useful on Android devices but does not provide a portable cross-platform screen-time system.

respect.note: Android's built-in tools let users inspect screen time, app opens, notifications, app timers and bedtime/focus settings without buying another product.

accessibility.note: Digital Wellbeing is available through Android settings and the Google Play app listing for many Android users.

economical.note: Digital Wellbeing is included with supported Android devices and does not require a separate purchase.

products.description: The Android built-in floor for checking and limiting screen habits, convenient and free but embedded in Google's mobile ecosystem.

products.name: Freedom

privacy.note: Freedom's privacy policy describes collection and use of personal information for account, product, billing, support and service-operation purposes.

openness.note: Freedom is proprietary commercial blocker software, not open-source or self-hostable.

portability.note: Freedom syncs blocking sessions across Mac, Windows, iOS, Android and Chrome, giving it stronger cross-device coverage than built-in phone controls.

respect.note: Freedom says it avoids dopamine-triggering streaks, points, leaderboards and rewards, and designs features to reduce distractions rather than create app dependency.

accessibility.note: Freedom covers computers, phones and tablets with scheduled focus sessions and app/website blocking, though setup is broader than built-in controls.

economical.note: Freedom's premium page describes paid plans for cross-platform blocking, with the App Store listing a 7-day trial and $39.99/year US subscription pricing.

products.description: Polished cross-platform blocker for people who need schedules across devices, with a good anti-engagement stance but paid proprietary tradeoffs.

products.name: Cold Turkey Blocker

privacy.note: Cold Turkey publishes a privacy policy for its blocker products and does not present itself as an ad-funded service.

openness.note: Cold Turkey Blocker is proprietary desktop software rather than an open-source blocker.

portability.note: Cold Turkey pricing says one purchase can be used on all computers the purchaser personally uses, but it is still primarily a desktop blocker.

respect.note: Cold Turkey focuses on hard-to-bypass blocking for websites, apps, games, searches and even the entire internet, which can help users honor pre-set intentions.

accessibility.note: Cold Turkey is simple to set up for desktop blocking, but its strict lock mode can be unforgiving for users who need flexible exceptions.

economical.note: Cold Turkey offers a free blocker and a paid Pro upgrade with a free 7-day trial and one purchase for the user's personal computers.

products.description: Strict desktop blocker for people who want friction that is genuinely hard to bypass, with less mobile breadth and less openness than community tools.

products.name: one sec

privacy.note: one sec says it is privacy-first and that data remains offline by default, with partner processing only for optional features such as support, subscription purchase or iCloud sync.

openness.note: one sec is proprietary app software rather than an open-source blocker.

portability.note: one sec is available on major mobile platforms and describes app and website interventions, but it remains an app-specific workflow rather than a portable standard.

respect.note: one sec adds a pause before distracting apps instead of simply blocking everything, which supports reflection rather than punishment.

accessibility.note: The app is designed for everyday app-opening friction, making it approachable for users who dislike strict all-or-nothing blockers.

economical.note: one sec uses an app subscription model for advanced/cross-platform use while keeping basic app-store access available.

products.description: A softer screen-time tool that adds mindful friction before distracting apps, strong on autonomy and privacy claims but still proprietary.

products.name: Opal

privacy.note: Opal says iOS Screen Time data and detailed Android usage data remain on-device, while the service still has account/community/subscription surfaces.

openness.note: Opal is a proprietary commercial app and community product rather than open-source screen-time software.

portability.note: Opal is available across mobile and desktop contexts, but its focus sessions, analytics, rewards and community features are tied to the Opal account/product.
