respect.note: Opal helps users block apps and websites, but its focus score, rewards, community and leaderboard framing make it more app-shaped than simpler blockers.

accessibility.note: Opal offers a polished mainstream focus app for iPhone, Mac and Android with app blocking, real-time feedback and recurring sessions.

economical.note: Opal offers free access and paid Pro plans, but its own pricing page frames the product as a subscription service for full use.

products.description: Polished mainstream screen-time app with strong blocking UX, but a more expensive and gamified proprietary model than built-in or open-source options.

products.name: SelfControl

privacy.note: SelfControl is a local Mac app for blocking access to selected websites or mail servers, without a hosted account model.

openness.note: SelfControl is free and open-source software under the GNU GPL with public source code.

portability.note: SelfControl is macOS-only, so its excellent local-control model does not carry across Windows, Android or iOS.

respect.note: SelfControl's timer cannot be undone by restarting the computer or deleting the application, which can support serious precommitment without an engagement layer.

accessibility.note: The app is simple but blunt and Mac-only, with less hand-holding than modern subscription focus apps.

economical.note: SelfControl is free open-source software for macOS.

products.description: Free open-source Mac blocker for serious website precommitment, excellent if you want a local blunt instrument and poor if you need mobile or cross-platform coverage.

products.name: LeechBlock NG

privacy.note: LeechBlock NG is an open-source browser extension rather than a hosted account service, though users still grant browser permissions for blocking to work.

openness.note: LeechBlock NG's source is public under the MPL-2.0 license.

portability.note: LeechBlock NG is available as a browser extension, including Firefox add-on distribution, but its scope is browser-site blocking rather than full-device control.

respect.note: LeechBlock NG lets users define which time-wasting sites to block and when, without subscriptions, rewards or social accountability layers.

accessibility.note: The browser-extension model is easier than self-hosting and harder than built-in phone controls; it works best for web distractions.

economical.note: LeechBlock NG is a free productivity browser extension.

products.description: Free open-source browser blocker for web distractions, strong on transparency and cost but narrower than whole-device screen-time systems.

products.name: Blacklight

privacy.note: Blacklight scans a website and reveals user-tracking technologies such as ad trackers, pixels and other third-party surveillance signals.

openness.note: The Markup publishes some Blacklight collector code, but not all of the production system is represented as a reusable open-source tool.

portability.note: The scanner is web-based and lets users test sites across selectable location and device contexts.

respect.note: Blacklight comes from The Markup's public-interest technology reporting and is built to reveal tracking practices.

accessibility.note: Users can enter a URL and get a readable privacy scan without installing a browser extension.

economical.note: The public Blacklight scan tool is free to use.

products.description: A free website privacy inspector that makes hidden trackers and pixels visible for ordinary web users.

products.name: PrivacyTests.org

privacy.note: PrivacyTests.org compares browser privacy protections by running automated leak and tracking tests.

openness.note: The test program and result-rendering website are open source under the MIT license.

portability.note: The site compares many desktop and mobile browsers, helping users choose across ecosystems rather than only one vendor.

respect.note: The project's stated goal is to help users choose more private browsers and encourage browser makers to fix leaks.

accessibility.note: The result tables are public and visual, but interpreting browser-leak categories still requires some privacy literacy.

economical.note: PrivacyTests.org is free to use on the public web.

products.description: An open browser-privacy test suite that helps people compare privacy leaks across browsers instead of relying on brand claims.

products.name: Webbkoll

privacy.note: Webbkoll checks what data-protecting measures a website has taken and how much behavior monitoring is shared with third parties.

openness.note: The Webbkoll source repository is public and the project describes itself as an online privacy-checking tool.

portability.note: The tool is a public web scanner that can be used on any site URL without installing client software.

respect.note: Webbkoll combines scanning with recommendations for not tracking or gossiping about users in digital environments.

accessibility.note: The site is easy to run, but some results such as headers and third-party requests are more useful to technically curious users.

economical.note: Webbkoll is available as a free public scanner.

products.description: A public website privacy checker that exposes third-party requests, headers and other privacy signals for a given URL.

products.name: DuckDuckGo App Tracking Protection

privacy.note: App Tracking Protection blocks many third-party trackers in Android apps, including when those apps are not actively being used.

openness.note: The feature is documented publicly but is part of DuckDuckGo's proprietary Android browser app rather than a standalone open-source blocker.

portability.note: The feature is available in DuckDuckGo Private Browser for Android, so it is useful but platform- and app-bound.

respect.note: DuckDuckGo says the feature works locally on the device and does not collect personal data.

accessibility.note: Users can enable it in the Android browser, but the VPN-like permission model and exceptions can be confusing for less technical users.

economical.note: DuckDuckGo App Tracking Protection is included in the free Android browser app.

products.description: An Android feature that blocks many third-party app trackers locally, useful for seeing how much mobile tracking happens outside the browser.

products.name: NetGuard

privacy.note: NetGuard blocks internet access per Android app without root and can individually allow or deny Wi-Fi and mobile access.

openness.note: NetGuard describes itself as a free, open-source, no-root Android firewall and publishes source code.

portability.note: NetGuard is Android-specific and uses Android's VPN slot, so it does not cover desktop systems or combine with another local VPN.

respect.note: The project says it has no calling home, no tracking or analytics, and no advertisements.

accessibility.note: NetGuard emphasizes simple no-root use while still exposing advanced per-app and per-address firewall controls.

economical.note: NetGuard is free software, with optional paid/supporter features depending on distribution route.

products.description: A no-root Android firewall for blocking internet access app by app, useful when you want a simple local control layer instead of trusting app settings.

products.name: TrackerControl

privacy.note: TrackerControl monitors and controls hidden tracker and ad collection in Android apps, analyzing traffic locally with no external VPN server by default.

openness.note: TrackerControl publishes its Android app source code and project repositories publicly.

portability.note: TrackerControl is Android-specific and relies on Android VPN functionality, so it is not a general desktop or router firewall.

respect.note: The project says no personal data leaves the device by default, making it a local-control tool rather than a hosted filtering service.

accessibility.note: TrackerControl offers tracker-blocking modes and insights, but stricter blocking can break app behavior and needs user judgment.

economical.note: TrackerControl is distributed as free open-source software.

products.description: An Android tracker-control app for seeing and blocking hidden app trackers, stronger on learning and control than set-and-forget simplicity.

products.name: LuLu

privacy.note: LuLu protects macOS network connections and can alert on outgoing activity from apps and malware.

openness.note: LuLu is a free open-source macOS firewall with public GPL-3.0 source code.

portability.note: LuLu is macOS-specific, so its strong app-firewall model does not transfer to Windows, Android or Linux.

respect.note: The tool is local, free and open-source, funded through optional support rather than ads or tracking.

accessibility.note: LuLu is simpler than many technical firewalls, but connection prompts and rule choices still require user attention.

economical.note: LuLu is free to download and use.

products.description: A free open-source outbound firewall for Macs, useful for seeing and stopping apps that phone home.

products.name: Little Snitch

privacy.note: Little Snitch shows where Mac apps connect on the internet and lets users allow or deny those connections.

openness.note: Little Snitch is a proprietary Objective Development app rather than an open-source firewall.

portability.note: Little Snitch is primarily a macOS product, with separate Linux network-monitor work that is not equivalent to the macOS security tool.

respect.note: The product is paid local software focused on network visibility, but the closed model requires trusting the vendor.

accessibility.note: Little Snitch is polished and long-running, with network monitor views and rule controls aimed at ordinary Mac users.

economical.note: Little Snitch offers a demo mode, but full ongoing use requires a paid license key.

products.description: The polished mainstream Mac app firewall: excellent visibility and usability, but closed-source and paid.

products.name: Portmaster

privacy.note: Portmaster monitors network connections and lets users set per-application rules for what to block.

openness.note: Portmaster describes itself as free and open source, with public source repositories.

portability.note: Portmaster offers Windows and Linux downloads, but not a macOS or mobile route.

respect.note: Portmaster is built around local network-control defaults, with optional paid privacy-network features rather than ads.

accessibility.note: Portmaster aims to do the heavy lifting with defaults while still allowing detailed per-app control.

economical.note: Portmaster's core firewall is free, with paid optional network/privacy services.

products.description: A Windows/Linux application firewall for people who want per-app network control with privacy-oriented defaults.

products.name: OpenSnitch

privacy.note: OpenSnitch provides interactive outbound connection filtering and system-wide blocking of ads, trackers or malware domains.

openness.note: OpenSnitch is public open-source software for GNU/Linux.

portability.note: OpenSnitch is a Linux firewall and does not cover macOS, Windows or mobile devices.

respect.note: The tool is local open-source firewall software rather than a hosted filtering or advertising service.

accessibility.note: OpenSnitch includes a GUI, but Linux firewall installation and rule management are still more technical than mainstream consumer tools.

economical.note: OpenSnitch is free open-source software.

products.description: A Linux application firewall inspired by Little Snitch, strongest for users comfortable installing and managing desktop firewall rules.

products.name: GlassWire

privacy.note: GlassWire visualizes network activity and includes firewall/network-monitor features, but it is not an open-source privacy-first tool.

openness.note: GlassWire is a proprietary commercial app rather than an open-source firewall.

portability.note: GlassWire is available across Windows and Android use cases, giving it broader mainstream reach than single-platform firewalls.

respect.note: The model is freemium/premium software rather than ad-supported tracking, but users trade source auditability for a polished commercial app.

accessibility.note: GlassWire emphasizes visual network monitoring, suspicious-activity alerts and a mainstream-friendly interface.

economical.note: GlassWire offers a free tier for basic monitoring with paid upgrades for full features.

products.description: A polished mainstream network monitor/firewall option for Windows and Android users, easier than most open-source tools but less auditable.

products.name: NoScript

privacy.note: NoScript blocks JavaScript and other active content by default unless a user trusts the site, reducing script-based tracking and attack surface.

openness.note: NoScript publishes its source code publicly.

portability.note: NoScript is available for Firefox, Chrome and other browser families, though configuration must travel with the extension ecosystem.

respect.note: The Chrome Web Store listing states NoScript collects zero data and gives users trust-based content control.

accessibility.note: NoScript is powerful but often breaks sites until users understand and manage trust levels.

economical.note: NoScript is free to install.

products.description: A powerful script-control extension for high-control browsing; excellent protection potential, but a steep learning curve.

products.name: Cookie AutoDelete

privacy.note: Cookie AutoDelete deletes unused cookies after tabs close and lets users keep cookies only for trusted sites.

openness.note: The extension source and documentation are public on GitHub.

portability.note: Cookie AutoDelete is a WebExtension for Firefox and Chrome-style browsers, with configuration tied to the extension.

respect.note: The tool gives users direct control over cookie persistence rather than selling a hosted privacy service.

accessibility.note: Automatic deletion is simple after setup, but whitelists and container interactions require care.

economical.note: Cookie AutoDelete is free to install from the Firefox add-ons store.

products.description: An open extension for automatically clearing unwanted cookies and site data after tabs close.

products.name: Firefox Multi-Account Containers

privacy.note: The extension separates website storage into tab-specific containers so cookies from one container are not available to another.

openness.note: Mozilla publishes the Multi-Account Containers source under an open license.

portability.note: The approach is Firefox-specific, so it is less portable across browsers than generic web scanners or DNS settings.

respect.note: Containers give users more boundary-setting between work, personal, shopping and other browsing contexts.

accessibility.note: Color-coded tabs and automatic site assignment make the concept usable, but users must understand container boundaries.

economical.note: Firefox Multi-Account Containers is free to install.

products.description: A Firefox extension for separating online roles into cookie-isolated containers, useful for account separation and calmer browsing boundaries.

products.name: Facebook Container

privacy.note: Facebook Container isolates Facebook identity into a separate container tab to make cross-site Facebook tracking harder.

openness.note: Mozilla publishes the Facebook Container extension source publicly.

portability.note: The extension is specific to Firefox and to Facebook/Meta tracking rather than a general browser-independent privacy layer.

respect.note: Mozilla frames the extension as a way to keep using Facebook while limiting how much off-platform browsing it can connect to a user.

accessibility.note: The extension is easy to install and runs automatically, though it is narrow and may overlap with modern browser cookie isolation.

economical.note: Facebook Container is free to install.

products.description: A narrow but useful Firefox extension for isolating Facebook/Meta identity from the rest of the web.

products.name: AdGuard Browser Extension

privacy.note: AdGuard's browser extension blocks ads and trackers and includes privacy-protection features against profiling.

openness.note: AdGuard states the browser extension is completely free and open source, with code published on GitHub.

portability.note: AdGuard documents browser-extension support across Chrome, Firefox, Opera and Edge.

respect.note: The extension is open and free, but it sits within a larger commercial AdGuard product ecosystem.

accessibility.note: A mainstream installable extension with configurable filters is easier for many users than manual DNS or script-blocker setup.

economical.note: AdGuard's browser extension is free, unlike some standalone AdGuard apps and services.

products.description: A mainstream free open-source browser extension for blocking ads and trackers across major browser families.

products.name: Tor Browser

privacy.note: Tor Browser routes traffic through the Tor network to defend against tracking, surveillance and censorship.

openness.note: Tor Project distributes open-source privacy software.

portability.note: Browser is standards-based and available cross-platform, though Tor-specific behavior is not a general account-migration system.

respect.note: Nonprofit privacy/censorship-resistance mission with no advertising business.

accessibility.note: Available for major platforms, but slower browsing and some site breakage make it harder for everyday use.

economical.note: Tor Browser is free.

products.description: The strongest mainstream anti-tracking/anonymity browser, open source and free, with speed and usability tradeoffs.

products.name: Firefox

privacy.note: Firefox Enhanced Tracking Protection blocks many cross-site trackers and harmful scripts by default.

openness.note: Firefox is open-source browser software.

portability.note: Open web standards, bookmarks/password export and cross-platform apps make leaving/using other tools feasible.

respect.note: Mozilla positions Firefox around privacy protection rather than ad-platform lock-in, though Mozilla has commercial search deals.

accessibility.note: Mature mainstream browser with good site compatibility, extensions and cross-platform support.

economical.note: Firefox is free.

products.description: An open-source browser with strong built-in tracking protection and broad compatibility, backed by Mozilla.

products.name: Brave

privacy.note: Brave says it blocks privacy-invasive ads and trackers and fingerprinting protections by default.

openness.note: Brave Browser source is publicly available and Chromium-based.

portability.note: Chromium compatibility, extensions and standard browser data flows make migration manageable.

respect.note: Default blocking is respectful, but the optional Brave Ads/Rewards model keeps advertising inside the product.

accessibility.note: Chrome-like UX and extension compatibility make it easy to adopt.

economical.note: Brave is free.

products.description: A Chromium browser with strong default ad/tracker blocking, but a mixed trust story because of its ads/rewards/crypto layer.

products.name: Safari

privacy.note: Apple says Safari's Intelligent Tracking Prevention uses on-device intelligence to limit cross-site tracking.

openness.note: Safari is closed Apple software, although WebKit is open source.

portability.note: Web standards help portability, but browser sync and full experience are Apple-device centered.

respect.note: Apple is not primarily an ad-funded browser company, but Safari reinforces Apple ecosystem lock-in.

accessibility.note: Excellent integration and accessibility on Apple platforms; limited outside Apple hardware.

economical.note: Free on Apple devices.

products.description: Apple's default browser, strong on anti-tracking within Apple devices but closed and tightly tied to the ecosystem.

products.name: Google Chrome

privacy.note: Google's policy covers Chrome-synced browsing history and identifiers across apps, browsers and devices.

openness.note: Chromium is open source, but Google Chrome includes proprietary Google components.

portability.note: Bookmarks/password export and web standards help, but Google Account sync can deepen lock-in.

respect.note: DOJ's Google Search remedies cited exclusive contracts involving Search and Chrome, reinforcing the browser's role in Google's default-access ecosystem.

accessibility.note: Best-in-class compatibility, speed, extensions and device sync make it highly accessible.

economical.note: Chrome is free.

products.description: The dominant browser with excellent compatibility and sync, but tightly connected to Google's data and default-search ecosystem.

products.name: Microsoft Edge

privacy.note: Edge offers tracking prevention, but Microsoft privacy terms cover broad diagnostic, account and service data processing.

openness.note: Edge is Chromium-based but Microsoft's browser product is proprietary.

portability.note: Chromium compatibility and exportable browser data help, but Microsoft account/Windows integration can add lock-in.

respect.note: Microsoft services, promotions and data flows make it less calm than independent browsers.

accessibility.note: Mature browser with Windows integration, compatibility and accessibility features.

economical.note: Edge is free.

products.description: A capable Chromium browser with strong Windows integration and accessibility, but heavy Microsoft data and promotion hooks.

products.name: LibreWolf

privacy.note: LibreWolf says it hardens Firefox against tracking and fingerprinting, removes telemetry/data collection and includes uBlock Origin.

openness.note: LibreWolf links its source code and describes itself as a community-driven open-source browser project.

portability.note: LibreWolf stays close to Firefox but intentionally disables some convenience defaults such as DRM and relies on users or package managers for updates.

respect.note: LibreWolf emphasizes privacy, security and user freedom over experiments, adware, annoyances or platform-growth features.

accessibility.note: LibreWolf is usable as a daily Firefox-style browser, but hardened defaults, no built-in auto-update and DRM tradeoffs make it less beginner-friendly.

economical.note: LibreWolf is free to download and use.

products.description: A hardened Firefox fork for people who want privacy-first defaults and open code, accepting extra breakage and maintenance responsibility.

products.name: DuckDuckGo Browser

privacy.note: DuckDuckGo says its browser blocks third-party trackers, many ads and cookie pop-ups by default and does not track searches.

openness.note: DuckDuckGo documents its web-tracking protections, but the consumer browser is an operated proprietary app rather than a fully open browser project.

portability.note: The browser is available on Windows, Mac, iOS and Android, but its strongest privacy bundle is DuckDuckGo-specific.

respect.note: DuckDuckGo frames the browser around data protection rather than data collection, with one-button deletion and tracker-blocking defaults.

accessibility.note: DuckDuckGo positions the browser as a mainstream one-download privacy upgrade across major desktop and mobile platforms.

economical.note: DuckDuckGo Browser is free to download and use, with some adjacent privacy services offered as paid upgrades.

products.description: A mainstream privacy browser that makes tracker blocking easy, with weaker openness than Firefox-derived alternatives.

products.name: Opera Browser

privacy.note: Opera offers ad blocking, tracker blocking and a no-log browser VPN, but Opera's privacy notice also describes technical, usage and marketing data processing.

openness.note: Opera is a proprietary Chromium-based browser product rather than an open-source browser distribution.

portability.note: Chromium compatibility, bookmarks and sync make basic browser switching feasible, though Opera's built-in features are Opera-specific.

respect.note: Opera includes privacy tools, but the product also foregrounds built-in AI, partner services, accounts and advertising-adjacent monetization.

accessibility.note: Opera is a mature, easy-to-install mainstream browser with built-in ad blocker, tracker blocker, VPN and AI features.

economical.note: Opera's browser and browser-only VPN are free, while VPN Pro and other upgrades are paid.

products.description: A recognizable mainstream alternative with useful built-ins and a free VPN, but proprietary and less calm than privacy-first browsers.

products.name: Zen Browser

privacy.note: Zen describes itself as privacy-focused and says it cares about user experience, not user data.

openness.note: Zen's project repository is public, describes Zen as open source and lists an MPL-2.0 license.

portability.note: Zen is Firefox-based and cross-platform, but its distinctive vertical-tab and productivity experience is still a newer browser layer.

respect.note: Zen frames its core values around a balance of beauty, performance and privacy rather than ads or surveillance features.

accessibility.note: Zen is available to download, but it is still a newer browser with beta-era positioning and a smaller support ecosystem than Firefox or Chrome.

economical.note: Zen Browser is free to download and use.

products.description: A newer open-source, Firefox-based browser for people who want Arc-like productivity without giving up privacy-oriented defaults.

products.name: Orion Browser

privacy.note: Kagi says Orion has zero telemetry, built-in ad blocking and anti-tracking, and no AI data collection.

openness.note: Orion is a proprietary Kagi browser rather than an open-source browser project, despite using WebKit and supporting many extensions.

portability.note: Orion supports Safari, Chrome and Firefox extensions, with macOS/iOS/iPadOS available, Linux in beta and Windows still in development.

respect.note: Kagi's Orion docs say the browser has no built-in telemetry and is designed not to phone home by default.

accessibility.note: Orion is strongest for Apple users today, with Linux beta and Windows not yet generally available, limiting broad adoption.

economical.note: Orion is user-funded through Orion Plus subscriptions or lifetime licenses for ongoing development, with core browser access available through downloads.

products.description: A Kagi-funded WebKit browser with strong zero-telemetry claims and extension support, best today for Apple users and privacy-focused power users.

products.name: uBlock Origin

privacy.note: uBlock Origin blocks ads, trackers, coin miners, popups, malware domains and other unwanted requests by default.

openness.note: uBlock Origin is a public open-source project with its source code and issue tracker on GitHub.

portability.note: uBlock Origin supports major browser families, though full power depends on browser extension rules and platform support.

respect.note: The project is a wide-spectrum blocker rather than an advertising allowlist business.

accessibility.note: It is free and effective, but users may need to understand filter lists and browser-extension compatibility.

economical.note: uBlock Origin is free to use.

products.description: A powerful open-source content blocker that makes the surveillance web lighter, faster and less manipulative.

products.name: Privacy Badger

privacy.note: EFF describes Privacy Badger as a free browser extension that stops companies from spying on users online.

openness.note: Privacy Badger publishes its extension source code publicly under EFF's GitHub organization.

portability.note: Privacy Badger is distributed as a browser extension for mainstream desktop browsers and Firefox for Android.

respect.note: EFF says Privacy Badger sends Global Privacy Control and Do Not Track signals and blocks trackers that ignore them.

accessibility.note: Simple installation and automatic tracker blocking make it easy for non-experts, with less tuning than filter-list blockers.

economical.note: Privacy Badger is free.

products.description: EFF's tracker-blocking extension is a good low-effort privacy upgrade, especially for people who will not tune filter lists.

products.name: DuckDuckGo Privacy Extension

privacy.note: DuckDuckGo says its browser extension adds tracker blocking, cookie protection, private search and email protection.

openness.note: DuckDuckGo publishes the Privacy Extensions source code under the Apache 2.0 license.

portability.note: The extension is available for Firefox, Chrome, Edge and Opera according to its repository.

respect.note: The add-on is useful and privacy-aligned, but it also steers users toward DuckDuckGo's own search and browser ecosystem.

accessibility.note: It is designed as a simple install-and-go privacy layer for mainstream browsers.

economical.note: DuckDuckGo's privacy extension is free.

products.description: A convenient privacy extension that bundles tracker blocking and private-search defaults, with some DuckDuckGo ecosystem lock-in.

products.name: ClearURLs

privacy.note: ClearURLs removes tracking elements from URLs while browsing.

openness.note: ClearURLs publishes its add-on and rules database as public source repositories.

portability.note: ClearURLs is built as a WebExtensions add-on for Firefox and some Chromium-based browsers.

respect.note: The tool targets tracking parameters rather than monetizing attention or steering users into a closed service.

accessibility.note: It is useful after installation, but narrower and more technical than a general blocker.

economical.note: ClearURLs is free.

products.description: A focused open-source add-on that strips tracking parameters from links, useful as a small privacy hygiene layer.

products.name: Consent-O-Matic

privacy.note: Consent-O-Matic recognizes consent pop-ups and submits the user's saved preferences, defaulting toward privacy-preserving settings where categories are unclear.

openness.note: Consent-O-Matic is an open-source project with public rules and extension code.

portability.note: The tool is distributed as a browser extension for common desktop browsers and Safari/iOS.

respect.note: Aarhus University describes the extension as a response to confusing cookie dialogs and dark-pattern consent design.

accessibility.note: It reduces repetitive consent-banner decisions, but only works where the pop-up pattern is recognized.

economical.note: Consent-O-Matic is free.

products.description: A university-built extension that automates cookie-banner choices so dark patterns have fewer chances to wear you down.

products.name: Terms of Service; Didn't Read

privacy.note: ToS;DR does not block tracking directly, but it surfaces privacy-policy and terms risks before users accept them.

openness.note: ToS;DR publishes its site and browser-extension code in public repositories.

portability.note: The service offers a website, API and browser extensions for multiple browsers.

respect.note: The project is explicitly built to help users understand the terms and privacy policies they are asked to accept.

accessibility.note: Browser extensions show ratings and summaries in context, though coverage depends on volunteer-reviewed services.

economical.note: ToS;DR is free to use.

products.description: A terms-and-privacy literacy project that turns opaque agreements into browsable ratings and summaries.

products.name: Adblock Plus

privacy.note: Adblock Plus says it blocks tracking and malware sites, while its privacy policy still describes limited personal-data collection for the service.

openness.note: Adblock Plus says it is an open-source project licensed under GPLv3.

portability.note: Adblock Plus is available for major desktop browsers and mobile devices.

respect.note: Its Acceptable Ads program allowlists ads that meet the standard, so the default model is not full ad blocking.

accessibility.note: It is easy to install, widely known and maintains compatibility with current Chrome extension changes.

economical.note: Adblock Plus is free to use.

products.description: A very easy mainstream ad blocker, useful for beginners but less values-aligned because acceptable ads are allowed by default.

products.name: DuckDuckGo

privacy.note: DuckDuckGo says it does not save search history or track users across the web.

openness.note: Some components and apps are public, but the search service is not a fully open-source search index.

portability.note: No account requirement reduces lock-in, though search preferences are not a rich portable data model.

respect.note: Ads are based on search keywords rather than behavioral profiles.

accessibility.note: Simple search UI and no-account use make it easy to adopt.

economical.note: DuckDuckGo search is free.

products.description: A private-search brand that avoids search-history tracking and uses non-tracking ads, but is not a fully open search stack.

products.name: Startpage

privacy.note: Startpage says it does not track users and returns search results without saving personal search history.

openness.note: The service is privacy-oriented but closed rather than an open-source search stack.

portability.note: No account requirement keeps lock-in low, though there is little user-owned data to export.

respect.note: Private-search model avoids behavioral tracking, while still using search ads.

accessibility.note: Simple Google-like search UX is easy for ordinary users.

economical.note: Startpage is free to use.

products.description: A private-search service offering Google-style results through a no-tracking search proxy model.

products.name: Kagi

privacy.note: Kagi says it does not track users for advertising and keeps search private.

openness.note: Kagi is not an open-source search engine, though some tools/projects are public.

portability.note: Search settings/lenses can be managed, but the value is mostly a hosted paid service rather than a portable data commons.

respect.note: Kagi's paid, no-ad model aligns the service with subscribers rather than advertisers.

accessibility.note: Clean web search is easy to use, but account/payment requirement limits access.

economical.note: Paid subscription makes it less economical than free search.

products.description: A paid search engine with no ads and strong user-alignment, trading cost for a cleaner incentive model.

products.name: Google Search

privacy.note: Google's privacy policy describes search terms, ad interactions, unique identifiers and activity across services as collected data.

openness.note: Google Search is a closed ranking/index service.

portability.note: Google Takeout/data controls exist, but search ranking, index access and user-interaction signals are not user-portable in an open-protocol sense.

respect.note: DOJ says Google used default-distribution deals to lock up search access, reduce choice and maintain monopoly power.

accessibility.note: Best-known search UX, broad language support and default placement make it extremely accessible.

economical.note: Free to use, funded by advertising.

products.description: The most accessible search engine, but also the canonical ad-funded, profile-driven default with recent monopoly remedies.

products.name: Mastodon

privacy.note: Mastodon avoids a central ad-tracking company, but privacy and admin access vary by server/instance.

openness.note: Mastodon is open-source and part of the ActivityPub/fediverse ecosystem.

portability.note: Mastodon documents account migration between servers, though follower/content portability has limits.

respect.note: Federated/community-run model has no platform-wide engagement-ad business.

accessibility.note: Setup and choosing a server adds friction versus centralized social apps.

economical.note: Mastodon is free for users on many instances, with servers often donation-funded.

products.description: An open-source federated social network with no central ad model, but instance choice and moderation vary.

products.name: Bluesky

privacy.note: Bluesky says posts/comments are public and direct messages are stored/processed unencrypted for Trust & Safety access.

openness.note: AT Protocol is described as an open-source framework and standard for public conversation.

portability.note: AT Protocol is designed for account portability and user-owned identity.

respect.note: More open/portable than legacy social; still a public social feed with moderation and discovery algorithms.

accessibility.note: Main app is simple and mainstream-friendly compared with most federated social tools.

economical.note: Bluesky is free to use.

products.description: A fast-growing social network built on AT Protocol, more portable than legacy social but public-by-design and not private chat.

products.name: X (Twitter)

privacy.note: X privacy materials describe collecting, using and sharing data for service operation, ads and personalization.

openness.note: X is a mostly closed social platform rather than an open protocol.

portability.note: Users can download an archive of X data, but social graph and audience are not truly portable.

respect.note: Ad-funded, algorithmic public feed creates strong engagement incentives.

accessibility.note: Large network, web/mobile access and published accessibility features make it accessible, though policies and paid tiers affect reach.

economical.note: Free tier exists with paid upgrades such as Premium.

products.description: A large social/news network with export tools, but ad-driven, data-heavy, closed, and engagement-optimized.

products.name: Instagram

privacy.note: Instagram Help says end-to-end encrypted messaging on Instagram is no longer supported as of May 8, 2026.

openness.note: Instagram is a closed Meta platform rather than open protocol/social software.

portability.note: Instagram lets users download account information, but audience/network portability remains limited.

respect.note: BEUC's 2026 analysis says Meta's latest Facebook/Instagram consent-for-ads model still fails to offer free, specific, informed and unambiguous consent.

accessibility.note: Very polished, widely adopted mobile app with broad creator/business tooling.

economical.note: Free to use, funded by ads and commerce features.

products.description: A mainstream Meta social app with excellent reach and UX, but closed, ad-funded, deeply engagement-oriented, and no longer an encrypted-DM option.

products.name: TikTok

privacy.note: The FTC's FY2026 budget justification says DOJ sued TikTok/ByteDance on the FTC's referral for allegedly violating COPPA and a 2019 consent order.

openness.note: TikTok is a closed proprietary social/video platform.

portability.note: TikTok supports requesting/downloading account data, but social graph and recommendation reach are locked in.

respect.note: The FTC's FY2026 budget justification says the complaint alleged TikTok/ByteDance knew of compliance failures that put children's data and privacy at risk.

accessibility.note: Extremely easy mobile video creation/consumption and global popularity make it highly accessible.

economical.note: Free to use, funded through ads/commerce and platform monetization.

products.description: A highly accessible video feed with maximal engagement design, extensive data collection disclosures, and a current U.S. children's-privacy enforcement case.

products.name: Proton Drive

privacy.note: Proton Drive says files are end-to-end encrypted so Proton cannot access file contents.

openness.note: Proton publishes app source code, though the full hosted service is not self-hostable.

portability.note: Files can be downloaded/exported, but collaboration and sharing are still inside a hosted Proton account.

respect.note: User-funded privacy suite with no ad-surveillance business.

accessibility.note: Consumer cloud-drive UX with web/mobile/desktop apps, though collaboration features are less mature than Google Drive.

economical.note: Free storage tier exists with paid upgrades.

products.description: End-to-end encrypted cloud storage from Proton, strong on privacy with a familiar freemium cloud model.

products.name: Nextcloud

privacy.note: Self-hosting lets users control where documents, contacts, calendars and files are stored.

openness.note: Nextcloud presents itself as self-hosted open-source cloud file storage/collaboration technology.

portability.note: Own-server model and standard sync/file workflows make data portability strong.

respect.note: No ad-surveillance model; control depends on the host/admin chosen.

accessibility.note: Powerful but setup, hosting and maintenance create friction for nontechnical users.

economical.note: Community/self-hosted software can be free, but hosting/admin time may cost money.

products.description: A self-hostable, open-source cloud collaboration suite that maximizes control at the cost of setup and maintenance.

products.name: Google Drive

privacy.note: Google Drive terms point users to Google's broad privacy policy for managing/exporting/deleting information.

openness.note: Google Drive is a closed hosted collaboration service.

portability.note: Google Takeout can export Drive and other account data, but collaborative docs and sharing context may not travel cleanly.

respect.note: Not a Drive ad product directly, but it sits inside Google's account and advertising ecosystem.

accessibility.note: Best-in-class web collaboration, sharing, mobile apps and office-suite integration.

economical.note: Free storage tier with paid Google One/Workspace upgrades.

products.description: A powerful, accessible collaboration suite with useful export controls, but housed inside Google's closed data ecosystem.

products.name: Google Docs / Workspace

privacy.note: Google says Docs, Sheets, Slides and Vids do not use personal-content app information for advertising, but the suite remains inside Google's account ecosystem.

openness.note: Google Docs/Workspace is a proprietary hosted office suite, not an open-source or self-hostable editor.

portability.note: Google Takeout can export account data, but collaborative document history, comments and sharing context do not fully transfer as an open workspace.

respect.note: Google's Docs privacy page makes a no-content-for-ads claim, but the service still depends on a closed Google account and product ecosystem.

accessibility.note: Google Docs is web-first, free to start, and has very strong real-time collaboration, sharing, mobile and accessibility support.

economical.note: Google Docs is available at no extra cost for individual Google accounts, with paid Workspace tiers for organizations.

products.description: The default shared-document tool for many people: excellent collaboration and low friction, but closed and account-bound.

products.name: Microsoft 365 / Office

privacy.note: Microsoft says documents you create belong to you and Trust Center privacy principles say Microsoft will not use your data without agreement, but the suite remains a closed cloud/account system.

openness.note: Microsoft 365 apps and cloud services are proprietary products rather than open-source or self-hostable office software.

portability.note: Microsoft documents GDPR/CCPA data-subject request workflows for discovering, deleting and exporting data from Office 365 services, usually via tenant/admin processes.

respect.note: Microsoft's trust center says your data belongs to you and can be accessed, modified or deleted, but Copilot/cloud-connected features add complexity.

accessibility.note: Microsoft 365 is widely available across PC, Mac, mobile and web, with real-time collaboration and mature accessibility support.

economical.note: Free web/mobile options exist, but full desktop apps, larger storage and Copilot features sit behind paid Microsoft 365 subscriptions.

products.description: A mature mainstream office suite with excellent compatibility and access, but a closed subscription/cloud ecosystem.

products.name: CryptPad

privacy.note: CryptPad describes itself as an end-to-end encrypted collaborative office suite, so hosted operators cannot read document contents in the usual way.

openness.note: CryptPad presents itself as open-source/free software and can be run as an own instance.

portability.note: CryptPad supports collaborative documents, sheets, forms, kanban and other tools, but moving a whole workspace still depends on export/import and instance choices.

respect.note: The product is explicitly privacy-first, end-to-end encrypted and not built as an advertising platform.

accessibility.note: CryptPad is browser-based and usable from a public instance, but encrypted collaboration can be less familiar than Google Docs.

economical.note: The flagship instance offers a free account and paid plans for more storage; own-instance support is also available.

products.description: A privacy-first office suite for collaborative documents, sheets and boards, with end-to-end encryption and open-source code.

products.name: ONLYOFFICE

privacy.note: ONLYOFFICE emphasizes private-server deployment, file encryption, secure sharing and GDPR compliance for office collaboration.

openness.note: ONLYOFFICE publishes community/open-source editions and public repositories, though product tiers and editions vary.

portability.note: ONLYOFFICE Docs focuses on standard office documents, spreadsheets, presentations and forms and can integrate with self-hosted storage.

respect.note: Self-hosted and private-server options let organizations avoid an ad-funded productivity platform and keep more control over document processing.

accessibility.note: ONLYOFFICE offers familiar document, spreadsheet and presentation editors, but self-hosting/integration is more complex than mainstream SaaS.

economical.note: ONLYOFFICE Community/DocSpace community paths are free/open-source for limited use, with paid editions for scale and support.

products.description: A Microsoft-format-friendly office suite with self-hosted/community paths, useful when compatibility matters but control still matters too.

products.name: Collabora Online

privacy.note: Collabora Online is designed to integrate into your own infrastructure or a trusted hosting partner, keeping data under chosen governance.

openness.note: Collabora describes the product as an open-source document editing suite, and publishes Collabora Online source/release artifacts publicly.

portability.note: Collabora is based around open document workflows and integrates with self-hosted platforms such as Nextcloud/ownCloud-style storage.

respect.note: The pitch centers on digital sovereignty and user-controlled infrastructure rather than advertising or lock-in.

accessibility.note: Collabora provides browser document editing, but setup and hosting choices make it less plug-and-play than Google or Microsoft.

economical.note: CODE is a free self-hosted development edition for developers, home users and small teams, while production support is commercial.

products.description: A LibreOffice-derived online office suite for organizations that want browser collaboration without giving the documents to a big SaaS default.

products.name: Zotero

privacy.note: Zotero says it is designed as a local program that saves data to your own computer by default and does not require sharing data to be usable.

openness.note: Zotero source code is available under the AGPLv3 license and hosted publicly.

portability.note: Zotero documents whole-library, collection and item export, with Zotero RDF recommended for the most complete transfer.

respect.note: Zotero is built around local research libraries and optional sync/storage rather than advertising or publisher analytics.

accessibility.note: Zotero is available for Mac, Windows, Linux, iOS and Android, with browser capture and citation workflows.

economical.note: Zotero is free to use, with 300 MB free file storage and paid storage tiers for larger synced libraries.

products.description: The strongest default for many research workflows: free, open, local-first, citation-friendly, and portable, with paid storage only if you want hosted file sync.

products.name: Mendeley Reference Manager

privacy.note: Mendeley uses an Elsevier account; Elsevier's privacy center says account activity such as searching, reading and library building can support personalized services.

openness.note: Mendeley is a proprietary Elsevier reference-management service, not an open-source or self-hostable research library.

portability.note: Mendeley Reference Manager can export all references as BibTeX, EndNote XML or RIS from the desktop app.

respect.note: Mendeley is convenient and free to start, but it sits inside Elsevier's commercial research-content and account ecosystem.

accessibility.note: Mendeley is a free web and desktop reference manager with Word/web-importer workflows and online access.

economical.note: Mendeley publishes a free plan with 2 GB storage, with paid upgrades for unlimited storage and AI workspace features.

products.description: A mainstream free-to-start academic reference manager with good import/export basics, but a weak fit for people avoiding publisher/platform data ecosystems.

products.name: EndNote

privacy.note: EndNote is governed by Clarivate privacy practices for collection, use and sharing of personal data.

openness.note: EndNote is a proprietary Clarivate product rather than an open-source or self-hostable reference manager.

portability.note: EndNote online supports exporting references with RIS/RefMan-style export workflows, and desktop supports many output styles.

respect.note: EndNote is a paid academic workflow product with cloud/AI additions, not an advertising product, but it remains closed and vendor-bound.

accessibility.note: EndNote integrates with major writing workflows such as Cite While You Write for Word and web/desktop reference management.

economical.note: EndNote is sold as a purchased desktop/cloud reference-management product, often through individual or institutional licensing.

products.description: A long-running institutional reference-management default: powerful for formal academic workflows, but closed, paid, and less values-aligned for open portable research.

products.name: Paperpile

privacy.note: Paperpile says library data and uploaded files are saved on its servers, with optional sync of files to Google Drive.

openness.note: Paperpile is a proprietary web reference manager rather than open-source software.

portability.note: Paperpile can export selected items, folders, labels or a full library to formats such as BibTeX, RIS, CSV or JSON.

respect.note: Paperpile is not ad-funded and has explicit export paths, but it is web/server based and deeply integrated with Google Docs/Drive workflows.

accessibility.note: Paperpile is designed for browser-based reference management with Google Docs, Word, mobile apps, PDF annotation and sharing.

economical.note: Paperpile offers a free trial, then paid individual or team subscriptions for the full reference manager.

products.description: A polished web reference manager for Google Docs-heavy researchers, with good export support but weaker privacy/openness because the library lives on Paperpile servers.

products.name: JabRef

privacy.note: JabRef is a desktop reference manager built around local bibliography files rather than a mandatory hosted account.

openness.note: JabRef describes itself as an open-source, cross-platform citation and reference management tool.

portability.note: JabRef's native workflow is BibTeX/BibLaTeX bibliography management, which keeps citation data in portable text files.

respect.note: JabRef is volunteer/open-source research software, not an ad-funded or publisher-owned hosted analytics platform.

accessibility.note: JabRef is cross-platform and powerful for LaTeX/BibTeX users, but less friendly for casual Google Docs or mobile-first users.

economical.note: JabRef is free software.

products.description: A high-control, BibTeX-native reference manager for researchers who want their bibliography as files they can inspect, back up, and move.

products.name: Overleaf

privacy.note: Overleaf publishes privacy, security and acceptable-use terms for its hosted LaTeX service.

openness.note: Overleaf publishes a Community Edition repository and describes it as an open-source collaborative LaTeX editor that can be run locally.

portability.note: Overleaf supports Git integration for cloning projects locally and treating a project as a remote repository, though this is a premium cloud feature.

respect.note: Overleaf's value is collaborative academic writing rather than ads, but the hosted service is still a subscription platform with account-based project storage.

accessibility.note: Overleaf is a browser-based LaTeX editor with no local installation, real-time collaboration, templates and institutional plans.

economical.note: Overleaf has a free plan with unlimited projects and one collaborator, plus paid plans for more collaboration and integrations.

products.description: The easiest collaborative LaTeX path for many students and researchers: strong for access and reproducible text files, less strong as a hosted subscription workflow.

products.name: Hypothesis

privacy.note: Hypothesis publishes privacy policies for open-web and LMS use; the service involves account-linked annotations and course integrations.

openness.note: The Hypothesis organization publishes open-source annotation software repositories for annotating the web.

portability.note: Hypothesis creates web/PDF annotations around URLs and groups, but social annotation data remains tied to account, group and service context.

respect.note: Hypothesis is built for learning and collaborative reading rather than advertising or attention feeds.

accessibility.note: Hypothesis integrates with learning-management systems and browser/web reading workflows for higher education.

economical.note: Hypothesis supports open-web use and also sells higher-education/LMS deployments, so cost depends on context.

products.description: A public-interest social annotation layer for close reading and class discussion; useful for digital literacy, but annotations can be socially/contextually sensitive.

products.name: Google Scholar

privacy.note: Google Scholar uses cookies/settings and sits inside Google's broader privacy policy and account ecosystem.

openness.note: Google Scholar is a proprietary academic search index, and its help page says bulk access is not provided.

portability.note: Google Scholar supports citation export to BibTeX, EndNote, RefMan and RefWorks one result at a time, but not bulk records.

respect.note: Scholar is valuable for broad discovery, but ranking, coverage and data access are opaque compared with open scholarly catalogs.

accessibility.note: Google Scholar searches scholarly literature across disciplines and helps locate PDFs, citations, related articles and library links.

economical.note: Google Scholar is free to use, though full-text access often depends on open access or library subscriptions.

products.description: The familiar scholarly-search default: excellent for quick discovery, but opaque and not suitable as an open, bulk, auditable research index.

products.name: Semantic Scholar

privacy.note: Semantic Scholar is governed by Ai2 privacy practices for the sites and services that link to Ai2's privacy notice.

openness.note: Semantic Scholar offers an Academic Graph API and downloadable datasets, though the web product itself is not an open-source client.

portability.note: The Semantic Scholar API provides programmatic access to paper, author, citation, venue and dataset services.

respect.note: Semantic Scholar is a free Ai2 research-discovery tool rather than an advertising search product, but it uses AI ranking and account features.

accessibility.note: Semantic Scholar is a free AI-powered research tool for scientific literature.

economical.note: Semantic Scholar's FAQ describes it as a free AI-powered search and discovery tool.

products.description: A strong free scholarly-search alternative when AI ranking and citation graph access help, with better API access than Google Scholar but still a hosted service.

products.name: OpenAlex

privacy.note: OpenAlex is primarily an open scholarly metadata catalog and API, so ordinary use does not require building a personal reading profile.

openness.note: OpenAlex describes itself as a fully open catalog of the global research system.

portability.note: OpenAlex provides API and data snapshot access to a comprehensive catalog of works, authors, sources, institutions and topics.

respect.note: OpenAlex is open research infrastructure from OurResearch, oriented around reusable metadata rather than attention capture.

accessibility.note: OpenAlex Web is usable by humans and the API is powerful for builders, but it is less beginner-friendly than Google Scholar.

economical.note: OpenAlex makes scholarly metadata openly available through web, API and snapshot channels.

products.description: Open scholarly infrastructure for people who want research metadata they can inspect, reuse, and build on rather than a closed academic search box.

products.name: PubMed

privacy.note: NCBI says it provides its websites as a public service and does not collect personally identifiable information for commercial marketing.

openness.note: PubMed is a public NLM/NCBI database of biomedical citations with links to full text where available.

portability.note: PubMed supports advanced search, citation records and NCBI data/usage policies for public biomedical search infrastructure.

respect.note: PubMed is public biomedical information infrastructure rather than an ad-funded or publisher-owned research platform.

accessibility.note: PubMed comprises more than 40 million biomedical-literature citations and is freely searchable on the web.

economical.note: PubMed search is free, though some linked full text may require subscriptions or institutional access.

products.description: The public biomedical-literature baseline: free, high-trust, and not ad-driven, with the caveat that many linked articles still depend on publishers or libraries.

products.name: Unpaywall

privacy.note: Unpaywall's FAQ says the browser extension sends a DOI to its API only when checking for an open-access location.

openness.note: Unpaywall describes itself as an open database of free scholarly articles harvested from publishers and repositories.

portability.note: Unpaywall provides free programmatic API access to its open-access database.

respect.note: Unpaywall's purpose is finding legal open-access versions of articles rather than locking users into a reading platform.

accessibility.note: Unpaywall is most useful as a browser extension or API alongside article pages, rather than as a general search engine.

economical.note: Unpaywall offers free access to the API and open-access discovery database.

products.description: A practical open-access literacy tool: it helps users find legal free copies of scholarly articles and exposes that data through an API.

products.name: Etherpad

privacy.note: Etherpad says your server is the only server and its site emphasizes running under your governance without telemetry.

openness.note: Etherpad is open source and publishes its code on GitHub under an Apache-style license.

portability.note: Etherpad emphasizes open data format, built-in full export and preserved revision history.

respect.note: The project explicitly frames sovereignty as default: no telemetry, no upsells and no silent hosted-service changes when self-hosted.

accessibility.note: Etherpad is lightweight and browser-based, but it is primarily a collaborative pad rather than a full office suite.

economical.note: Etherpad is free open-source software; the main cost is hosting or using a trusted public instance.

products.description: A simple, open, self-hostable collaborative text editor for shared notes and live drafting, not a full Google Docs replacement.

products.name: Google Calendar

privacy.note: Google says Calendar content is stored encrypted in transit and at rest and is not used for advertising, while still processed for product features and reliability.

openness.note: Calendar is a closed Google service even though it supports common calendar import/export patterns.

portability.note: Google Takeout explicitly supports exporting Calendar data for backup or transfer.

respect.note: Google provides controls and says Calendar content is not used for ads, but account-level data processing and ecosystem lock-in remain material trade-offs.

accessibility.note: Calendar is a widely available web, mobile and Workspace product with broad integration support.

economical.note: The consumer calendar is free with a Google Account, with paid Workspace plans for organizations.

products.description: The default mainstream calendar for many people: very convenient and portable through Takeout, but still a closed Google-account dependency.

products.name: Outlook Calendar

privacy.note: Microsoft's Trust Center frames privacy as a core principle, but Outlook Calendar remains a cloud service under Microsoft account and organization policies.

openness.note: Outlook Calendar is proprietary Microsoft software and service infrastructure.

portability.note: Microsoft documents exporting Outlook calendars as iCalendar files and importing calendars into Outlook.

respect.note: The product has mature sharing and privacy controls, but the strongest experience is tied to Microsoft accounts, Microsoft 365 and Exchange ecosystems.

accessibility.note: Outlook Calendar is available on web, desktop and mobile and bundled into the broader Microsoft 365 stack.

economical.note: Microsoft lists a free Outlook plan and paid Microsoft 365 tiers with more storage and ad-free features.

products.description: The Microsoft-account calendar default, strongest for people already living in Outlook, Exchange or Microsoft 365.

products.name: Proton Calendar

privacy.note: Proton says Calendar uses end-to-end encryption for event details, participants and locations, with zero-access encryption for stored data.

openness.note: Proton publishes open-source app code and cryptographic details, but the hosted calendar service itself is not a self-hostable open stack.

portability.note: Proton documents importing and exporting calendars using ICS files.

respect.note: The product is explicitly positioned around private scheduling without surveillance advertising.

accessibility.note: Proton Calendar is available on web and mobile, but works best inside the Proton account ecosystem.

economical.note: Proton offers a free tier and paid plans that unlock larger storage and more ecosystem features.

products.description: A privacy-first calendar for people who want encrypted schedules and are comfortable living inside the Proton ecosystem.

products.name: Tuta Calendar

privacy.note: Tuta describes its calendar as zero-knowledge encrypted and built so only the user can access calendar data.

openness.note: Tuta states that its apps are open source and publishes the client code publicly.

portability.note: Tuta documents calendar import/export workflows, but its encrypted ecosystem is less protocol-portable than a plain CalDAV server.

respect.note: Tuta is positioned around private, ad-free encrypted email and calendar rather than behavioral advertising.

accessibility.note: Tuta Calendar is available through Tuta apps, with encrypted design trading off some interoperability convenience.

economical.note: Tuta lists a free plan and paid plans with more calendars, aliases, storage and business features.

products.description: An encrypted calendar bundled with Tuta, strongest for users prioritizing privacy over broad calendar-protocol interoperability.

products.name: Nextcloud Calendar

privacy.note: Nextcloud Calendar can be run on infrastructure the user or organization controls, so privacy depends heavily on the chosen host and admin practices.

openness.note: The Calendar app publishes its source code openly in the Nextcloud GitHub repository.

portability.note: Nextcloud Calendar is built around standard calendar sync and sharing patterns including CalDAV.

respect.note: A self-hosted or trusted-provider Nextcloud setup avoids the surveillance-ad-funded calendar model, but governance depends on the operator.

accessibility.note: The product is powerful for Nextcloud users but requires choosing a provider or operating a server.

economical.note: The app itself is free open-source software; practical cost depends on hosting, administration and provider choice.

products.description: A self-hostable calendar for people or organizations that want standard calendar sync under their own provider or server governance.

products.name: Cal.com

privacy.note: Hosted Cal.com necessarily connects to calendars for booking availability, while Cal.diy offers a self-host path for users who can operate it.

openness.note: Cal.com moved its production codebase private while keeping Cal.diy as the open-source community edition.

portability.note: Cal.com offers developer APIs, integrations and a Cal.diy self-host option, though hosted account data is still a platform dependency.

respect.note: Cal.com is more developer- and self-host-friendly than many hosted schedulers, but its commercial hosted product is no longer fully open source.

accessibility.note: The hosted product is easy to sign up for and supports common calendar integrations; self-hosting requires technical administration.

economical.note: Cal.com advertises free individual scheduling with paid plans for teams and advanced use.

products.description: A modern scheduling-link platform, stronger than most mainstream schedulers for people who care about APIs and a self-hostable community edition.

products.name: Calendly

privacy.note: Calendly's privacy notice describes collecting account, calendar-integration, scheduling and device data, with disclosures to service providers and partners.

openness.note: Calendly is a proprietary hosted scheduling platform rather than open-source software.

portability.note: Calendly integrates with major calendars and business tools, but the scheduling workflow is centered on a hosted Calendly account.

respect.note: Calendly offers security controls and account settings, but its data model is a mainstream SaaS model rather than local-first or self-hostable.

accessibility.note: Calendly is one of the easiest and most widely recognized booking-link tools, with broad app integrations and a simple web workflow.

economical.note: Calendly lists a free plan plus paid tiers for more automation, routing and team features.

products.description: The mainstream booking-link default: extremely easy, but closed, account-centric and less aligned with privacy/self-hosting values.

products.name: Doodle

privacy.note: Doodle's privacy policy describes collecting account, scheduling, device, usage and marketing data, plus sharing with processors and partners.

openness.note: Doodle is a proprietary hosted polling and scheduling product.

portability.note: Doodle is strong for quick poll coordination but less data-portable than open calendar or CSV-first community tools.

respect.note: Doodle reserves ad-free experience and some tracking/contact-request controls for paid Professional plans.

accessibility.note: Doodle is simple for group polls, booking pages and sign-up sheets and has high mainstream recognition.

economical.note: Doodle documents a free account for group meetings, booking pages and sign-up sheets, with paid Professional plans for advanced features.

products.description: A fast, recognizable scheduling-poll tool, useful as the honest mainstream floor for people comparing privacy and openness.

products.name: Framadate

privacy.note: Framasoft describes Framadate as a free open-source service that respects privacy and personal data.

openness.note: Framadate is published as free/libre software, with public project code and licensing information.

portability.note: Framadate documents exporting poll results in CSV format from the administration page.

respect.note: The service is run by Framasoft as a values-oriented alternative to proprietary poll schedulers.

accessibility.note: Framadate is simple and account-light for date polls, but it is less polished than mainstream commercial schedulers.

economical.note: Framadate is offered as a free public service and free/libre software.

products.description: A free/libre Doodle-style poll scheduler for lightweight coordination when privacy, simplicity and open software matter more than automation.

products.name: Google Forms

privacy.note: Forms files are encrypted in transit and at rest, but data sits inside Google's broader account and privacy-policy ecosystem.

openness.note: Google Forms is a proprietary hosted service rather than open-source or self-hostable software.

portability.note: Google documents exporting raw response data into Google Sheets for deeper analysis.

respect.note: The service is convenient and free, but it is tied to Google's larger data collection and account infrastructure.

accessibility.note: Forms is widely available, template-driven and designed for respondents to complete on any device.

economical.note: Google Forms is available as a no-cost form tool with deeper Workspace integration for organizations.

products.description: The recognizable free default for forms and classroom surveys: very easy to use, but embedded in Google's proprietary account and data ecosystem.

products.name: Typeform

privacy.note: Typeform says it treats security and privacy seriously, but respondents' data is processed by a proprietary hosted service.

openness.note: Typeform is a proprietary SaaS form builder, not open-source or self-hostable.

portability.note: Typeform supports result handling through its hosted product, but the strongest export and analysis workflows depend on plan and integrations.

respect.note: The product emphasizes polished conversational forms, while paid tiers and proprietary hosting limit user control.

accessibility.note: Typeform offers a polished, mainstream form-building experience with many templates and integrations.

economical.note: Typeform offers a free starting point, but meaningful response volume and advanced features are gated behind paid plans.

products.description: A polished conversational-form platform that is strong on user experience and recognition, but weaker on openness, self-hosting and cost-sensitive control.

products.name: SurveyMonkey

privacy.note: SurveyMonkey's privacy notice covers survey, form and application data processed through its hosted service.

openness.note: SurveyMonkey is a proprietary hosted survey platform rather than open-source or self-hostable software.

portability.note: SurveyMonkey documents exports for survey results including PDF, PPT, XLS, CSV and SPSS formats.

respect.note: Strong export options help users leave, but the service remains a proprietary data-collection platform.

accessibility.note: SurveyMonkey is a mainstream survey tool with broad templates, analysis features and organization workflows.

economical.note: A free tier exists, but individual and team pricing gates many survey features and response workflows.

products.description: A familiar mainstream survey platform with good export routes and mature analysis tools, balanced by proprietary hosting and paid-plan gates.

products.name: Tally

privacy.note: Tally says it is GDPR-compliant, hosted in Europe, avoids cookie tracking and encrypts form data in transit and at rest.

openness.note: Tally is a proprietary hosted form builder rather than open-source or self-hostable software.

portability.note: Tally supports data-moving workflows through Google Sheets, Airtable, Zapier, Make and webhooks.

respect.note: Tally emphasizes no cookie tracking, EU hosting and data-retention controls on business plans.

accessibility.note: Tally offers a document-like builder, templates, embeds and many form blocks with a low learning curve.

economical.note: Tally advertises unlimited forms and submissions for free within fair-use guidelines.

products.description: A generous, modern form builder for people who want low friction and low cost without moving all the way to self-hosted software.

products.name: BlockSurvey

privacy.note: BlockSurvey presents itself as end-to-end encrypted, with survey data encrypted before being sent to its servers.

openness.note: The service is privacy-first but not presented as open-source or self-hostable on its public product pages.

portability.note: BlockSurvey supports form and survey workflows, but public positioning emphasizes encrypted collection more than broad open-format portability.

respect.note: BlockSurvey says users hold encryption keys and that it cannot access user data.

accessibility.note: The product is a hosted no-code builder, but it is less universally familiar than Google Forms or SurveyMonkey.

economical.note: BlockSurvey offers trial or paid hosted plans, so it is less cost-accessible than free mainstream form builders.

products.description: A hosted privacy-first survey builder for sensitive collection, prioritizing end-to-end encryption over broad familiarity or lowest cost.

products.name: LimeSurvey

privacy.note: LimeSurvey emphasizes keeping survey data under user control, especially when self-hosted.

openness.note: LimeSurvey presents itself as open-source survey software with both self-hosted and hosted options.

portability.note: LimeSurvey pricing and feature material describes exports to formats including SPSS, R, Stata, CSV, Excel and PDF.

respect.note: Self-hosting and open-source licensing give organizations more control than proprietary SaaS defaults.

accessibility.note: LimeSurvey is powerful but more administration-heavy than mainstream hosted form builders.

economical.note: The community edition can be self-hosted, while hosted plans add convenience at subscription prices.

products.description: A serious open-source survey platform for organizations that want control, export depth and self-hosting more than instant consumer polish.

products.name: Nextcloud Forms

privacy.note: Forms keeps submissions inside the user's Nextcloud environment when installed on a Nextcloud server.

openness.note: Nextcloud Forms is published as an open-source Nextcloud app with public source code.

portability.note: The app listing describes exporting results, and the project positions Forms as a simple survey and questionnaire tool.

respect.note: Self-hosting through Nextcloud avoids sending form responses to a separate ad-funded or proprietary survey platform.

accessibility.note: The tool is straightforward for existing Nextcloud users, but it requires access to a Nextcloud instance.

economical.note: The app itself is free/open-source, though users still need a Nextcloud server or provider.

products.description: A simple open-source forms app for people already living in Nextcloud or willing to trade polish for self-hosted control.

products.name: CryptPad Forms

privacy.note: CryptPad says form data is end-to-end encrypted so even the hosted service cannot read it.

openness.note: CryptPad describes itself as an open-source, end-to-end encrypted collaborative office suite.

portability.note: CryptPad forms support response collection and collaboration, but the form app is less focused on broad analytics exports than survey suites.

respect.note: CryptPad emphasizes no ads, no data mining and granular access control for forms.

accessibility.note: The hosted app is usable without operating infrastructure, but encrypted collaboration has a smaller mainstream footprint.

economical.note: CryptPad offers hosted free use with paid storage plans, and the software can be self-hosted.

products.description: An encrypted open-source form option for sensitive small-group collection, strongest when privacy and non-extractive hosting matter more than analytics polish.

products.name: Docusign eSignature

privacy.note: Docusign documents encryption at rest and in transit, access controls, retention controls, and regional data storage for agreement data.

openness.note: Docusign eSignature is a proprietary hosted agreement platform rather than open-source or self-hostable software.

portability.note: Docusign documents envelope retention, purge controls and retained audit-log data used to attest transaction details.

respect.note: The privacy documentation gives customers some retention and key-management controls, but signature metadata remains part of the hosted agreement record.

accessibility.note: Docusign is a mainstream agreement platform with web, mobile, templates, integrations and broad signing recognition.

economical.note: Docusign's sending workflow is primarily sold through paid eSignature plans, making it less cost-accessible than free or self-hosted options.

products.description: The recognizable mainstream e-signature default: mature, secure and widely accepted, but proprietary, subscription-based and centered on hosted agreement metadata.

products.name: Adobe Acrobat Sign

privacy.note: Adobe publishes additional privacy information specifically for Acrobat Sign electronic signature services.

openness.note: Acrobat Sign is a proprietary Adobe cloud service, not an open-source or self-hosted signing tool.

portability.note: Acrobat Sign supports tracking, document status and signed-record workflows inside Adobe's PDF-centered signing platform.

respect.note: The service is strong for compliance workflows, but users remain inside Adobe's hosted account, PDF and plan ecosystem.

accessibility.note: Adobe sells Acrobat Sign as an integrated PDF and e-signature workflow for individual, team and business users.

economical.note: Adobe's business e-signature route is bundled into paid Acrobat or Acrobat Sign plans, with enterprise features behind sales-led tiers.

products.description: Adobe's PDF-native signing route, useful for organizations already in Acrobat workflows but weaker for openness, independence and low-cost simplicity.

products.name: Dropbox Sign

privacy.note: Dropbox Sign publishes privacy, security and compliance material for its signing services through its trust center.

openness.note: Dropbox Sign is a proprietary hosted service rather than open-source or self-hosted signing software.

portability.note: Dropbox Sign emphasizes tamperproof documents, complete audit trails and API-based signing workflows.

respect.note: Dropbox Sign has useful audit and security features, but its privacy policy describes personal data processing across Dropbox Sign services.

accessibility.note: Dropbox Sign is a polished mainstream signing workflow with templates, APIs and Dropbox account integration.

economical.note: Dropbox Sign offers individual and team paid plans, with the primary sending features priced per user or organization.

products.description: A clean commercial signing product, strongest for teams that want an easy hosted workflow and weaker for source transparency or self-hosted control.

products.name: PandaDoc

privacy.note: PandaDoc documents SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA and encryption controls for agreement and document workflows.

openness.note: PandaDoc is proprietary hosted document-workflow software rather than open-source or self-hostable infrastructure.

portability.note: PandaDoc includes document, template, API and integration workflows, but the editing and analytics experience stays inside the hosted platform.
