respect.note: The product is paid encrypted storage with security controls rather than an advertising-funded personal-data platform.

accessibility.note: Tresorit Basic works across desktop, mobile and web, but storage and device limits are tighter than mainstream free clouds.

economical.note: Tresorit has a small free Basic plan and paid personal plans; its privacy-first positioning comes with higher-cost storage than mainstream clouds.

products.description: A polished encrypted storage and sharing service for sensitive files, stronger on privacy than price or openness.

products.name: pCloud

privacy.note: pCloud markets Swiss privacy and secure storage, but zero-knowledge client-side encryption is a separate pCloud Encryption feature.

openness.note: pCloud is a proprietary hosted cloud storage product.

portability.note: pCloud is ordinary file storage with sync and sharing, so files are portable even though account features remain platform-bound.

respect.note: pCloud is subscription/lifetime storage rather than ad-social, but strongest zero-knowledge protections require using the encrypted folder feature.

accessibility.note: pCloud emphasizes access from any device, media playback, file sharing and automatic backup workflows.

economical.note: pCloud offers a free tier, subscription plans and lifetime-plan options.

products.description: A consumer-friendly cloud drive with good media/file usability and lifetime-plan appeal, but zero-knowledge protection is not the default whole-drive model.

products.name: Filen

privacy.note: Filen says it uses zero-knowledge client-side encryption and that the provider cannot access user files.

openness.note: Filen states that its apps are open source and publishes organization code repositories on GitHub.

portability.note: Filen offers sync, network-drive, CLI, WebDAV/S3 bridge and file-sharing workflows for moving ordinary files around.

respect.note: The service is built around paid encrypted storage, no hidden fees and no speed restrictions rather than advertising monetization.

accessibility.note: Filen supports web, desktop, mobile and CLI tools, but it is less mainstream than Apple, Google, Microsoft or Dropbox.

economical.note: Filen lists low-cost paid tiers and says encryption is included in the price, with free signup available.

products.description: A newer Germany-based encrypted cloud drive with open-source apps and strong privacy posture, but less mainstream polish and recognition.

products.name: Internxt

privacy.note: Internxt says files are automatically encrypted using end-to-end and post-quantum cryptography so only the user can access data.

openness.note: Internxt says its code is public on GitHub and can be reviewed and verified.

portability.note: Internxt Drive supports file sync and sharing, but advanced collaboration and versioning are more limited than mainstream suites.

respect.note: The product is framed around privacy, zero-knowledge encryption and open-source transparency rather than advertising data use.

accessibility.note: Internxt offers encrypted storage across common desktop, mobile and web workflows, but with a smaller ecosystem than mainstream clouds.

economical.note: Internxt pricing lists a free encrypted cloud-storage tier and paid annual, lifetime and business plans.

products.description: An open-source, zero-knowledge cloud storage option for privacy-first users who can accept a smaller feature ecosystem.

products.name: Backblaze Computer Backup

privacy.note: Backblaze encrypts backup data and offers a private encryption key option, but its architecture prioritizes transparent restore over fully self-managed encryption.

openness.note: Backblaze Computer Backup is a proprietary hosted backup service rather than open-source or self-hostable backup software.

portability.note: Backblaze supports download, B2 and USB restore routes, but the backup set is tied to Backblaze's hosted restore workflow.

respect.note: Backblaze remains a paid backup service rather than an ad platform, but 2026 reporting and official docs highlight exclusions and unlimited-use caveats users should inspect.

accessibility.note: Backblaze emphasizes automatic unlimited backup for Macs and PCs with simple restore-app and web restore options.

economical.note: Backblaze lists a flat personal price for unlimited computer backup, with monthly, yearly and two-year billing options.

products.description: A highly recognizable automatic computer-backup service with strong ease and price, but proprietary restore workflows and important exclusion/retention caveats.

products.name: IDrive Online Backup

privacy.note: IDrive uses AES-256 encryption and supports a private encryption key that it says is not stored on its servers.

openness.note: IDrive is a proprietary hosted backup service rather than open-source or self-hostable backup software.

portability.note: IDrive supports multiple-device backup, web/desktop/mobile restore and IDrive Express physical shipment for large backup or restore jobs.

respect.note: Private-key setup gives users stronger control, but default encryption and account-plan terms still require trusting the hosted provider.

accessibility.note: IDrive backs up PCs, Macs, Linux devices, iPhones, iPads and Android devices into one account.

economical.note: IDrive lists low-cost personal plans, but also discloses overuse charges if storage limits are exceeded.

products.description: A mainstream multi-device backup service with a stronger private-key option than many consumer defaults, but proprietary hosting and storage-plan limits.

products.name: Carbonite Safe

privacy.note: Carbonite markets encrypted automatic backup and documents a private-key option for Windows, but it remains a proprietary hosted backup service.

openness.note: Carbonite Safe is a closed, hosted OpenText consumer backup product rather than open-source or self-hostable software.

portability.note: Carbonite lets users restore selected files or full backups, but recovery depends on Carbonite's account, app and restore workflow.

respect.note: The model is paid backup rather than advertising, but bundled security-suite upsells and proprietary restore flows keep user control moderate.

accessibility.note: Carbonite emphasizes automatic, encrypted, unlimited backup and one-click file restoration for home users.

economical.note: Carbonite lists personal plans around a flat yearly computer-backup price with discounted promotional pricing.

products.description: A familiar consumer backup floor: easy, automatic and flat-priced, but closed and less portable than user-controlled backup stacks.

products.name: Arq Backup

privacy.note: Arq says backups are encrypted before upload and the encryption password never leaves the user's computer.

openness.note: Arq is proprietary software, even though it lets users choose external storage destinations instead of only Arq's cloud.

portability.note: Arq backs up to a cloud account, attached disk or both, explicitly positioning itself around no vendor lock-in.

respect.note: Arq's paid app model and user-chosen storage reduce platform dependence compared with all-in-one hosted backup defaults.

accessibility.note: Arq supports Mac and Windows with support included, but users must still understand backup destinations and storage choices.

economical.note: Arq lists a one-time per-computer app price and a Premium subscription including storage for up to five computers.

products.description: A paid backup app for people who want client-side encryption and control over storage location without going fully command-line.

products.name: Duplicati

privacy.note: Duplicati says backup data is encrypted locally with AES-256 before reaching the network or cloud.

openness.note: Duplicati is free and open source, with public code and a backup client for encrypted incremental backups.

portability.note: Duplicati supports many storage backends, including S3, Backblaze B2, Box, Dropbox, Google Drive, MEGA, OneDrive, SFTP and WebDAV.

respect.note: The free local backup client gives users control of encryption and storage destination, though hosted monitoring features introduce optional service dependence.

accessibility.note: Duplicati offers a graphical backup client, but users still need to choose and maintain a storage target.

economical.note: Duplicati lists a free plan for basic use and optional paid monitoring/management tiers.

products.description: An open-source backup client for encrypted backups to many cloud or remote storage targets, stronger on control than novice simplicity.

products.name: restic

privacy.note: restic describes itself as using cryptography carefully in every part of the backup process.

openness.note: restic is open-source software licensed under the BSD 2-Clause License.

portability.note: restic backs up Linux, BSD, Mac and Windows systems to many storage types, including self-hosted and online services.

respect.note: A local command-line backup tool has no advertising model or hosted account dependency unless the user chooses a hosted storage backend.

accessibility.note: restic is a single executable, but its command-line workflow and storage-backend setup make it more technical than consumer backup apps.

economical.note: restic is free software; user cost comes from the storage target they choose.

products.description: A respected open-source command-line backup tool for people who want portable encrypted backups and can manage their own storage target.

products.name: Kopia

privacy.note: Kopia uses end-to-end encryption with user-controlled keys before backup data leaves the machine.

openness.note: Kopia describes itself as fast and secure open-source backup software, with public source available.

portability.note: Kopia can save encrypted snapshots to remote/cloud storage, network storage, a server or local storage chosen by the user.

respect.note: Kopia is a local open-source tool where users choose storage and keys, avoiding ad or hosted-account dependence by default.

accessibility.note: Kopia supports GUI and CLI workflows on Windows, macOS and Linux, making it more approachable than CLI-only backup tools.

economical.note: Kopia is free open-source software; user cost depends on the storage location they choose.

products.description: An open-source encrypted backup tool with GUI and CLI options for users who want strong key control without fully giving up usability.

products.name: Cryptomator

privacy.note: Cryptomator encrypts cloud files client-side so encrypted vault contents are useless without the user's key.

openness.note: Cryptomator is provided as a free open-source project with public source repositories.

portability.note: Cryptomator pricing says personal vaults work with any cloud storage, though supported services vary by platform.

respect.note: The project is donation-supported with optional paid mobile apps and no ad-surveillance model.

accessibility.note: Cryptomator's desktop app is free and designed as a more accessible cloud-encryption route than technical command-line tools.

economical.note: Cryptomator lists free personal desktop use, with optional one-time mobile purchases and upgrades.

products.description: A user-friendly open-source vault app for encrypting files before they sync through Dropbox, Google Drive, iCloud, OneDrive or another cloud.

products.name: VeraCrypt

privacy.note: VeraCrypt is disk/container encryption software for creating encrypted volumes or encrypting storage devices.

openness.note: VeraCrypt publishes source and license terms, though its mixed TrueCrypt-derived licensing is more complex than a simple permissive license.

portability.note: VeraCrypt downloads are available for Windows, macOS and Linux, supporting cross-platform encrypted containers.

respect.note: VeraCrypt is local encryption software with no hosted account or advertising model.

accessibility.note: VeraCrypt is powerful but more technical than consumer cloud-vault tools because users must manage volumes, mounts and passwords carefully.

economical.note: VeraCrypt is distributed as free open-source disk encryption software.

products.description: A durable encrypted-container and disk-encryption tool for users comfortable managing volumes and recovery risk directly.

products.name: Picocrypt

privacy.note: Picocrypt uses XChaCha20 and Argon2id for simple file encryption.

openness.note: Picocrypt is public source software under the GPL-3.0 license.

portability.note: Picocrypt is designed as a small file-encryption tool rather than a cloud-sync platform, so encrypted outputs are portable but workflow integration is limited.

respect.note: The original project is archived and read-only, which keeps it usable but limits ongoing maintenance and responsiveness.

accessibility.note: Picocrypt emphasizes drag-and-drop simplicity for encrypting and decrypting files.

economical.note: Picocrypt is free software with public source code.

products.description: A tiny drag-and-drop file-encryption tool that is easy to understand, but now archived and less suitable as a long-term default.

products.name: rclone crypt

privacy.note: rclone crypt performs client-side encryption before upload and leaves data encrypted at rest in the wrapped remote.

openness.note: rclone describes itself as mature open-source software inspired by rsync.

portability.note: rclone supports more than 70 storage products and virtual backends including crypt, making encrypted storage highly portable across providers.

respect.note: The tool is local and user-controlled; users choose the storage backend and encryption layer rather than adopting a hosted account model.

accessibility.note: rclone is primarily command-line software, powerful for technical users but less approachable for ordinary cloud-storage users.

economical.note: rclone is free open-source software; user cost comes from whichever storage provider they choose.

products.description: A technical but powerful way to add client-side encryption across many cloud storage providers and backup targets.

products.name: age

privacy.note: age is designed as a simple modern secure file-encryption tool and format with small explicit keys.

openness.note: age is public source software under a BSD-3-Clause license.

portability.note: age provides a file-encryption format, Go library and interoperable implementations, but it is not a full cloud-sync or GUI vault.

respect.note: age is a local tool and format with no hosted account, advertising or tracking business model.

accessibility.note: age is intentionally simple for command-line users, but still expects comfort with keys, recipients and terminal workflows.

economical.note: age is free open-source software.

products.description: A modern command-line file-encryption tool for technical users who want a small, auditable format rather than a hosted service.

products.name: GnuPG

privacy.note: GnuPG implements OpenPGP and lets users encrypt and sign data and communications.

openness.note: GnuPG is a complete free implementation of the OpenPGP standard with free-software distribution routes.

portability.note: GnuPG is a standard-backed tool with frontends and libraries, but practical use depends on compatible key and recipient workflows.

respect.note: GnuPG is local cryptographic software rather than a hosted account or ad-backed platform.

accessibility.note: GnuPG is powerful but its key-management model and command-line roots create a steep learning curve for many users.

economical.note: GnuPG is free software and commonly available through operating-system package channels.

products.description: The classic OpenPGP route for encrypting and signing files or messages: powerful and open, but difficult for everyday users.

products.name: hat.sh

privacy.note: hat.sh provides local in-browser file encryption using chunked AEAD stream encryption and decryption.

openness.note: hat.sh is public source software under the MIT license.

portability.note: Because hat.sh runs in the browser, encrypted outputs can be made on many systems without installing a native app.

respect.note: The tool is local file encryption rather than a cloud account, though browser-delivered crypto requires trusting the loaded web app version.

accessibility.note: A browser UI makes one-off file encryption easier than command-line tools, while still requiring users to manage passwords and encrypted outputs.

economical.note: hat.sh is free public-source software.

products.description: A lightweight browser-based file-encryption tool for quick local encryption, best used with awareness of web-app supply-chain trust.

products.name: 7-Zip encrypted archives

privacy.note: 7-Zip supports AES-256 encryption in 7z archives, but this is archive/password encryption rather than a full key-managed vault or sync tool.

openness.note: 7-Zip is free software with open source, mostly under GNU LGPL with some BSD and unRAR license restrictions.

portability.note: 7z archives are portable files, but recipients need compatible extraction software and password handling.

respect.note: 7-Zip is local archive software with no hosted account, ad tracking or subscription model.

accessibility.note: 7-Zip is widely used and integrates with Windows file workflows, making basic encrypted archives approachable for many users.

economical.note: 7-Zip is free to use on any computer, including in commercial organizations.

products.description: The familiar archive-tool route for encrypting a file bundle: easy and free, but less purpose-built than dedicated cloud or key-management encryption tools.

products.name: WeTransfer

privacy.note: WeTransfer's privacy policy says it processes uploaded user content, account/contact data, usage data, technical data, cookies, and advertising or measurement partner data.

openness.note: The core consumer transfer service is a proprietary hosted product rather than an open-source protocol or self-hostable tool.

portability.note: Transfers are simple download links, but files are only available for the service's stated retention period and deeper export/control depends on the account and plan context.

respect.note: The mainstream free transfer model is convenient, but the privacy policy allows marketing, advertising measurement, cookies, inferred information, and partner data use.

accessibility.note: Browser-based transfer links make WeTransfer easy for nontechnical senders and recipients, including people who do not want to install software.

economical.note: WeTransfer offers free file sending and paid plans for heavier use, branding, storage, and collaboration features.

products.description: Popular browser-based file transfer service with very low friction and a clear convenience floor, but weaker privacy and openness than encrypted or open-source sharing tools.

products.name: Dropbox Transfer

privacy.note: Dropbox's privacy policy says it processes account data, files and related content, contacts, usage data, device data, cookies, and may share data with service providers, affiliates, admins, and collaborators.

openness.note: Dropbox Transfer is a proprietary Dropbox service rather than an open-source transfer protocol or self-hostable application.

portability.note: Recipients can download transfer files without a Dropbox account, and transfer expiration/delete controls give senders a defined file handoff model.

respect.note: Transfers are recipient-friendly, but Dropbox remains an account-based cloud platform with broad operational data processing and paid controls such as custom expiration and passwords.

accessibility.note: Dropbox says Transfer is available to all Dropbox users and recipients do not need a Dropbox account to receive files.

economical.note: Basic users can send transfers up to 2 GB, while larger transfer sizes and advanced controls are tied to paid Dropbox plans.

products.description: Dropbox's dedicated transfer product is easy for existing Dropbox users and recipients, with strong mainstream usability but proprietary cloud-platform tradeoffs.

products.name: SwissTransfer

privacy.note: SwissTransfer is operated by Infomaniak, whose privacy policy emphasizes Swiss-hosted services and GDPR/Swiss-law-oriented data protection commitments.

openness.note: SwissTransfer is a proprietary hosted transfer service, not an open-source or self-hostable file transfer project.

portability.note: Infomaniak's SwissTransfer FAQ says recipients can download files individually or as a ZIP archive.

respect.note: SwissTransfer positions itself as a free, secure, privacy-conscious alternative and does not center advertising or account lock-in in the transfer flow.

accessibility.note: The service supports browser-based transfers up to 50 GB, but Infomaniak lists a number of countries where creation is unavailable.

economical.note: SwissTransfer is presented as a free service for sending large files, with the FAQ describing free transfers up to 50 GB.

products.description: Free large-file transfer service from Infomaniak with strong value for simple sharing, though it remains proprietary and creation is unavailable in some countries.

products.name: Wormhole

privacy.note: Wormhole's security documentation says files are encrypted in the browser before upload, the encryption key stays in the URL fragment, and the server never receives that key.

openness.note: Wormhole documents its browser encryption design, but the hosted consumer service is not presented as a fully open-source, self-hostable project.

portability.note: Transfers produce expiring links, and recipients can download the original file without joining a cloud drive ecosystem.

respect.note: Wormhole's legal and security materials emphasize not collecting sensitive file contents and using end-to-end encryption for shared files.

accessibility.note: The web app supports simple browser-based sending up to 10 GB with expiring links, making private transfer usable without command-line tools.

economical.note: Wormhole presents its transfer service as free to use for browser-based encrypted file sending.

products.description: Browser-friendly encrypted file transfer with expiring links and a strong privacy design, though it is less open than fully self-hostable tools.

products.name: OnionShare

privacy.note: OnionShare is designed for secure and anonymous file sharing, website hosting, and chat over Tor onion services.

openness.note: OnionShare describes itself as open source and GPLv3 licensed, with public documentation and source code.

portability.note: OnionShare is available for Windows, macOS, Linux, and privacy-focused systems such as Qubes OS, Tails, and Parrot OS.

respect.note: The project is built around user-controlled anonymous sharing rather than account lock-in, advertising, or behavioral monetization.

accessibility.note: Desktop apps are available, but users need Tor-oriented workflows and both sides must handle onion-service links, which raises the usability floor.

economical.note: OnionShare is free software distributed under the GPLv3 license.

products.description: Open-source Tor-based sharing tool for people who need anonymity and control more than mainstream convenience.

products.name: LocalSend

privacy.note: LocalSend's privacy policy says the app does not collect, store, process, or use personal or non-personal data.

openness.note: LocalSend is open source and licensed under Apache License 2.0.

portability.note: LocalSend is cross-platform and designed to share files nearby without needing an internet connection.

respect.note: The project is free, local-first, accountless, and does not use advertising or data collection as a service model.

accessibility.note: Graphical apps across common platforms make local network sharing much easier than command-line or Tor-based transfer tools.

economical.note: LocalSend is free software with public source code and no subscription requirement.

products.description: Open-source local-network file sharing app for sending files between nearby devices without accounts, cloud storage, or internet dependency.

products.name: PairDrop

privacy.note: PairDrop's project documentation describes peer-to-peer local transfer in the browser, with internet transfers supported through temporary public rooms and relay fallback when needed.

openness.note: PairDrop is open source and licensed under GPL-3.0.

portability.note: PairDrop works in modern browsers and can move images, documents, and text across platforms without installing a native app.

respect.note: The service emphasizes no setup, no sign-up, temporary rooms, and direct sharing instead of a cloud-storage account model.

accessibility.note: A browser-first interface makes PairDrop approachable for quick cross-device sharing, though network and browser conditions can still affect transfers.

economical.note: PairDrop is free to use and its source code is public under GPL-3.0.

products.description: Open-source browser-based device-to-device sharing tool, strongest for quick local or paired transfers without making a cloud account.

products.name: Magic Wormhole

privacy.note: Magic Wormhole uses single-use wormhole codes to move files, directories, or text between computers without putting them into a long-lived cloud account.

openness.note: Magic Wormhole is an open-source project with public source code and documentation.

portability.note: The project supports arbitrary-sized files, directories, and text, and is available as a library and command-line tool.

respect.note: The single-use-code design supports intentional one-time transfers instead of account lock-in, advertising, or persistent cloud hosting.

accessibility.note: Magic Wormhole is powerful for technical users, but its primary command-line workflow makes it less approachable than browser or graphical transfer apps.

economical.note: Magic Wormhole is free and open-source software.

products.description: Open-source command-line transfer tool for deliberate one-time sends, excellent for technical users and less suitable as a mainstream family-and-friends default.

products.name: Google Photos

privacy.note: Google Photos says photo data is not used for ads, but the service still sits inside a broad Google account and cloud ecosystem.

openness.note: Google Photos is a proprietary Google service rather than an open-source or federated photo library.

portability.note: Google Takeout supports exporting Google Photos data, though albums, sharing context and AI organization remain platform-bound.

respect.note: The service emphasizes private backup and control, but AI organization and Google-account integration create a larger data relationship than encrypted-first tools.

accessibility.note: Google Photos is widely available, easy to search and organize, and designed for automatic backup across mainstream devices.

economical.note: Google offers 15 GB of shared account storage before paid Google One plans are needed.

products.description: The default photo backup for many Android and Google-account households: extremely easy, searchable and portable enough to export, but proprietary and not end-to-end encrypted.

products.name: iCloud Photos

privacy.note: Apple says iCloud Photos stores full-resolution originals in iCloud, and Advanced Data Protection can extend end-to-end encryption to Photos when enabled.

openness.note: iCloud Photos is a proprietary Apple cloud service, not an open-source or federated photo system.

portability.note: Apple documents ways to download copies of iCloud photos and videos, but the tightest experience stays inside Apple devices and Photos libraries.

respect.note: The strongest privacy posture depends on users enabling Advanced Data Protection, while non-Apple workflows remain less central.

accessibility.note: For Apple-device users, iCloud Photos is built into the system and syncs photos and edits across devices automatically.

economical.note: Apple includes 5 GB of free iCloud storage, with larger iCloud+ storage tiers requiring a paid plan.

products.description: The native Apple photo sync layer: excellent for iPhone and Mac households, with optional stronger iCloud encryption, but proprietary and ecosystem-shaped.

products.name: Amazon Photos

privacy.note: Amazon Photos is governed by Amazon's broader privacy notice and account ecosystem rather than end-to-end encrypted photo storage.

openness.note: Amazon Photos is a proprietary Amazon service, not an open-source or federated photo platform.

portability.note: Amazon help documents downloading photos and videos, but albums, sharing and account features remain Amazon-bound.

respect.note: The service is convenient for Prime and Alexa/Fire TV households, but the data relationship is tied to a large commerce and device platform.

accessibility.note: Amazon Photos supports automatic backup, sharing and mainstream device access, especially for Amazon-account households.

economical.note: Amazon advertises free photo storage for Prime members and a limited free tier for other Amazon customers.

products.description: A convenient photo-backup option for Amazon and Prime households, with strong ease and price appeal but weaker privacy and openness signals.

products.name: Ente Photos

privacy.note: Ente says photos, videos and metadata are end-to-end encrypted before upload, with zero-knowledge storage.

openness.note: Ente publishes its client and server code as open source and documents self-hosting for the same codebase.

portability.note: Ente provides cross-platform apps, export paths and a self-hosting route, reducing lock-in compared with mainstream clouds.

respect.note: The product is built around paid, private storage rather than ad targeting or broad platform data reuse.

accessibility.note: Ente offers polished mobile, desktop and web apps, though it is still less universally preinstalled than Google, Apple or Amazon defaults.

economical.note: Ente offers a free starting tier and paid encrypted storage plans, so it is accessible but not the cheapest at large libraries.

products.description: A polished end-to-end encrypted photo backup service for people who want mainstream usability without handing their library to an advertising or device ecosystem.

products.name: Immich

privacy.note: Immich is self-hosted, so privacy depends on the user's own server and backup hygiene rather than a third-party photo cloud.

openness.note: Immich publishes its source code under an open license for a self-hosted photo and video management server.

portability.note: Self-hosting keeps the media library under user control, but users must manage exports, storage and backups themselves.

respect.note: The project is community/open-source infrastructure rather than an ad-funded or closed photo platform.

accessibility.note: Immich provides familiar mobile backup and photo-library features, but setup and maintenance require server comfort.

economical.note: The software is free to run, but users bear hosting, storage, backup and administration costs.

products.description: A leading open-source self-hosted photo backup and library for people who want Google Photos-like convenience under their own control.

products.name: PhotoPrism

privacy.note: PhotoPrism is self-hosted personal photo-management software, so library control depends on the user's own deployment and storage choices.

openness.note: PhotoPrism publishes its source code and describes itself as free open-source software for photo management.

portability.note: PhotoPrism organizes existing photo files without requiring import into a closed hosted service, but migration still depends on user storage layout.

respect.note: The product is a self-hosted library and membership-supported project, not an advertising photo network.

accessibility.note: PhotoPrism is powerful for self-hosters but less turnkey for automatic phone backup than mainstream cloud-photo apps.

economical.note: The community edition can be self-hosted without a license fee, while paid memberships support extra features and the project.

products.description: A mature self-hosted photo library and organizer for people who want local control, search and curation more than turnkey consumer-cloud backup.

products.name: Flickr

privacy.note: Flickr's privacy notice describes account, device, EXIF, location, cookie and advertising/analytics data collection.

openness.note: Flickr is a proprietary hosted photo community rather than an open-source or federated photo protocol.

portability.note: Flickr supports downloading account data and media, but audience, comments, groups and social context are platform-bound.

respect.note: The service has meaningful sharing controls, but its privacy notice includes ad, analytics and third-party service integrations.

accessibility.note: Flickr remains a large, recognizable photo-hosting community with albums, sharing, discovery and mobile access.

economical.note: Flickr's free accounts are limited, while Pro unlocks higher capacity and broader account features.

products.description: A recognizable photo-hosting community with strong discoverability and sharing, but a proprietary social platform and a more complex privacy/ads surface.

products.name: SmugMug

privacy.note: SmugMug's privacy policy describes account, photo, EXIF/location and site-usage data collection, with owner-controlled gallery privacy settings.

openness.note: SmugMug is a proprietary paid photo-hosting service, not an open-source or federated photo library.

portability.note: SmugMug help documents downloading owner photos and gallery images, but site design, sales tools and audience live inside the hosted service.

respect.note: SmugMug markets full-resolution paid photo storage with privacy controls and no photo-mining or selling claim.

accessibility.note: The service is polished for photographers and client galleries, but it is less universal as a default household backup tool.

economical.note: SmugMug is primarily a paid subscription service after trial, making it less cost-flexible than free or freemium photo backup.

products.description: A paid, photographer-oriented hosting service with full-resolution storage and privacy controls, trading openness and low cost for polished galleries and control.

products.name: LinkedIn

privacy.note: LinkedIn's privacy policy covers profile, contact, usage, ad, plugin and Microsoft-affiliate data collection and use.

openness.note: LinkedIn is a closed professional network rather than an open social protocol.

portability.note: LinkedIn lets members download account data, but professional graph, recommendations and audience reach remain platform-bound.

respect.note: The service is useful for work, but the privacy policy describes ads, plugins, inference and AI-supported personalization across a professional graph.

accessibility.note: Very accessible for professional identity, job search, recruiting and business networking.

economical.note: Core account use is free, with paid Premium, recruiting and sales products.

products.description: The mainstream professional graph: highly useful for work and hiring, but closed, data-rich, and hard to leave socially.

products.name: YouTube

privacy.note: YouTube Help says search and watch history can improve recommendations and make ads more relevant.

openness.note: YouTube is a proprietary Google video platform rather than an open video commons.

portability.note: Google Takeout can export YouTube/account data, but subscriber graph, recommendations and audience reach do not migrate cleanly.

respect.note: YouTube's own privacy materials describe activity-based recommendations and ad personalization controls, signaling a strong attention/ad model.

accessibility.note: Extremely broad web/mobile/TV access, creator supply and search make it one of the easiest media services to use.

economical.note: Core viewing is free with ads; Premium is a paid ad-free tier.

products.description: The default online video platform: unmatched access and creator reach, paired with Google data, ads, recommendations, and lock-in.

products.name: Lemmy

privacy.note: Lemmy avoids a central ad-tracking company, but privacy still depends on the server and what users post publicly.

openness.note: Lemmy is open source and its official repository describes it as an AGPL decentralized link aggregator/forum for the fediverse.

portability.note: Lemmy is federated over ActivityPub, so users can interact across servers, though account and moderation portability still depend on instance tooling.

respect.note: Lemmy's homepage describes no tracking, no advertising, no secret algorithms and donation-funded open development.

accessibility.note: Choosing an instance adds friction, but Lemmy has web access and multiple apps across iOS, Android, desktop and web.

economical.note: Lemmy is free/open software, with servers typically run by communities or donations rather than users paying a platform fee.

products.description: A federated, open-source discussion platform that gives Reddit-like forums a community-run alternative.

products.name: Pixelfed

privacy.note: Pixelfed is instance-based and avoids a central Instagram-style ad graph, but privacy depends on the chosen server and public posting choices.

openness.note: Pixelfed is open-source AGPL software for federated photo sharing.

portability.note: Pixelfed participates in the ActivityPub fediverse, allowing interoperability with compatible federated platforms.

respect.note: Pixelfed positions itself as decentralized photo sharing rather than algorithmic ad-feed social media.

accessibility.note: The Instagram-like format is familiar, but instance choice and smaller network effects add friction.

economical.note: Pixelfed is free/open software; user costs depend on the instance or self-hosting.

products.description: A federated, open-source photo sharing network that offers an Instagram-like experience without one central platform owner.

products.name: PeerTube

privacy.note: PeerTube is instance-based and avoids one central video-ad profile, though privacy and moderation depend on the host instance.

openness.note: PeerTube is free/open-source AGPL software for self-hosted and federated video hosting.

portability.note: PeerTube is ActivityPub-federated and supports a network of interoperable video hosting providers.

respect.note: PeerTube explicitly presents itself as a decentralized alternative to platforms that centralize data and attention.

accessibility.note: It supports web video and live streaming, but discovery and creator reach are much smaller than YouTube.

economical.note: PeerTube is free/open software; hosting a serious video instance still carries server and bandwidth costs.

products.description: A federated, open-source video platform for communities that want self-hosted alternatives to central video networks.

products.name: Threads

privacy.note: Threads has a supplemental privacy notice on top of Meta's broader policy, with Threads-specific collection and processing details.

openness.note: Threads has fediverse sharing features, but they are opt-in and the service remains a Meta/Instagram-controlled platform.

portability.note: Threads offers official data download/export tools, though social reach and network position do not fully port.

respect.note: Threads is tied to Meta's social-feed and recommendation ecosystem, so its incentives still lean toward engagement growth and data use.

accessibility.note: Threads was built by Instagram's team and launched as a mainstream text-sharing app using Instagram accounts.

economical.note: Threads is free to use, with the tradeoff of operating inside Meta's advertising and data ecosystem.

products.description: Meta's mainstream text-social network, easy to join from Instagram but still embedded in a large ad-funded platform stack.

products.name: Snapchat

privacy.note: Snap's privacy policy describes collection from user-provided information, app use, other users, affiliates and third parties.

openness.note: Snapchat is a proprietary social-camera platform rather than an open protocol or self-hostable service.

portability.note: Snapchat has a Download My Data process, but social graph, lenses, streaks and reach are not meaningfully portable.

respect.note: Snapchat's policy includes advertising, measurement, personalization and third-party data contexts, which weakens user-respecting incentives.

accessibility.note: Snapchat is a highly polished mainstream mobile camera and messaging app with a low barrier to casual use.

economical.note: Snapchat is free to use, with advertising and optional paid features shaping the business model.

products.description: A mainstream social camera and messaging app with polished usability but weak openness and data-portability tradeoffs.

products.name: Pinterest

privacy.note: Pinterest's privacy policy says collected information is used for personalized content, recommendations and ads.

openness.note: Pinterest is a proprietary discovery and social-commerce platform rather than an open protocol.

portability.note: Pinterest offers privacy and data settings, but boards, recommendations, followers and shopping/discovery context do not fully port away.

respect.note: Pinterest's personalization help explains that activity on and off Pinterest can inform personalized experiences and ads.

accessibility.note: Pinterest has a familiar, low-friction visual search and inspiration workflow across web and mobile.

economical.note: Pinterest is free to use, with advertising and commerce incentives supporting the platform.

products.description: A visual discovery platform that is useful for ideas and shopping inspiration, but strongly tied to personalization and ad incentives.

products.name: Twitch

privacy.note: Twitch's privacy notice describes data collection and use for recommendations, advertising, marketing, payments, community features and chat.

openness.note: Twitch is a proprietary Amazon-owned live-streaming platform rather than an open protocol or self-hostable network.

portability.note: Twitch privacy choices include access/copy requests for personal data, but audience, chat history and monetization are platform-bound.

respect.note: Twitch supports real communities, but recommendations, advertising, marketing, subscriptions and paid engagement create attention-platform incentives.

accessibility.note: Twitch makes live streaming and chat easy across web, mobile and TV-style viewing contexts.

economical.note: Twitch is free to watch, with optional subscriptions, Bits and other paid features layered on top.

products.description: A dominant live-streaming and chat platform that is easy to use, but proprietary and driven by attention, ads and platform monetization.

products.name: Quad9

privacy.note: Quad9 says normal use logs no data containing a user's IP address and treats IP addresses as personally identifiable information.

openness.note: Quad9 publishes service profiles, setup options and governance information, but ordinary users consume a hosted resolver rather than running a self-hosted stack.

portability.note: Quad9 can be configured directly by IP, DNS-over-HTTPS, DNS-over-TLS or DNSCrypt on routers and devices.

respect.note: Quad9 is operated by the Swiss-based Quad9 Foundation as a free security and privacy DNS service, not as an advertising platform.

accessibility.note: Quad9 can be used without an account or contract, but changing DNS settings is still more technical than installing a normal app.

economical.note: Quad9 describes the resolver as a free service.

products.description: A free Swiss public DNS resolver that blocks malicious domains while making unusually strong privacy commitments for DNS.

products.name: NextDNS

privacy.note: NextDNS says it does not sell or share user data, logs nothing unless requested, and lets users export or delete retained data.

openness.note: NextDNS publishes several public repositories, including its CLI client and blocklist metadata, but the hosted service itself is not a fully self-hostable stack.

portability.note: NextDNS supports DNS-over-HTTPS and DNS-over-TLS setup across major platforms and stores configurable settings in portable profiles.

respect.note: NextDNS is a paid-aligned firewall service with blocklists, logging controls and data residency options rather than an ad-funded attention product.

accessibility.note: NextDNS says setup is natively supported on major platforms and can be tried without signup, while advanced configuration adds some learning curve.

economical.note: NextDNS has a free tier capped at 300,000 queries per month and paid personal plans for unlimited queries.

products.description: A flexible DNS firewall for people who want malware, tracker, parental-control and analytics controls without running their own server.

products.name: AdGuard DNS

privacy.note: AdGuard says public AdGuard DNS processes no personal data and its privacy policy emphasizes minimization.

openness.note: AdGuard Home is free and open-source network-wide DNS blocking software, though the hosted AdGuard DNS service remains a managed product.

portability.note: AdGuard DNS works through public DNS servers, personal DNS profiles and router/device setup rather than requiring one browser extension.

respect.note: AdGuard DNS is built around blocking ads, trackers and malicious domains, but it is also part of a broader paid AdGuard product ecosystem.

accessibility.note: AdGuard DNS offers public free servers and paid personal DNS dashboards, with guides for many devices.

economical.note: AdGuard says public DNS servers are free and a Starter plan is available, with paid personal and team plans for advanced use.

products.description: A polished DNS filtering service that can block ads, trackers, malware and family-unsafe content, with a self-hostable sibling in AdGuard Home.

products.name: Pi-hole

privacy.note: Pi-hole runs on hardware you control, so DNS logs and blocklists can stay on the local network instead of a third-party resolver.

openness.note: Pi-hole is open-source software with public source code, issue tracking and install methods.

portability.note: Pi-hole can protect all devices using a network DNS server, but it depends on maintaining local hardware or a server.

respect.note: Pi-hole is a community-supported blocking tool rather than a hosted advertising or data-brokerage service.

accessibility.note: Pi-hole has an automated installer and web dashboard, but setup still requires router or server administration.

economical.note: Pi-hole describes itself as free open-source software, though users need their own hardware or hosting.

products.description: A self-hosted DNS sinkhole for people comfortable maintaining a small server and wanting local control over network-wide blocking.

products.name: RethinkDNS

privacy.note: RethinkDNS routes DNS through encrypted DNS protocols and is positioned around blocking spyware, ads and trackers across apps.

openness.note: RethinkDNS describes its app as free and open source, and publishes the Android firewall/DNS client repository under Apache-2.0.

portability.note: RethinkDNS is strongest on Android with DNS, firewall and WireGuard modes, while cross-platform use centers on DNS resolver configuration.

respect.note: RethinkDNS frames the product as user control over the translation layer, not an advertising or engagement platform.

accessibility.note: RethinkDNS can be configured for free, but its strongest features are power-user DNS and Android firewall controls.

economical.note: RethinkDNS says the app is free and open source and the cloud DNS service has a free tier.

products.description: An open-source DNS and Android firewall toolkit for people who want to see and constrain what apps are doing on the network.

products.name: Control D

privacy.note: Control D says its free DNS servers do not store individual browsing history, timestamps or logs.

openness.note: Control D is a hosted commercial DNS service; it publishes setup docs and an open-source router daemon, but not the full hosted platform.

portability.note: Control D supports modern encrypted DNS protocols and multiple filtering configurations across devices and routers.

respect.note: Control D offers explicit malware, ads, tracking, social and family filtering profiles instead of an ad-funded consumer platform.

accessibility.note: Control D provides quick free DNS setups and custom configurations, with more complex controls in paid business plans.

economical.note: Control D offers free public DNS profiles plus paid SMB and enterprise plans.

products.description: A practical hosted DNS filtering service with free profiles and more granular paid controls for households, schools and teams.

products.name: Cloudflare 1.1.1.1

privacy.note: Cloudflare says 1.1.1.1 will not sell/share resolver personal data for ads, truncates IPs, and deletes public resolver logs within 25 hours.

openness.note: Cloudflare publishes resolver documentation and setup details, but 1.1.1.1 is a proprietary hosted Cloudflare service.

portability.note: 1.1.1.1 can be configured on devices and routers and supports encrypted DNS setup paths including DoH and DoT.

respect.note: Cloudflare's resolver is not ad-targeted and offers optional Families filtering, though it remains part of a very large infrastructure company.

accessibility.note: Cloudflare provides simple apps and device/router setup guides, making 1.1.1.1 one of the easiest DNS switches for mainstream users.

economical.note: Cloudflare markets 1.1.1.1 as a free app and public resolver, with optional paid WARP+ features.

products.description: A very accessible public DNS resolver with clear privacy commitments, but still a proprietary hosted service from a major infrastructure company.

products.name: Google Public DNS

privacy.note: Google says Public DNS does not use personal data for ad targeting, but temporary logs include IP address and query details for 24-48 hours.

openness.note: Google Public DNS is a proprietary hosted resolver with public documentation, not an open-source or self-hostable resolver stack.

portability.note: Google Public DNS works through standard IPs and also supports DNS-over-TLS and DNS-over-HTTPS.

respect.note: Google does not use Public DNS personal information for ad targeting, but the service still routes DNS through Google's broader ecosystem.

accessibility.note: Google Public DNS is easy to configure using memorable IP addresses and widely documented setup instructions.

economical.note: Google describes Public DNS as a free global DNS resolution service.

products.description: A free and technically solid public resolver, but less values-aligned for privacy-first users because it sends DNS to Google and keeps temporary query logs.

products.name: OpenDNS FamilyShield

privacy.note: OpenDNS is now part of Cisco and points users to Cisco's broad privacy statement for Personal Data processing and sharing practices.

openness.note: OpenDNS FamilyShield is a proprietary Cisco-hosted DNS service, not an open-source or self-hostable resolver.

portability.note: OpenDNS settings apply at the device or home-network level and can cover laptops, phones, game consoles, TVs and other connected devices.

respect.note: FamilyShield provides preconfigured family and phishing protection, but with lower transparency and more enterprise-platform lock-in than smaller privacy-first resolvers.

accessibility.note: OpenDNS FamilyShield is preconfigured and designed as a set-it-and-forget-it household DNS option.

economical.note: OpenDNS lists FamilyShield as free.

products.description: A simple free family-filtering DNS option from Cisco/OpenDNS, useful as a floor comparison for ease versus privacy and openness.

products.name: CleanBrowsing

privacy.note: CleanBrowsing says free DNS filters do not log or store personally identifiable information such as IP addresses tied to requests.

openness.note: CleanBrowsing publishes free resolver addresses and documentation, but the resolver and filtering platform are proprietary services.

portability.note: CleanBrowsing provides IPv4, IPv6, DNS-over-HTTPS and DNS-over-TLS options for family, adult and security filters.

respect.note: CleanBrowsing is focused on safety and content filtering, with free filters and paid configurable options rather than advertising incentives.

accessibility.note: CleanBrowsing offers no-account free filters and setup articles, though DNS setup is still more technical than app-store installation.

economical.note: CleanBrowsing offers free DNS filters and paid plans with more filters, support and configurability.

products.description: A family- and safety-oriented DNS filtering service with free resolvers and more configurable paid plans.

products.name: Mullvad DNS

privacy.note: Mullvad says it keeps no activity logs and its public encrypted DNS protects queries between device and DNS server.

openness.note: Mullvad publishes detailed DNS setup docs and configuration profiles, but the public resolver is still a hosted Mullvad service.

portability.note: Mullvad DNS supports DNS-over-HTTPS and DNS-over-TLS across browsers, Android, iOS, Windows, macOS and Linux.

respect.note: Mullvad offers privacy-oriented DNS with optional blockers for ads, trackers, malware, adult content, gambling and social media.

accessibility.note: Mullvad provides clear setup instructions, but encrypted DNS configuration still requires manual device or browser changes.

economical.note: Mullvad's public encrypted DNS documentation does not require a paid VPN account to use the resolver endpoints.

products.description: A privacy-oriented encrypted DNS service from Mullvad with optional blocking profiles and strong no-logging posture.

products.name: DNS4EU

privacy.note: DNS4EU says client IP addresses are anonymised before logging, no private data is collected, and the service aligns with GDPR.

openness.note: DNS4EU publishes resolver options and policies, but the public resolver is an operated service rather than an open self-hosted project.

portability.note: DNS4EU offers IPv4, IPv6, DNS-over-HTTPS and DNS-over-TLS endpoints across protective, child-protection, ad-blocking and unfiltered modes.

respect.note: DNS4EU is backed by the European Union and emphasizes digital sovereignty, EU jurisdiction, privacy and optional filtering rather than advertising.

accessibility.note: DNS4EU provides setup guidance and test pages, but the public service is intended for individual citizens and DNS configuration is still technical.

economical.note: DNS4EU says its public service is completely free for citizens.

products.description: An EU-backed public resolver for individual citizens, with protective, child-safety, ad-blocking and unfiltered encrypted DNS options.

products.name: Brave Search

privacy.note: Brave says its search engine does not profile users or collect personal data for search profiling.

openness.note: Brave Search is powered by Brave's independent web index, though the hosted search service itself is proprietary.

portability.note: Brave Search works as a normal web search engine in any browser and also exposes a commercial API.

respect.note: Brave positions Search around private results and no profiling, with ads separated from behavioral search tracking.

accessibility.note: Brave Search is available on the public web and as the default search engine for many Brave browser users.

economical.note: Brave Search is free to use on the web, with optional paid/API products for heavier or developer use.

products.description: A mainstream private-search option with its own independent web index, useful for people moving away from Google Search without losing everyday ease.

products.name: Mojeek

privacy.note: Mojeek states a strict no-tracking privacy policy and says it does not track users.

openness.note: Mojeek emphasizes its own crawler and independent search index, but the ranking system and hosted service are proprietary.

portability.note: Mojeek can be used directly from the web or added to a browser as a search provider.

respect.note: Mojeek's privacy position is built around data minimisation and non-tracking rather than surveillance advertising.

accessibility.note: Mojeek is simple to try in a browser, though its independent index may feel less complete than dominant search engines.

economical.note: Mojeek's public search page is free to use.

products.description: A UK-based independent search engine with a no-tracking stance and its own crawler/index rather than simply proxying a dominant engine.

products.name: Qwant

privacy.note: Qwant says it does not store search data, does not sell personal data, and is hosted in Europe.

openness.note: Qwant publishes privacy promises and user-facing search access, but the search service is not an open-source/self-hostable engine.

portability.note: Qwant can be used from the web as a browser search engine, but it does not provide user-owned search infrastructure.

respect.note: Qwant frames itself as a search engine that values the user rather than treating them as a product.

accessibility.note: Qwant is a mainstream-feeling search page with instant answers and web search access in a normal browser.

economical.note: Qwant's public search engine is free for ordinary web search use.

products.description: A French search engine emphasizing privacy, European hosting and a familiar search experience.

products.name: MetaGer

privacy.note: MetaGer presents itself as privacy-protected search run by the nonprofit SUMA-EV.

openness.note: MetaGer says its source code is free and open source.

portability.note: MetaGer can be used as a web metasearch engine, but results depend on MetaGer's hosted service and upstream sources.

respect.note: MetaGer is developed by a nonprofit association for free access to knowledge and supports itself through membership/donations.

accessibility.note: MetaGer is available on the public web, though its metasearch and privacy posture may feel less mainstream than default search engines.

economical.note: MetaGer offers public search access and ad-free/member-supported options through SUMA-EV.

products.description: A German nonprofit metasearch engine with open-source code and a privacy-forward operating model.

products.name: Thunderbird

privacy.note: Thunderbird says it does not collect personal data, sell ads in your inbox, or train AI on private conversations.

openness.note: Thunderbird presents itself as open source and part of the Mozilla family.

portability.note: Thunderbird is a cross-platform client for standard email accounts, so users can bring many existing providers rather than being locked to one mailbox.

respect.note: Thunderbird says it is funded by user donations rather than inbox advertising.

accessibility.note: Thunderbird offers desktop downloads and Android work under the Thunderbird family, but setup still requires email-account configuration.

economical.note: Thunderbird is free to download and use.

products.description: A mature open-source email client for people who want email without handing the whole inbox workflow to a webmail platform.

products.name: K-9 Mail

privacy.note: K-9 Mail is described as a privacy-focused Android email client and is now part of the Thunderbird family.

openness.note: K-9 Mail says it is an open-source email client, with Thunderbird Android source available publicly.

portability.note: K-9 Mail works with email providers through standard client workflows, so users can keep their existing mailbox provider.

respect.note: The Thunderbird Android project says it is built on open-source technology and does not treat private data as a product.

accessibility.note: K-9 Mail is available for Android users, but it is Android-specific and still requires email account setup.

economical.note: K-9 Mail is available as a free Android email client.

products.description: An open-source Android email client for bringing privacy-minded email workflows to mobile without switching providers.

products.name: FairEmail

privacy.note: FairEmail describes itself as a fully featured, privacy-oriented email app.

openness.note: FairEmail says it is 100% open source and publishes its Android app source on GitHub.

portability.note: FairEmail works with virtually all email providers and is a client rather than a new mailbox service.

respect.note: FairEmail is positioned as an email client for people who value privacy rather than an advertising-backed webmail platform.

accessibility.note: FairEmail supports many providers and accounts, but its power-user feature set can be less simple than minimalist email apps.

economical.note: FairEmail is available as an Android app with open-source distribution and optional paid/pro features.

products.description: A privacy-oriented Android email client for people who want fine-grained controls and broad provider compatibility.

products.name: Syncthing

privacy.note: Syncthing says your data is your data alone and lets you choose where it is stored and how it is transmitted.

openness.note: Syncthing is an open-source continuous file synchronization program with public source code.

portability.note: Syncthing syncs folders between multiple computers without requiring a single proprietary cloud provider.

respect.note: Syncthing is designed around user-controlled storage and transport rather than third-party cloud lock-in.

accessibility.note: Syncthing is powerful and cross-platform, but pairing devices and managing folders is more technical than using a default cloud drive.

economical.note: Syncthing is free open-source software.

products.description: A free, open-source way to sync files directly between your devices without making a commercial cloud drive the default middleman.

products.name: BigBlueButton

privacy.note: BigBlueButton can be self-hosted for online learning, so privacy depends heavily on the hosting organization and deployment.

openness.note: BigBlueButton describes itself as open-source virtual classroom software.

portability.note: BigBlueButton can be installed, customized, developed, scaled and integrated by organizations with the source code.

respect.note: BigBlueButton is built for education and learning workflows rather than consumer ad-funded video calling.

accessibility.note: BigBlueButton is strong for schools and institutions, but self-hosting or choosing a host is more complex than joining a mainstream meeting app.

economical.note: The software is open source, though real-world use usually requires hosting, administration or a paid host.

products.description: An open-source video/classroom platform especially relevant for schools, public-interest learning programs and self-hosted education infrastructure.

products.name: Nextcloud Talk

privacy.note: Nextcloud says Talk keeps conversations on your own server or a trusted local provider and emphasizes control over data.

openness.note: Nextcloud Talk is open source and has public source under the Nextcloud spreed repository.

portability.note: Talk integrates with Nextcloud Hub, files, chat and conferencing, but is still most portable when a user or organization controls the Nextcloud instance.

respect.note: Nextcloud frames Talk as digital sovereignty without vendor lock-in and dependencies on proprietary vendors.

accessibility.note: Talk is straightforward inside a configured Nextcloud instance, but setup is harder than joining a consumer video-call service.

economical.note: Nextcloud Talk software is open source, though hosting and high-performance deployments can add cost.

products.description: A self-hostable chat and video-conferencing route for people or organizations already thinking about Nextcloud as their private collaboration base.

products.name: Whereby

privacy.note: Whereby says it does not store users' video and audio data for Meetings rooms, with local recording saved locally until download.

openness.note: Whereby publishes security/privacy information, but the meeting platform is a proprietary hosted service.

portability.note: Whereby is browser-based and easy to join, but rooms, hosting and account workflows remain tied to Whereby's service.

respect.note: Whereby's security page emphasizes meeting privacy and not storing audio/video, though it remains a commercial SaaS platform.

accessibility.note: Whereby supports browser-based meetings with a free plan and simple room links, making it easy for non-technical guests.

economical.note: Whereby offers a Free Meetings plan, but group limits and longer use push many users to paid plans.

products.description: A very easy browser-meeting option with better convenience than openness; a useful midpoint between fully self-hosted calls and large default platforms.

products.name: Discourse

privacy.note: Discourse can be self-hosted for community control, while privacy depends on each site's operators and configuration.

openness.note: Discourse says it is a 100% open-source community platform for users who want control over where their site runs.

portability.note: Discourse supports self-hosting and API/webhook access in hosted plans, but communities still need administrators to manage migration and exports.

respect.note: Discourse is oriented around owned community discussion rather than social-media feed manipulation or ad tracking.

accessibility.note: Discourse is mature and widely used, but running a community forum requires moderation and hosting expertise.

economical.note: The software is open source for self-hosters, while official hosted plans are paid.

products.description: A mature open-source forum/community platform for groups that want owned discussion spaces instead of defaulting to commercial social platforms.

products.name: Flarum

privacy.note: Flarum can be self-hosted, so community privacy depends on the site operator rather than a single social platform.

openness.note: Flarum describes itself as free, open-source forum software built by the community.

portability.note: Flarum is deployable forum software with public source code, but moving a live community still requires admin and hosting work.

respect.note: Flarum is community forum infrastructure rather than a centralized engagement-maximizing social feed.

accessibility.note: Flarum is designed to be fast and simple, though self-hosting remains a more technical path than using a hosted social group.

economical.note: Flarum's software is free and open source, with hosting costs depending on deployment.

products.description: A lighter open-source forum path for smaller communities that want an owned discussion space without a heavy platform footprint.

products.name: Mobilizon

privacy.note: Mobilizon is designed to help groups manage communities and events without relying on Facebook groups/events or Meetup-style platforms.

openness.note: Mobilizon documentation says the software is under a Free license and can be hosted by anyone as an instance.

portability.note: Mobilizon instances can federate, allowing people on one instance to register for events created on another.

respect.note: Mobilizon's purpose is to free groups from dominant event/social platforms and support community organization.

accessibility.note: Mobilizon is simple as event software, but choosing an instance or hosting one is less familiar than using Facebook Events.

economical.note: Mobilizon is free/libre software; costs depend on whether a group uses an existing instance or hosts one.

products.description: A federated, free-software path for events and groups that want to organize without relying on Facebook Events or Meetup-style centralized platforms.

products.name: Nostr

privacy.note: Nostr is controlled through user keys and relays, but public social posts and relay metadata mean privacy depends on client/relay choices.

openness.note: Nostr presents itself as a free and open-source protocol for social media and other uses.

portability.note: Nostr avoids a trusted central server and uses cryptographic keys and relays, giving account identity more portability than platform-tied social accounts.

respect.note: Nostr's core pitch is user control rather than platform control, with multiple clients and relays instead of one owner.

accessibility.note: Nostr remains much more technical for ordinary users because they must understand keys, clients and relays.

economical.note: The protocol is open and free to use, though paid relays, identifiers or clients may exist.

products.description: A decentralized social protocol that maximizes portability and user control, but still asks more technical literacy from newcomers than mainstream networks.

products.name: Friendica

privacy.note: Friendica can be run as decentralized social communication software, with privacy depending on the chosen server and administrators.

openness.note: Friendica's source describes it as an open and free social network platform.

portability.note: Friendica links to independent social and corporate services, supporting broader decentralized social communication.

respect.note: Friendica supports the free social web through smaller sites rather than a single centralized platform owner.

accessibility.note: Friendica is powerful but less familiar to new users than Mastodon or mainstream social networks.

economical.note: Friendica is free/open-source software; practical costs depend on the selected instance or hosting.

products.description: A decentralized social-network server for people who want more interoperability and local control than centralized social media usually offers.

products.name: Penpot

privacy.note: Penpot can be self-hosted, giving teams more ownership and deployment control than closed hosted design suites.

openness.note: Penpot describes itself as an open-source design platform for teams.

portability.note: Penpot emphasizes design-code collaboration and self-hosted ownership without vendor lock-in.

respect.note: Penpot's open-source and self-hostable model gives teams a clearer escape route from proprietary design lock-in.

accessibility.note: Penpot offers cloud signup and self-host install, but it is still less familiar to many design teams than Figma or Canva.

economical.note: Penpot pricing lists a $0 professional cloud plan and self-hosting options.

products.description: An open-source, self-hostable design collaboration platform for teams that want Figma-like workflows with less vendor lock-in.

products.name: Figma

privacy.note: Figma's privacy policy says it collects customer content and usage data when people use the service.

openness.note: Figma is a proprietary hosted design platform, though it publishes legal, privacy and data portability documentation.

portability.note: Figma lets users save local copies of files, but permissions and product boundaries can still limit export workflows.

respect.note: Figma offers admin controls for AI content training, but users may need to turn training off or use team settings.

accessibility.note: Figma is a widely adopted browser-based design tool with free viewer/collaboration capabilities.

economical.note: Figma offers free/starter access and education options, with more team and AI capabilities on paid plans.

products.description: The mainstream collaborative design default: very accessible and useful, but proprietary, cloud-centered and weaker on privacy/openness than open design tools.

products.name: Canva

privacy.note: Canva's privacy policy describes collection and use of information when people use the service.

openness.note: Canva is a proprietary hosted design suite rather than open-source/self-hostable software.

portability.note: Canva offers bulk export of personal data, uploads and designs in a portable ZIP format.

respect.note: Canva says privacy settings control whether Canva and technology partners may use data to improve AI services.

accessibility.note: Canva is a highly accessible template-based design tool with broad browser and mobile availability.

economical.note: Canva lists a free plan, with paid plans for Pro, Teams and Enterprise features.

products.description: The mass-market easy design suite: excellent for access and learning-by-making, but a proprietary cloud platform with real privacy and AI-settings tradeoffs.

products.name: Excalidraw

privacy.note: Excalidraw says free-user data is stored locally and shared drawings are protected by end-to-end encryption.

openness.note: Excalidraw describes itself as a free and open-source virtual hand-drawn-style whiteboard.

portability.note: Excalidraw supports export workflows such as PNG, SVG and clipboard output for drawings.

respect.note: Excalidraw's collaboration design uses end-to-end encryption and local-first storage for free users.

accessibility.note: Excalidraw is available as a no-signup web whiteboard for quick diagrams and sketches.

economical.note: The public Excalidraw whiteboard is free, with optional paid Excalidraw+ for hosted team features.

products.description: A fast, friendly open-source whiteboard for diagrams and teaching moments, with unusually good privacy defaults for casual collaboration.

products.name: Miro

privacy.note: Miro's privacy policy describes collection and processing of personal data and customer content through the service.

openness.note: Miro is a proprietary hosted innovation/whiteboard workspace, though it publishes security, privacy and developer documentation.

portability.note: Miro supports exporting boards as image, PDF, SVG or CSV in documented export workflows, with some plan-dependent limitations.

respect.note: Miro publishes security/compliance information, but remains a commercial centralized collaboration platform.

accessibility.note: Miro has a broad, polished collaborative whiteboard workflow and states it strives to meet WCAG 2.2 AA.

economical.note: Miro offers a free plan and paid plans for larger or more advanced collaboration.

products.description: A mainstream collaborative whiteboard with strong usability and team adoption, balanced by proprietary cloud lock-in and weaker privacy/openness signals.

products.name: AppFlowy

privacy.note: AppFlowy is an open-source workspace with local app use and optional cloud or self-hosted deployment choices.

openness.note: AppFlowy publishes its source code publicly and describes itself as an open-source alternative to Notion.

portability.note: AppFlowy documents export workflows, though complex workspace/database structures can still be app-specific.

respect.note: The product is subscription/cloud or self-host funded rather than advertising-funded, with open-source escape routes.

accessibility.note: AppFlowy offers polished desktop/mobile apps, but self-hosting and open-workspace concepts can be less beginner-friendly than Notion.

economical.note: AppFlowy lists a free individual plan plus paid cloud and self-hosted options.

products.description: An open-source Notion-style workspace with local, cloud and self-hosted paths for people who want more control than a closed cloud notebook.

products.name: AFFiNE

privacy.note: AFFiNE describes local-first workspaces with optional sync and self-hosting, which reduces forced cloud dependence.

openness.note: AFFiNE publishes its source code publicly as an open-source all-in-one workspace.

portability.note: AFFiNE documents export options, including Markdown and HTML-oriented workflows.

respect.note: AFFiNE is funded through paid cloud and team plans rather than a surveillance advertising model.

accessibility.note: AFFiNE combines docs, whiteboards and databases, which is powerful but more complex than a simple notes app.

economical.note: AFFiNE lists a free plan and paid Pro/Team tiers for sync, AI and collaboration features.

products.description: A local-first, open-source workspace that blends docs, whiteboards and databases for people escaping closed knowledge tools.

products.name: Outline

privacy.note: Outline supports hosted and self-hosted knowledge bases, allowing organizations to choose their deployment model.

openness.note: Outline publishes its source code publicly for the collaborative knowledge-base app.

portability.note: Outline documents workspace export for moving documents out of the service.

respect.note: Outline is subscription-funded for hosted teams and open-source for self-hosting, rather than ad-funded.

accessibility.note: Outline is designed as a polished team wiki with Slack/Google/Microsoft sign-in flows for workplace adoption.

economical.note: Outline has a paid hosted plan and a self-hosted route that can lower software costs for technical teams.

products.description: A polished open-source team wiki, strongest for organizations that want knowledge-base usability with a self-hosting escape route.

products.name: BookStack

privacy.note: BookStack is self-hosted wiki software, so organizations can run it on infrastructure they control.

openness.note: BookStack describes itself as free and open-source wiki software and publishes its code publicly.

portability.note: BookStack supports exporting content in formats such as PDF, HTML, plain text and Markdown depending on context.

respect.note: BookStack is a self-hosted project without an ad business or forced hosted workspace model.

accessibility.note: BookStack is intentionally simple for documentation, though installation and maintenance require admin capacity.

economical.note: BookStack is free open-source software, with optional paid hosting/support only through third parties.

products.description: A calm, self-hosted documentation wiki for teams that want ownership and simplicity over all-in-one workspace polish.

products.name: OpenProject

privacy.note: OpenProject offers self-hosted and cloud editions, giving teams a data-control choice.

openness.note: OpenProject publishes a free open-source Community edition under the GPL.

portability.note: OpenProject documents backup and restore workflows and project-data administration, but migration still needs admin skill.

respect.note: The business model is open-core subscriptions and services, not advertising or behavioral-data monetization.

accessibility.note: OpenProject is feature-rich for professional project management, but less frictionless than simple kanban tools.

economical.note: The Community edition is free, with paid Enterprise and cloud options for advanced features and support.

products.description: A serious open-source project-management suite for teams that need Jira-like depth without fully closed cloud lock-in.

products.name: Plane

privacy.note: Plane documents self-hosting with Docker Compose, so teams can run the project-management app outside the hosted cloud.

openness.note: Plane publishes its source code publicly as an open-source project-management platform.

portability.note: Plane supports project and issue workflows, but broad portability depends on exports, API use and admin practices.

respect.note: Plane is funded through cloud and paid plan features rather than an advertising model.

accessibility.note: Plane is designed as a modern issue and project tracker, though it still assumes team/project-management literacy.

economical.note: Plane lists a free plan and paid Starter/Business options, with self-hosting available.

products.description: A modern open-source issue and project tracker for teams that want a lighter, self-hostable alternative to Jira-style systems.

products.name: Taiga
